abstract: We describe a model that can recognize two-dimensional shapes in an unsegmented image, independent of their orientation, position, and scale. The model, called TRAFFIC, efficiently represents the structural relation between an object and each of its component features by encoding the fixed viewpoint-invariant transformation from the feature's reference frame to the object's in the weights of a connectionist network. Using a hierarchy of such transformations, with increasing complexity of features at each successive layer, the network can recognize multiple objects in parallel. An implemen(cid:173) tation of TRAFFIC is described, along with experimental results demonstrating the network's ability to recognize constellations of stars in a viewpoint-invariant manner.

paragraphs: TRAFFIC is a model for recognizing two-dimensional shapes in images that have not already been divided into separate objects. Recognition is designed to work regardless of an object's position, orientation, or scale. The approach focuses on the structural relationship between an object and the features that make it up.

Each feature has a reference frame, and the network's weights encode a fixed transformation from that frame to the object's frame. This represents how a component relates to the whole in a way that remains consistent across the stated viewpoint changes. A hierarchy combines these transformations, with successive layers representing increasingly complex features.

The hierarchical construction allows the network to recognize multiple objects in parallel. The paper describes an implementation and experiments recognizing constellations of stars despite changes in viewpoint. These results demonstrate the proposed use of component-to-object transformations in a concrete recognition setting. The central idea is that encoding stable structural relationships can support recognition even when the image coordinates of the object change.
summary.tldr: TRAFFIC recognizes shapes across position, rotation, and scale changes by combining hierarchical transformations between feature and object reference frames.

title: TRAFFIC: Recognizing Objects Using Hierarchical Reference Frame Transformations

abstract: Sex identification in animals has biological importance. Humans are good at making this determination visually, but machines have not matched this ability. A neural network was trained to discriminate sex in human faces, and performed as well as humans on a set of 90 exemplars. Images sampled at 30x30 were compressed using a 900x40x900 fully-connected back-propagation network; activities of hidden units served as input to a back-propagation "SexNet" trained to produce values of 1 for male and o for female faces. The network's average error rate of 8.1% compared favorably to humans, who averaged 11.6%. Some SexNet errors mimicked those of humans.

A neural network was trained to discriminate sex in human faces, and performed as well as humans on a set of 90 exemplars. Images sampled at 30x30 were compressed using a 900x40x900 fully-connected back-propagation network; activities of hidden units served as input to a back-propagation "SexNet" trained to produce values of 1 for male and o for female faces. The network's average error rate of 8.1% compared favorably to humans, who averaged 11.6%. Some SexNet errors mimicked those of humans.

paragraphs: This paper studies a neural network trained to assign human face images to the study's male and female categories. It compares the network's classifications with human judgments on a set of 90 exemplars. The task is framed as testing whether learned visual processing can approach human performance on those image categories.

The system has two stages. First, a fully connected backpropagation network compresses images sampled at 30 by 30 pixels. Its architecture has 900 input units, 40 hidden units, and 900 output units. The activities of the 40 hidden units then become the input to a separate backpropagation classifier, SexNet, trained to output the binary category labels.

The reported average error is 8.1% for SexNet and 11.6% for the human participants. Some network mistakes resemble human mistakes. These results support the stated comparison on the 90 exemplars and show that the compressed representation retained information useful for the classification task. The architectural contribution is the use of learned image compression as an intermediate representation for a second learned classifier.
summary.tldr: A two-stage neural system classified faces into the study's male/female categories with 8.1% average error on 90 exemplars, compared with humans' 11.6%.

title: SEXNET: A Neural Network Identifies Sex From Human Faces

paragraphs: This paper addresses the choice of learning rate in stochastic gradient descent, a framework encompassing LMS, online backpropagation, and adaptive k-means clustering. The learning rate controls the size of updates, so its behavior affects both the search for a useful solution and the eventual process of settling toward one.

The authors describe weaknesses in standard fixed and adaptive schedules. Their earlier search-then-converge schedules achieve the theoretically optimal asymptotic convergence rate and improve the ability to escape poor local minima. Those schedules still require the user to choose a key parameter, leaving an important part of the learning procedure dependent on manual configuration.

The proposed contribution is a methodology for constructing fully automatic adaptive learning rates that retain the optimal convergence rate. Its importance lies in bringing automatic adjustment together with the stated theoretical behavior. The paper targets a remaining tuning requirement in an already promising family of schedules, aiming to preserve their convergence properties while reducing user intervention.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes fully automatic adaptive learning rates that achieve the optimal convergence rate for stochastic gradient search.

title: Towards Faster Stochastic Gradient Search

paragraphs: The paper studies how online gradient descent changes a two-layer neural network over time. The network updates its weights after each independent training example, so the number of examples acts as a clock for the learning process. An analytic solution is used to investigate how the learning rate controls this evolution and its convergence.

The analysis uses a teacher-student setting. A teacher network defines the desired mapping, and a student network learns from examples of that mapping. Their numbers of hidden units may differ. Generalization error measures the disagreement between the student's learned function and the target, connecting weight dynamics to predictive ability.

The discussion is restricted to a soft-committee machine: hidden units have fixed positive output weights of one, and only input-to-hidden weights adapt. The hidden activation is an error function. These choices define the setting in which the analytic account is developed. The paper's contribution is to make the learning trajectory mathematically accessible, providing a way to examine how learning-rate choices influence progress toward the target function.
summary.tldr: An analytic account of online learning examines how the learning rate shapes generalization and convergence in two-layer networks.

title: Dynamics of On-Line Gradient Descent Learning for Multilayer Neural Networks

abstract: Recently researchers have derived formal complexity analysis of analog computation in the setting of discrete-time dynamical systems. As an empirical constrast, training recurrent neural networks (RNNs) produces self -organized systems that are realizations of analog mechanisms. Pre(cid:173) vious work showed that a RNN can learn to process a simple context-free language (CFL) by counting. Herein, we extend that work to show that a RNN can learn a harder CFL, a simple palindrome, by organizing its re(cid:173) sources into a symbol-sensitive counting solution, and we provide a dy(cid:173) namical systems analysis which demonstrates how the network: can not only count, but also copy and store counting infonnation.

As an empirical constrast, training recurrent neural networks (RNNs) produces self -organized systems that are realizations of analog mechanisms. Pre(cid:173) vious work showed that a RNN can learn to process a simple context-free language (CFL) by counting. Herein, we extend that work to show that a RNN can learn a harder CFL, a simple palindrome, by organizing its re(cid:173) sources into a symbol-sensitive counting solution, and we provide a dy(cid:173) namical systems analysis which demonstrates how the network: can not only count, but also copy and store counting infonnation.

paragraphs: The paper examines what computational mechanisms a recurrent neural network can develop through training. Earlier work had shown a network learning a simple context-free language by counting. Here, the authors extend that investigation to a harder language involving a simple palindrome, where the identity of symbols must also matter.

The trained network organizes its resources into a symbol-sensitive counting solution. This means its counting behavior carries information about symbols rather than merely recording a single undifferentiated total. The result connects language processing with an internal analog mechanism that emerges through learning, giving a concrete example alongside formal analyses of analog computation.

The authors also analyze the network as a dynamical system to explain how the solution operates. Their analysis shows that the network can count, copy counting information, and store it. The contribution therefore includes both successful learning of the language and an account of the internal operations that support it. These operations help explain how recurrent dynamics can coordinate information across a sequence.
summary.tldr: A recurrent network learns a simple palindrome language by counting, copying, and storing symbol-dependent information.

title: Recurrent Neural Networks Can Learn to Implement Symbol-Sensitive Counting

abstract: A new paradigm is proposed for sorting spikes in multi-electrode data using ratios of transfer functions between cells and electrodes. It is assumed that for every cell and electrode there is a stable linear relation. These are dictated by the properties of the tissue, the electrodes and their relative geometries. The main advantage of the method is that it is insensitive to variations in the shape and amplitude of a spike. Spike sorting is carried out in two separate steps. First, templates describing the statistics of each spike type are generated by clustering transfer function ratios then spikes are detected in the data using the spike statistics. These techniques were applied to data generated in the escape response system of the cockroach.

paragraphs: This paper proposes identifying neuronal spikes in multi-electrode recordings through relationships between recording channels. It assumes a stable linear relationship between each cell and each electrode, determined by tissue properties, electrode properties, and their relative geometry. These relationships are described by transfer functions, and the method works with ratios of those functions.

The stated advantage is insensitivity to changes in a spike's shape or amplitude. The method bases sorting on the relationships across electrodes, allowing those relationships to identify spike types even when individual waveforms vary. The stability and linearity assumptions are essential because they make the transfer-function relationships a dependable basis for grouping events.

Processing has two stages. First, the algorithm clusters transfer-function ratios to build templates describing the statistics of each spike type. It then detects spikes in the recordings using those statistics. The authors apply the techniques to data from the cockroach escape-response system, demonstrating the proposed workflow on a biological recording application.
summary.tldr: Clustering transfer-function ratios across electrodes sorts neuronal spikes while tolerating waveform and amplitude variation under a stable linear recording model.

title: Multi-Electrode Spike Sorting by Clustering Transfer Functions

abstract: I consider the problem of learning concepts from small numbers of pos(cid:173) itive examples, a feat which humans perform routinely but which com(cid:173) puters are rarely capable of. Bridging machine learning and cognitive science perspectives, I present both theoretical analysis and an empirical study with human subjects for the simple task oflearning concepts corre(cid:173) sponding to axis-aligned rectangles in a multidimensional feature space. Existing learning models, when applied to this task, cannot explain how subjects generalize from only a few examples of the concept. I propose a principled Bayesian model based on the assumption that the examples are a random sample from the concept to be learned. The model gives precise fits to human behavior on this simple task and provides qualitati ve insights into more complex, realistic cases of concept learning.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how people learn a concept from only a few examples that belong to it. It combines theoretical analysis with a human-subject study using concepts represented as axis-aligned rectangles in a multidimensional feature space. This simple setting makes it possible to examine how learners extend a concept beyond the examples they have seen.

The author reports that existing learning models, when applied to this task, cannot explain the subjects' generalization from small samples. The proposed Bayesian model rests on a specific assumption: the examples are sampled randomly from the concept being learned. The sampling process therefore becomes part of the explanation for how examples support different possible concepts.

The model closely fits human behavior on the rectangle task. The paper also uses it to offer qualitative insights into more realistic forms of concept learning. These are different levels of support: precise behavioral fits are reported for the simple task, while the broader cases receive qualitative interpretation. The work connects a probabilistic account of examples to observed human generalization.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian model assuming random positive examples closely explains human generalization in a simple concept-learning task.

title: Bayesian Modeling of Human Concept Learning

paragraphs: An object's appearance may not provide all the information needed to classify it. Other objects appearing alongside it can supply useful context. This paper addresses how to incorporate that information efficiently, focusing on a difficulty with approaches that consider joint assignments of identities: their computational cost can grow exponentially.

The authors propose a general framework that uses partial context at linear computational cost. The central choice is to incorporate a manageable amount of contextual information, making it possible for classification to depend on accompanying objects while avoiding the exponential cost associated with the conventional approaches discussed.

The framework is applied to recognition in microscopic urinalysis images. The authors report a significant improvement in recognition rate over an approach that ignores context, and state that conventional context-incorporation methods could not have delivered this gain in the application. The result shows the practical value of partial context: using some information about accompanying objects can improve recognition while keeping the contextual computation affordable.
summary.tldr: A framework using partial context at linear cost significantly improves microscopic urinalysis recognition over context-free classification.

title: Image Recognition in Context: Application to Microscopic Urinalysis

abstract: We present a new technique for time series analysis based on dy(cid:173) namic probabilistic networks. In this approach, the observed data are modeled in terms of unobserved, mutually independent factors, as in the recently introduced technique of Independent Factor Anal(cid:173) ysis (IFA). However, unlike in IFA, the factors are not Li.d.; each factor has its own temporal statistical characteristics. We derive a family of EM algorithms that learn the structure of the underlying factors and their relation to the data. These algorithms perform source separation and noise reduction in an integrated manner, and demonstrate superior performance compared to IFA.

In this approach, the observed data are modeled in terms of unobserved, mutually independent factors, as in the recently introduced technique of Independent Factor Anal(cid:173) ysis (IFA). However, unlike in IFA, the factors are not Li.d.; each factor has its own temporal statistical characteristics. We derive a family of EM algorithms that learn the structure of the underlying factors and their relation to the data. These algorithms perform source separation and noise reduction in an integrated manner, and demonstrate superior performance compared to IFA.

paragraphs: This paper models an observed time series through hidden factors that are mutually independent. It builds on Independent Factor Analysis, but changes how each factor behaves over time. Instead of treating successive values as independent and identically distributed, the model gives each factor its own temporal statistical structure.

The distinction is between independence across factors and dependence within a factor's history. Separate sources can remain independent of one another while each follows a characteristic pattern through time. Dynamic probabilistic networks provide the representation, and the authors derive a family of expectation-maximization algorithms to learn the factors' structure and their relationship to the observations.

The resulting algorithms combine source separation with noise reduction in one learning procedure. The paper reports superior performance relative to Independent Factor Analysis. This supports the usefulness of incorporating temporal structure when analyzing time series: the method can use patterns across time as well as relationships among observed variables. The reported comparison supports this approach without establishing that every possible time series benefits equally.
summary.tldr: Giving independent hidden factors their own temporal structure enables integrated source separation and noise reduction with reported improvements over IFA.

title: Independent Factor Analysis with Temporally Structured Sources

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether methods for inferring small gene-regulation networks can be adapted to large microarray datasets. Its evidence is preliminary. The approach first groups genes with similar expression trajectories into a minimal set of coexpressed clusters, shifting the modeling task from individual genes to the average behavior of gene groups.

A continuous-time analog recurrent neural network represents the clusters' mean expression trajectories under the different measurement conditions. The regulatory model is fitted using simulated annealing with weight decay. The procedure then examines several fitted models for common features in their connection matrices, making shared structure across fits part of the analysis.

The intended use includes assessing whether gene-expression time-course datasets are adequate for determining regulatory relationships such as coregulation. This connects the inference problem to the information available in the measurements themselves. The contribution is a proposed route from large collections of expression trajectories to candidate relationships among gene classes, supported by preliminary evidence that the adaptation from smaller-scale methods is feasible.
summary.tldr: A preliminary workflow clusters gene-expression trajectories and compares fitted recurrent models to investigate regulation among gene classes.

title: From Coexpression to Coregulation: An Approach to Inferring Transcriptional Regulation among Gene Classes from Large-Scale Expression Data

abstract: We develop a maximum entropy (maxent) approach to generating recom- mendations in the context of a user’s current navigation stream, suitable for environments where data is sparse, high-dimensional, and dynamic— conditions typical of many recommendation applications. We address sparsity and dimensionality reduction by ﬁrst clustering items based on user access patterns so as to attempt to minimize the apriori probabil- ity that recommendations will cross cluster boundaries and then recom- mending only within clusters. We address the inherent dynamic nature of the problem by explicitly modeling the data as a time series; we show how this representational expressivity ﬁts naturally into a maxent frame- work. We conduct experiments on data from ResearchIndex, a popu- lar online repository of over 470,000 computer science documents. We show that our maxent formulation outperforms several competing algo- rithms in ofﬂine tests simulating the recommendation of documents to ResearchIndex users.

paragraphs: The paper develops a recommendation method that uses a person's current sequence of navigation actions. It addresses settings where the item collection is large, observations are sparse, and behavior changes over time. Its maximum entropy formulation provides a framework for representing recommendations in the context of an unfolding browsing session.

The approach separates two challenges. First, it clusters items using patterns of user access, attempting to make recommendations that cross cluster boundaries unlikely in advance. It then recommends only within clusters, reducing the scope of the recommendation problem. Second, it represents the observations explicitly as a time series, allowing the model to account for their sequential organization rather than treating browsing activity as an unordered collection.

The authors evaluate the method using ResearchIndex, a repository containing more than 470,000 computer science documents. In offline tests that simulate recommending documents to users, their formulation outperforms several competing algorithms. The result supports this combination of clustering and temporal modeling for the evaluated recommendation setting; it is evidence from simulated recommendations rather than a reported live deployment.
summary.tldr: A maximum entropy recommender combines item clustering with navigation time series and outperforms several alternatives in offline document-recommendation tests.

title: A Maximum Entropy Approach to Collaborative Filtering in Dynamic, Sparse, High-Dimensional Domains

abstract: Computational mysteries surround the kernels relating the magnitude and sign of changes in efficacy as a function of the time difference between pre- and post-synaptic activity at a synapse. One important idea34 is that kernels result from fil(cid:173) tering, ie an attempt by synapses to eliminate noise corrupting learning. This idea has hitherto been applied to trace learning rules; we apply it to experimentally-defined kernels, using it to reverse-engineer assumed signal statistics. We also extend it to consider the additional goal for filtering of weighting learning according to statistical surprise, as in the Z-score transform. This provides a fresh view of observed kernels and can lead to different, and more natural, signal statistics.

paragraphs: Plasticity kernels describe how the timing difference between activity before and after a synapse relates to the direction and magnitude of changes in synaptic strength. This paper investigates why experimentally observed kernels have their particular forms. It develops the idea that a kernel reflects filtering intended to remove noise that would otherwise corrupt learning.

Earlier applications of this filtering interpretation concerned trace learning rules. Here, the authors apply it to experimentally defined kernels and work backward to infer assumed signal statistics. The kernel becomes evidence about the statistical environment that would make a given filtering rule appropriate, rather than only a description of how synaptic changes depend on timing.

The paper also adds a second filtering goal: weighting learning according to statistical surprise, as in a Z-score transform. This extension can change the signal statistics inferred from a kernel and can make them more natural. The contribution is an interpretive framework linking observed timing-dependent plasticity to assumptions about noise, signal structure, and how unexpected an event is.
summary.tldr: Interpreting plasticity kernels as noise and surprise filters allows researchers to infer the signal statistics that could underlie them.

title: Plasticity Kernels and Temporal Statistics

abstract: We examine the use of hidden Markov and hidden semi-Markov mod- els for automatically segmenting an electrocardiogram waveform into its constituent waveform features. An undecimated wavelet transform is used to generate an overcomplete representation of the signal that is more appropriate for subsequent modelling. We show that the state dura- tions implicit in a standard hidden Markov model are ill-suited to those of real ECG features, and we investigate the use of hidden semi-Markov models for improved state duration modelling.

paragraphs: Automated ECG interval analysis requires separating an electrocardiogram into its constituent waveform features. This paper examines hidden Markov models and hidden semi-Markov models for that segmentation task. The modeling problem includes both identifying the sequence of features and representing how long each feature lasts.

Before modeling, the authors apply an undecimated wavelet transform to the signal. This produces an overcomplete representation that they describe as more appropriate for the subsequent models. The signal representation and the temporal model therefore address complementary parts of the task: expressing the waveform for analysis and describing how its components unfold over time.

The paper shows that the durations implicit in a standard hidden Markov model are poorly suited to real ECG features. It consequently investigates hidden semi-Markov models for improved duration modeling. This identifies a specific mismatch between the standard model and the signal's temporal structure. The contribution is the diagnosis of that mismatch and an examination of a model designed to handle feature duration more appropriately.
summary.tldr: ECG segmentation reveals a mismatch in standard hidden Markov duration assumptions, motivating hidden semi-Markov models.

title: Markov Models for Automated ECG Interval Analysis

abstract: In this paper, we propose a new method, Parametric Embedding (PE), for visualizing the posteriors estimated over a mixture model. PE simultane- ously embeds both objects and their classes in a low-dimensional space. PE takes as input a set of class posterior vectors for given data points, and tries to preserve the posterior structure in an embedding space by minimizing a sum of Kullback-Leibler divergences, under the assump- tion that samples are generated by a Gaussian mixture with equal covari- ances in the embedding space. PE has many potential uses depending on the source of the input data, providing insight into the classiﬁer’s be- havior in supervised, semi-supervised and unsupervised settings. The PE algorithm has a computational advantage over conventional embedding methods based on pairwise object relations since its complexity scales with the product of the number of objects and the number of classes. We demonstrate PE by visualizing supervised categorization of web pages, semi-supervised categorization of digits, and the relations of words and latent topics found by an unsupervised algorithm, Latent Dirichlet Allo- cation.

We demonstrate PE by visualizing supervised categorization of web pages, semi-supervised categorization of digits, and the relations of words and latent topics found by an unsupervised algorithm, Latent Dirichlet Allo- cation.

paragraphs: Parametric Embedding visualizes the probabilities a model assigns to classes by placing both objects and classes in a shared low-dimensional space. Its input is a class-posterior vector for each object. The goal is to preserve these probability relationships so the display reveals how the model associates objects with classes.

The embedding minimizes a sum of Kullback-Leibler divergences under an explicit assumption: samples in the display space follow a Gaussian mixture whose components have equal covariances. Thus, the visualization is fitted to posterior structure through a particular probabilistic model. Its computational cost scales with the number of objects multiplied by the number of classes, offering an advantage over conventional methods based on pairwise object relationships.

The authors demonstrate supervised web-page categorization, semi-supervised digit categorization, and relationships between words and latent topics from Latent Dirichlet Allocation. These examples illustrate how the same visualization method can expose model behavior across different learning settings. The useful information being displayed is the pattern of class probabilities, rather than only similarities between original data points.
summary.tldr: Parametric Embedding jointly visualizes objects and classes by preserving class-probability structure under an equal-covariance Gaussian mixture assumption.

title: Parametric Embedding for Class Visualization

abstract: Theories of access consciousness address how it is that some mental states but not others are available for evaluation, choice behavior, and verbal report. Farah, O’Reilly, and Vecera (1994) argue that quality of representation is critical; Dehaene, Sergent, and Changeux (2003) argue that the ability to communicate representations is critical. We present a probabilistic information transmission or PIT model that suggests both of these conditions are essential for access consciousness. Having successfully modeled data from the repetition priming literature in the past, we use the PIT model to account for data from two experiments on subliminal priming, showing that the model produces priming even in the absence of accessibility and reportability of internal states. The model provides a mechanistic basis for understanding the dissociation of priming and awareness.

paragraphs: This paper examines access consciousness: why some mental states are available for evaluation, choice, and verbal report while others are not. It considers two proposed requirements, the quality of a representation and the ability to communicate it. The authors introduce a probabilistic information transmission model that suggests both requirements are essential.

The model had previously accounted for repetition-priming data. Here, the authors apply it to findings from two subliminal-priming experiments. The important behavior is that prior information can affect subsequent processing even when the relevant internal states are not accessible or reportable.

The model reproduces priming without accessibility and reportability, providing a mechanism for separating the effect of a mental state from conscious access to that state. This allows the two proposed requirements for access to be considered together in a working account of the experimental findings. The contribution is a model-based explanation of how priming and awareness can come apart, with representation quality and communication both playing a role.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic information-transmission model explains subliminal priming while suggesting that conscious access requires both representation quality and communication.

title: Theories of Access Consciousness

abstract: We describe an algorithmic framework for an abstract game which we term a convex repeated game. We show that various online learning and boosting algorithms can be all derived as special cases of our algorithmic framework. This unified view explains the properties of existing algorithms and also enables us to derive several new interesting algorithms. Our algorithmic framework stems from a connection that we build between the notions of regret in game theory and weak duality in convex optimization.

We show that various online learning and boosting algorithms can be all derived as special cases of our algorithmic framework. This unified view explains the properties of existing algorithms and also enables us to derive several new interesting algorithms. Our algorithmic framework stems from a connection that we build between the notions of regret in game theory and weak duality in convex optimization.

paragraphs: This paper develops a common algorithmic framework for an abstract setting called a convex repeated game. Its purpose is to connect methods that otherwise appear as separate algorithms. In particular, the authors show that various online learning and boosting methods can be obtained as special cases of the same framework.

The mathematical connection links regret in game theory with weak duality in convex optimization. Regret provides a way to assess decisions made over repeated rounds, while duality provides relationships between optimization formulations. Bringing these ideas together supplies the foundation from which the paper's family of algorithms is derived.

The resulting unified view serves two roles: it explains properties of existing methods and supports the derivation of several new algorithms. The contribution is therefore a reusable theoretical structure for understanding algorithm design. Its scope is the online learning and boosting algorithms captured by the framework, with the shared derivation helping reveal why their properties belong to a broader pattern.
summary.tldr: A connection between game-theoretic regret and convex duality unifies several online learning and boosting algorithms and yields new ones.

title: Convex Repeated Games and Fenchel Duality

abstract: We introduce a framework for actively learning visual categories from a mixture of weakly and strongly labeled image examples. We propose to allow the category-learner to strategically choose what annotations it receives---based on both the expected reduction in uncertainty as well as the relative costs of obtaining each annotation. We construct a multiple-instance discriminative classifier based on the initial training data. Then all remaining unlabeled and weakly labeled examples are surveyed to actively determine which annotation ought to be requested next. After each request, the current classifier is incrementally updated. Unlike previous work, our approach accounts for the fact that the optimal use of manual annotation may call for a combination of labels at multiple levels of granularity (e.g., a full segmentation on some images and a present/absent flag on others). As a result, it is possible to learn more accurate category models with a lower total expenditure of manual annotation effort.

paragraphs: Training visual category models involves choices about how much annotation to request for each image. A simple presence-or-absence label provides different information and requires different effort from a detailed segmentation. The paper introduces a framework that lets the learner choose among these annotation levels as learning proceeds.

The method starts by building a multiple-instance discriminative classifier from the available training data. It then examines unlabeled and weakly labeled examples to decide which annotation to request next. The decision considers both the expected reduction in uncertainty and the relative cost of obtaining the annotation. Each new response is used to update the classifier incrementally.

The key idea is that the best use of human effort may involve a mixture of coarse and detailed labels across images. Treating annotation level as a choice makes that tradeoff explicit. The authors state that this can produce more accurate category models with less total annotation effort, presenting a possibility enabled by strategic allocation rather than an unconditional outcome.
summary.tldr: An active learner selects both images and annotation detail by balancing expected information gain against human effort.

title: Multi-Level Active Prediction of Useful Image Annotations for Recognition

abstract: Despite the large amount of literature on upper bounds on complexity of convex analysis, surprisingly little is known about the fundamental hardness of these problems. The extensive use of convex optimization in machine learning and statistics makes such an understanding critical to understand fundamental computational limits of learning and estimation. In this paper, we study the complexity of stochastic convex optimization in an oracle model of computation. We improve upon known results and obtain tight minimax complexity estimates for some function classes. We also discuss implications of these results to the understanding the inherent complexity of large-scale learning and estimation problems.
originalAbstract: Despite the large amount of literature on upper bounds on complexity of convex analysis, surprisingly little is known about the fundamental hardness of these problems. The extensive use of convex optimization in machine learning and statistics makes such an understanding critical to understand fundamental computational limits of learning and estimation. In this paper, we study the complexity of stochastic convex optimization in an oracle model of computation. We improve upon known results and obtain tight minimax complexity estimates for some function classes. We also discuss implications of these results to the understanding the inherent complexity of large-scale learning and estimation problems.

paragraphs: An optimization algorithm's performance tells us how efficiently one method can solve a problem. A lower bound asks a different question: how much work must any method require under a specified model of computation? This paper studies that fundamental difficulty for stochastic convex optimization, motivated by its widespread use in learning and statistical estimation.

The analysis uses an oracle model, in which an algorithm obtains information about the optimization problem through queries. Information-theoretic lower bounds constrain what an algorithm can accomplish from the information available through those interactions. This makes the computational model part of the claim: the results describe difficulty within that framework.

The authors improve existing results and obtain tight minimax complexity estimates for some function classes. Tightness means that the lower and achievable complexity estimates align in the relevant sense for those classes. These results help distinguish room for better algorithms from barriers inherent to the problem formulation, with implications for large-scale learning and estimation.
summary.tldr: Information-theoretic analysis establishes improved lower bounds and tight minimax complexity estimates for some stochastic convex optimization classes.

title: Information-theoretic lower bounds on the oracle complexity of convex optimization

abstract: We discuss an online learning framework in which the agent is allowed to say I don't know'' as well as making incorrect predictions on given examples. We analyze the trade off between saying I don't know'' and making mistakes. If the number of don't know predictions is forced to be zero, the model reduces to the well-known mistake-bound model introduced by Littlestone [Lit88]. On the other hand, if no mistakes are allowed, the model reduces to KWIK framework introduced by Li et. al. [LLW08]. We propose a general, though inefficient, algorithm for general finite concept classes that minimizes the number of don't-know predictions if a certain number of mistakes are allowed. We then present specific polynomial-time algorithms for the concept classes of monotone disjunctions and linear separators.

On the other hand, if no mistakes are allowed, the model reduces to KWIK framework introduced by Li et. al. [LLW08]. We propose a general, though inefficient, algorithm for general finite concept classes that minimizes the number of don't-know predictions if a certain number of mistakes are allowed. We then present specific polynomial-time algorithms for the concept classes of monotone disjunctions and linear separators.

paragraphs: This paper studies an online learner that can either make a prediction or say that it does not know. Predictions may be wrong, while expressing uncertainty avoids committing to an answer. The central question is how allowing some mistakes changes the number of times the learner must withhold a prediction.

The framework joins two established extremes. If the learner is never allowed to say it does not know, the setting becomes mistake-bound learning. If it is never allowed to make a mistake, the setting becomes the KWIK framework. Studying the space between these extremes makes the permitted mistake budget an explicit part of the learning problem.

For general finite concept classes, the authors propose an algorithm that minimizes the number of don't-know responses given an allowance for mistakes. That general algorithm is computationally inefficient. They also provide polynomial-time algorithms for monotone disjunctions and linear separators. The contribution therefore includes both a general characterization of the tradeoff and efficient methods for specific classes of prediction rules.
summary.tldr: The paper formalizes the tradeoff between prediction mistakes and abstentions, with a general optimal but inefficient method and efficient algorithms for specific concept classes.

title: Trading off Mistakes and Don't-Know Predictions

abstract: Learning minimum volume sets of an underlying nominal distribution is a very effective approach to anomaly detection. Several approaches to learning minimum volume sets have been proposed in the literature, including the K-point nearest neighbor graph (K-kNNG) algorithm based on the geometric entropy minimization (GEM) principle [4]. The K-kNNG detector, while possessing several desirable characteristics, suffers from high computation complexity, and in [4] a simpler heuristic approximation, the leave-one-out kNNG (L1O-kNNG) was proposed. In this paper, we propose a novel bipartite k-nearest neighbor graph (BP-kNNG) anomaly detection scheme for estimating minimum volume sets. Our bipartite estimator retains all the desirable theoretical properties of the K-kNNG, while being computationally simpler than the K-kNNG and the surrogate L1O-kNNG detectors. We show that BP-kNNG is asymptotically consistent in recovering the p-value of each test point. Experimental results are given that illustrate the superior performance of BP-kNNG as compared to the L1O-kNNG and other state of the art anomaly detection schemes.

Experimental results are given that illustrate the superior performance of BP-kNNG as compared to the L1O-kNNG and other state of the art anomaly detection schemes.

paragraphs: The paper approaches anomaly detection by learning minimum-volume sets for the distribution of nominal, or normal, data. Such sets provide a compact description of normal observations. An existing nearest-neighbor graph method offers desirable theoretical properties, but its computational demands motivate simpler ways to estimate these sets.

The authors propose a bipartite nearest-neighbor graph estimator called BP-kNNG. They state that it preserves the desirable theoretical properties of the earlier K-kNNG method while requiring less computation than both that method and its leave-one-out heuristic approximation. The contribution therefore aims to retain the original statistical foundation while making the graph-based calculation more efficient.

A specific theoretical result establishes asymptotic consistency for recovering each test point's p-value. This is a statement about behavior as the available data grow, rather than exact recovery from every finite dataset. Experiments also illustrate superior performance relative to the leave-one-out approximation and other leading anomaly detectors. Together, these findings connect a simpler graph construction with both statistical justification and favorable empirical detection results.
summary.tldr: A bipartite nearest-neighbor anomaly detector reduces computation while preserving theoretical properties and consistently recovering test-point p-values asymptotically.

title: Efficient anomaly detection using bipartite k-NN graphs

abstract: An important challenge in Markov decision processes is to ensure robustness with respect to unexpected or adversarial system behavior while taking advantage of well-behaving parts of the system. We consider a problem setting where some unknown parts of the state space can have arbitrary transitions while other parts are purely stochastic. We devise an algorithm that is adaptive to potentially adversarial behavior and show that it achieves similar regret bounds as the purely stochastic case.
originalAbstract: An important challenge in Markov decision processes is to ensure robustness with respect to unexpected or adversarial system behavior while taking advantage of well-behaving parts of the system. We consider a problem setting where some unknown parts of the state space can have arbitrary transitions while other parts are purely stochastic. We devise an algorithm that is adaptive to potentially adversarial behavior and show that it achieves similar regret bounds as the purely stochastic case.

paragraphs: A learning agent may operate in an environment that is partly predictable and partly subject to unexpected or adversarial behavior. Treating the entire system as well behaved can miss this difficulty, while the stochastic portions still offer useful structure. This paper studies how reinforcement learning can accommodate both kinds of behavior within one Markov decision process.

The setting divides the state space into parts with arbitrary transitions and parts with purely stochastic transitions. Which parts have arbitrary behavior is unknown. The authors devise an algorithm that adapts to potentially adversarial behavior, addressing uncertainty about the environment's reliability alongside the usual problem of learning how to act.

They prove regret bounds similar to those for the purely stochastic case. Regret measures accumulated performance loss relative to the benchmark used in the analysis, so the result concerns learning performance over time. Its significance is that, in the stated mixed setting, allowing some unknown regions to behave arbitrarily need not eliminate the kind of regret guarantees available in a stochastic environment.
summary.tldr: An adaptive reinforcement-learning algorithm achieves stochastic-like regret bounds when unknown parts of the state space may have arbitrary transitions.

title: Reinforcement Learning in Robust Markov Decision Processes

abstract: This article offers an empirical exploration on the use of character-level convolutional networks (ConvNets) for text classification. We constructed several large-scale datasets to show that character-level convolutional networks could achieve state-of-the-art or competitive results. Comparisons are offered against traditional models such as bag of words, n-grams and their TFIDF variants, and deep learning models such as word-based ConvNets and recurrent neural networks.
originalAbstract: This article offers an empirical exploration on the use of character-level convolutional networks (ConvNets) for text classification. We constructed several large-scale datasets to show that character-level convolutional networks could achieve state-of-the-art or competitive results. Comparisons are offered against traditional models such as bag of words, n-grams and their TFIDF variants, and deep learning models such as word-based ConvNets and recurrent neural networks.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether convolutional neural networks operating at the character level can classify text effectively. The input representation makes individual characters the starting point for learning, rather than beginning with word-level representations. The study is empirical: its central question is how well this approach performs when evaluated against established text classification methods.

The authors construct several large-scale datasets and compare character-level networks with a range of alternatives. These include bag-of-words models, n-gram models, and versions using TFIDF weighting. They also compare with word-based convolutional networks and recurrent neural networks. This range of comparisons places the approach alongside both traditional text representations and other neural modeling choices.

The reported findings show that character-level convolutional networks can achieve competitive or state-of-the-art results. That establishes characters as a viable starting point for strong text classifiers in the studied settings. The claim is about demonstrated performance across the empirical study, rather than a guarantee that character-level models will always outperform word-based or traditional methods.
summary.tldr: Large-scale experiments show that character-level convolutional networks can achieve competitive or state-of-the-art text classification results.

title: Character-level Convolutional Networks for Text Classification

abstract: To predict sensory inputs or control motor trajectories, the brain must constantly learn temporal dynamics based on error feedback. However, it remains unclear how such supervised learning is implemented in biological neural networks. Learning in recurrent spiking networks is notoriously difficult because local changes in connectivity may have an unpredictable effect on the global dynamics. The most commonly used learning rules, such as temporal back-propagation, are not local and thus not biologically plausible. Furthermore, reproducing the Poisson-like statistics of neural responses requires the use of networks with balanced excitation and inhibition. Such balance is easily destroyed during learning. Using a top-down approach, we show how networks of integrate-and-fire neurons can learn arbitrary linear dynamical systems by feeding back their error as a feed-forward input. The network uses two types of recurrent connections: fast and slow. The fast connections learn to balance excitation and inhibition using a voltage-based plasticity rule. The slow connections are trained to minimize the error feedback using a current-based Hebbian learning rule. Importantly, the balance maintained by fast connections is crucial to ensure that global error signals are available locally in each neuron, in turn resulting in a local learning rule for the slow connections. This demonstrates that spiking networks can learn complex dynamics using purely local learning rules, using E/I balance as the key rather than an additional constraint. The resulting network implements a given function within the predictive coding scheme, with minimal dimensions and activity.

paragraphs: Learning temporal dynamics in a recurrent spiking network is difficult because a local connection change can have unpredictable effects throughout the network. Common training rules require nonlocal information, while learning can also disrupt the balance between excitation and inhibition associated with realistic neural response statistics. The paper makes that balance central to a local learning mechanism.

The proposed integrate-and-fire networks learn arbitrary linear dynamical systems by receiving their error as a feed-forward input. They contain fast and slow recurrent connections with different learning roles. Fast connections use a voltage-based plasticity rule to maintain excitatory-inhibitory balance. Slow connections use a current-based Hebbian rule to reduce the error feedback.

The key result is that the balance maintained by fast connections makes global error information locally available to individual neurons. This enables the slow connections to learn through a local rule. The resulting network implements a specified function within a predictive coding scheme with minimal dimensions and activity. The construction demonstrates a mechanism for local supervised learning in spiking networks, rather than establishing that biological brains use it.
summary.tldr: Maintaining excitatory-inhibitory balance enables recurrent spiking networks to learn linear dynamics through locally available error signals.

title: Enforcing balance allows local supervised learning in spiking recurrent networks

abstract: We propose Kernel Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (KMC), a gradient-free adaptive MCMC algorithm based on Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC). On target densities where classical HMC is not an option due to intractable gradients, KMC adaptively learns the target's gradient structure by fitting an exponential family model in a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space. Computational costs are reduced by two novel efficient approximations to this gradient. While being asymptotically exact, KMC mimics HMC in terms of sampling efficiency, and offers substantial mixing improvements over state-of-the-art gradient free samplers. We support our claims with experimental studies on both toy and real-world applications, including Approximate Bayesian Computation and exact-approximate MCMC.

On target densities where classical HMC is not an option due to intractable gradients, KMC adaptively learns the target's gradient structure by fitting an exponential family model in a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space. Computational costs are reduced by two novel efficient approximations to this gradient. While being asymptotically exact, KMC mimics HMC in terms of sampling efficiency, and offers substantial mixing improvements over state-of-the-art gradient free samplers. We support our claims with experimental studies on both toy and real-world applications, including Approximate Bayesian Computation and exact-approximate MCMC.

paragraphs: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo can explore probability distributions efficiently, but it normally needs gradients of the target density. Those gradients can be intractable in some inference problems. This paper proposes Kernel Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, or KMC, to retain useful HMC-like behavior when direct gradient access is unavailable.

KMC adaptively fits an exponential-family model in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space to learn the target’s gradient structure. Two efficient approximations reduce the cost of using this learned structure. The resulting algorithm is gradient-free with respect to the target and is described as asymptotically exact.

Experiments on toy and real-world problems, including Approximate Bayesian Computation and exact-approximate MCMC, report substantial mixing improvements over other gradient-free samplers. The asymptotic claim concerns eventual correctness, while the experiments address sampling efficiency. The abstract does not supply finite-run error guarantees or numerical speedups for particular applications.
summary.tldr: Kernel Hamiltonian Monte Carlo learns gradient structure to sample without target gradients.

title: Gradient-free Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with Efficient Kernel Exponential Families

abstract: The stochastic block model (SBM) has recently gathered significant attention due to new threshold phenomena. However, most developments rely on the knowledge of the model parameters, or at least on the number of communities. This paper introduces efficient algorithms that do not require such knowledge and yet achieve the optimal information-theoretic tradeoffs identified in Abbe-Sandon FOCS15. In the constant degree regime, an algorithm is developed that requires only a lower-bound on the relative sizes of the communities and achieves the optimal accuracy scaling for large degrees. This lower-bound requirement is removed for the regime of arbitrarily slowly diverging degrees, and the model parameters are learned efficiently. For the logarithmic degree regime, this is further enhanced into a fully agnostic algorithm that achieves the CH-limit for exact recovery in quasi-linear time. These provide the first algorithms affording efficiency, universality and information-theoretic optimality for strong and weak consistency in the SBM.
originalAbstract: The stochastic block model (SBM) has recently gathered significant attention due to new threshold phenomena. However, most developments rely on the knowledge of the model parameters, or at least on the number of communities. This paper introduces efficient algorithms that do not require such knowledge and yet achieve the optimal information-theoretic tradeoffs identified in Abbe-Sandon FOCS15. In the constant degree regime, an algorithm is developed that requires only a lower-bound on the relative sizes of the communities and achieves the optimal accuracy scaling for large degrees. This lower-bound requirement is removed for the regime of arbitrarily slowly diverging degrees, and the model parameters are learned efficiently. For the logarithmic degree regime, this is further enhanced into a fully agnostic algorithm that achieves the CH-limit for exact recovery in quasi-linear time. These provide the first algorithms affording efficiency, universality and information-theoretic optimality for strong and weak consistency in the SBM.

paragraphs: Community recovery in the stochastic block model often assumes knowledge of model parameters or the number of communities. This paper develops efficient algorithms that dispense with that information while achieving optimal information-theoretic tradeoffs. Its guarantees differ according to how graph degrees scale.

In the constant-degree regime, the algorithm still needs a lower bound on relative community sizes and achieves optimal accuracy scaling for large degrees. When degrees diverge arbitrarily slowly, the community-size requirement can be removed and the model parameters learned efficiently. These distinctions specify what prior information is needed in each setting.

For logarithmic degrees, the authors obtain a fully agnostic algorithm that reaches the CH-limit for exact recovery in quasi-linear time. The results combine computational efficiency with optimal recovery guarantees across the stated regimes. Their significance is that unknown parameters need not prevent optimal community recovery, while the precise recovery objective and assumptions remain tied to graph density.
summary.tldr: Efficient community-recovery algorithms attain optimal SBM tradeoffs without known parameters, with assumptions and guarantees depending on graph degree.

title: Recovering Communities in the General Stochastic Block Model Without Knowing the Parameters

abstract: Existing deep embedding methods in vision tasks are capable of learning a compact Euclidean space from images, where Euclidean distances correspond to a similarity metric. To make learning more effective and efficient, hard sample mining is usually employed, with samples identified through computing the Euclidean feature distance. However, the global Euclidean distance cannot faithfully characterize the true feature similarity in a complex visual feature space, where the intraclass distance in a high-density region may be larger than the interclass distance in low-density regions. In this paper, we introduce a Position-Dependent Deep Metric (PDDM) unit, which is capable of learning a similarity metric adaptive to local feature structure. The metric can be used to select genuinely hard samples in a local neighborhood to guide the deep embedding learning in an online and robust manner. The new layer is appealing in that it is pluggable to any convolutional networks and is trained end-to-end. Our local similarity-aware feature embedding not only demonstrates faster convergence and boosted performance on two complex image retrieval datasets, its large margin nature also leads to superior generalization results under the large and open set scenarios of transfer learning and zero-shot learning on ImageNet 2010 and ImageNet-10K datasets.

paragraphs: Deep image embeddings represent images as points whose distances express similarity. Training often emphasizes difficult examples selected using Euclidean distance. This paper argues that a single global distance can be misleading in a complex feature space: same-class examples in a dense region may be farther apart than different-class examples in a sparse region.

The proposed Position-Dependent Deep Metric unit learns a similarity measure that adapts to local feature structure. It uses this measure to identify difficult examples within local neighborhoods and guide embedding learning online. The unit can be inserted into convolutional networks and trained end to end, connecting local similarity estimation directly to representation learning.

The authors report faster convergence and improved performance on two challenging image retrieval datasets. They also report stronger generalization in large and open-set transfer-learning and zero-shot settings on ImageNet 2010 and ImageNet-10K, linking this behavior to the method’s large-margin nature. The findings support taking local feature structure into account when deciding which training examples are difficult.
summary.tldr: A learned, position-dependent similarity metric improves hard-example selection, convergence, and generalization in the reported image embedding experiments.

title: Local Similarity-Aware Deep Feature Embedding

abstract: Conditional probabilities are a core concept in machine learning. For example, optimal prediction of a label $Y$ given an input $X$ corresponds to maximizing the conditional probability of $Y$ given $X$. A common approach to inference tasks is learning a model of conditional probabilities. However, these models are often based on strong assumptions (e.g., log-linear models), and hence their estimate of conditional probabilities is not robust and is highly dependent on the validity of their assumptions. Here we propose a framework for reasoning about conditional probabilities without assuming anything about the underlying distributions, except knowledge of their second order marginals, which can be estimated from data. We show how this setting leads to guaranteed bounds on conditional probabilities, which can be calculated efficiently in a variety of settings, including structured-prediction. Finally, we apply them to semi-supervised deep learning, obtaining results competitive with variational autoencoders.

paragraphs: Predicting a label from an input often relies on estimating its conditional probability. Conventional models can make strong assumptions about the distribution producing the data, making their answers sensitive to whether those assumptions hold. This paper develops a way to reason about conditional probabilities while imposing much less structure on that distribution.

The framework assumes knowledge only of second-order marginals, which can be estimated from data. It uses this information to derive guaranteed bounds on conditional probabilities, rather than committing to a fully specified underlying distribution. The bounds express what the available marginal information supports while leaving other aspects of the distribution unspecified.

The authors show that these bounds can be computed efficiently in several settings, including structured prediction. They also apply the framework to semi-supervised deep learning and report results competitive with variational autoencoders. The contribution connects robustness to a concrete form of available information: the guarantees rely on the stated marginal knowledge, while the experiments demonstrate that this approach can also support useful learning performance.
summary.tldr: The framework derives guaranteed conditional-probability bounds from second-order marginals without specifying a full underlying distribution.

title: Robust Conditional Probabilities

abstract: We study implicit regularization when optimizing an underdetermined quadratic objective over a matrix $X$ with gradient descent on a factorization of X. We conjecture and provide empirical and theoretical evidence that with small enough step sizes and initialization close enough to the origin, gradient descent on a full dimensional factorization converges to the minimum nuclear norm solution.
originalAbstract: We study implicit regularization when optimizing an underdetermined quadratic objective over a matrix $X$ with gradient descent on a factorization of X. We conjecture and provide empirical and theoretical evidence that with small enough step sizes and initialization close enough to the origin, gradient descent on a full dimensional factorization converges to the minimum nuclear norm solution.

paragraphs: An underdetermined optimization problem leaves room for multiple solutions, making the solution selected by the learning procedure an important question. This paper studies that choice for a quadratic objective over a matrix. The matrix is represented through a factorization, and gradient descent operates on the factors.

The central conjecture is that this procedure converges to the minimum nuclear-norm solution when the step sizes are sufficiently small and initialization is sufficiently close to the origin. Nuclear norm measures the sum of a matrix's singular values. The factorization is full-dimensional, so the proposed preference concerns the behavior of optimization within that parameterization.

The authors provide both empirical and theoretical evidence for the conjecture. Its significance is a possible implicit regularization effect: the way a matrix is parameterized and optimized can favor a particular solution without explicitly adding that preference to the objective. The claim remains a conjecture supported by evidence, with small steps and near-origin initialization central to its stated form.
summary.tldr: The paper supports a conjecture that small-step gradient descent on matrix factors, initialized near zero, selects a minimum nuclear-norm solution.

title: Implicit Regularization in Matrix Factorization

abstract: In this paper we study the well-known greedy coordinate descent (GCD) algorithm to solve $\ell_1$-regularized problems and improve GCD by the two popular strategies: Nesterov's acceleration and stochastic optimization. Firstly, we propose a new rule for greedy selection based on an $\ell_1$-norm square approximation which is nontrivial to solve but convex; then an efficient algorithm called ``SOft ThreshOlding PrOjection (SOTOPO)'' is proposed to exactly solve the $\ell_1$-regularized $\ell_1$-norm square approximation problem, which is induced by the new rule. Based on the new rule and the SOTOPO algorithm, the Nesterov's acceleration and stochastic optimization strategies are then successfully applied to the GCD algorithm. The resulted algorithm called accelerated stochastic greedy coordinate descent (ASGCD) has the optimal convergence rate $O(\sqrt{1/\epsilon})$; meanwhile, it reduces the iteration complexity of greedy selection up to a factor of sample size. Both theoretically and empirically, we show that ASGCD has better performance for high-dimensional and dense problems with sparse solution.

paragraphs: The paper studies greedy coordinate descent for optimization problems with l1 regularization, a setting associated with sparse solutions. Greedy coordinate descent selects coordinates to update according to their apparent usefulness. The authors seek to improve this approach by combining it with Nesterov acceleration and stochastic optimization.

The key step is a new greedy selection rule based on an approximation involving the squared l1 norm. Solving the resulting regularized approximation is nontrivial, although the problem is convex. The authors introduce SOTOPO, an efficient soft-thresholding projection algorithm that solves this subproblem exactly. That solver makes the new selection rule usable within an accelerated stochastic method.

The resulting algorithm, ASGCD, achieves the stated optimal convergence rate of O(sqrt(1/epsilon)). It also reduces the iteration complexity of greedy selection by up to a factor equal to the sample size. Theoretical analysis and experiments indicate better performance for high-dimensional, dense problems whose solutions are sparse. This identifies the particular combination of problem structure and solution structure where the approach is especially useful.
summary.tldr: ASGCD combines a new greedy selection rule with acceleration and stochastic optimization to efficiently solve l1-regularized problems.

title: Accelerated Stochastic Greedy Coordinate Descent by Soft Thresholding Projection onto Simplex

abstract: In many machine learning applications, there are multiple decision-makers involved, both automated and human. The interaction between these agents often goes unaddressed in algorithmic development. In this work, we explore a simple version of this interaction with a two-stage framework containing an automated model and an external decision-maker. The model can choose to say PASS, and pass the decision downstream, as explored in rejection learning. We extend this concept by proposing "learning to defer", which generalizes rejection learning by considering the effect of other agents in the decision-making process. We propose a learning algorithm which accounts for potential biases held by external decision-makers in a system. Experiments demonstrate that learning to defer can make systems not only more accurate but also less biased. Even when working with inconsistent or biased users, we show that deferring models still greatly improve the accuracy and/or fairness of the entire system.
originalAbstract: In many machine learning applications, there are multiple decision-makers involved, both automated and human. The model can choose to say PASS, and pass the decision downstream, as explored in rejection learning. We extend this concept by proposing "learning to defer", which generalizes rejection learning by considering the effect of other agents in the decision-making process. We propose a learning algorithm which accounts for potential biases held by external decision-makers in a system. Experiments demonstrate that learning to defer can make systems not only more accurate but also less biased. Even when working with inconsistent or biased users, we show that deferring models still greatly improve the accuracy and/or fairness of the entire system.

paragraphs: Many prediction systems involve both an automated model and another decision-maker. This paper studies a two-stage system in which the model can make a decision or pass it downstream. The central issue is how to choose between those actions when the external decision-maker may have biases or behave inconsistently.

The authors extend rejection learning into learning to defer by accounting for the effects of the other agent. Their algorithm considers potential biases in the external decision-maker as part of learning. This shifts attention toward the performance of the combined decision process: passing a case changes who handles it, so the consequences depend on that person's behavior.

Experiments show that learning to defer can improve accuracy and reduce bias at the system level. Improvements in accuracy, fairness, or both are reported even with inconsistent or biased users. These findings support learning how the two stages should interact, while retaining the qualification that the reported gains need not improve both criteria simultaneously in every setting.
summary.tldr: Learning when to defer decisions, while accounting for downstream decision-makers, can improve system accuracy and fairness.

title: Predict Responsibly: Improving Fairness and Accuracy by Learning to Defer

abstract: Multiple modalities often co-occur when describing natural phenomena. Learning a joint representation of these modalities should yield deeper and more useful representations.Previous generative approaches to multi-modal input either do not learn a joint distribution or require additional computation to handle missing data. Here, we introduce a multimodal variational autoencoder (MVAE) that uses a product-of-experts inference network and a sub-sampled training paradigm to solve the multi-modal inference problem. Notably, our model shares parameters to efficiently learn under any combination of missing modalities. We apply the MVAE on four datasets and match state-of-the-art performance using many fewer parameters. In addition, we show that the MVAE is directly applicable to weakly-supervised learning, and is robust to incomplete supervision. We then consider two case studies, one of learning image transformations---edge detection, colorization, segmentation---as a set of modalities, followed by one of machine translation between two languages. We find appealing results across this range of tasks.

paragraphs: Different kinds of observations often describe the same underlying phenomenon, making a joint representation useful. Learning that representation becomes harder when some observations are missing. This paper introduces a multimodal variational autoencoder that learns across modalities while sharing parameters for every combination of available and missing inputs.

The model combines a product-of-experts inference network with a subsampled training scheme. These components address multimodal inference without requiring a separate collection of parameters for each missing-data pattern. The authors also show that the approach applies directly to weak supervision and remains robust when supervision is incomplete.

Across four datasets, the model matches state-of-the-art performance with many fewer parameters. Additional case studies treat edge detection, colorization, and segmentation as related modalities, and examine translation between two languages. The reported results support the same modeling framework across this range of tasks, with parameter sharing making joint learning practical even when examples do not provide every modality.
summary.tldr: A parameter-sharing multimodal variational autoencoder learns joint representations efficiently despite missing modalities and incomplete supervision.

title: Multimodal Generative Models for Scalable Weakly-Supervised Learning

abstract: We decompose the evidence lower bound to show the existence of a term measuring the total correlation between latent variables. We use this to motivate the beta-TCVAE (Total Correlation Variational Autoencoder) algorithm, a refinement and plug-in replacement of the beta-VAE for learning disentangled representations, requiring no additional hyperparameters during training. We further propose a principled classifier-free measure of disentanglement called the mutual information gap (MIG). We perform extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments, in both restricted and non-restricted settings, and show a strong relation between total correlation and disentanglement, when the model is trained using our framework.
originalAbstract: We decompose the evidence lower bound to show the existence of a term measuring the total correlation between latent variables. We use this to motivate the beta-TCVAE (Total Correlation Variational Autoencoder) algorithm, a refinement and plug-in replacement of the beta-VAE for learning disentangled representations, requiring no additional hyperparameters during training. We further propose a principled classifier-free measure of disentanglement called the mutual information gap (MIG).
