Machine-learning models can help predict peptide properties and improve identification, but comparing methods requires common data and evaluation conventions. This paper introduces PROSPECT as a labeled reference dataset spanning multiple proteomics tasks.

The work focuses on peptide retention-time prediction and tandem mass-spectrum prediction. Alongside the data, the authors review existing approaches and task formulations from a machine-learning perspective and recommend evaluation metrics and visualizations.

The intended benefit is more reproducible comparison and better assessment of generalization, while making the area accessible to machine-learning researchers. The abstract does not provide the dataset’s sample count or a new model’s numerical performance. Its contribution is primarily an evaluation resource and methodological guidance, rather than a claim that a particular predictor has already solved peptide characterization or demonstrated clinical utility.
summary.tldr: PROSPECT supplies labeled proteomics data and evaluation guidance for peptide-prediction tasks.

title: PROSPECT: Labeled Tandem Mass Spectrometry Dataset for Machine Learning in Proteomics

abstract: Multi-kernel learning (MKL) exhibits well-documented performance in online non-linear function approximation. Federated learning enables a group of learners (called clients) to train an MKL model on the data distributed among clients to perform online non-linear function approximation. There are some challenges in online federated MKL that need to be addressed: i) Communication efficiency especially when a large number of kernels are considered ii) Heterogeneous data distribution among clients. The present paper develops an algorithmic framework to enable clients to communicate with the server to send their updates with affordable communication cost while clients employ a large dictionary of kernels. Utilizing random feature (RF) approximation, the present paper proposes scalable online federated MKL algorithm. We prove that using the proposed online federated MKL algorithm, each client enjoys sub-linear regret with respect to the RF approximation of its best kernel in hindsight, which indicates that the proposed algorithm can effectively deal with heterogeneity of the data distributed among clients. Experimental results on real datasets showcase the advantages of the proposed algorithm compared with other online federated kernel learning ones.

paragraphs: This paper studies online nonlinear prediction when data is spread across collaborating clients. Each client can draw on a dictionary of kernels, offering multiple ways to model the data. Two challenges arise together: communicating updates becomes costly with many kernels, and different clients may have substantially different data distributions.

The proposed framework uses random-feature approximations to make online federated multi-kernel learning scalable. It enables clients to send updates to a server at an affordable communication cost while retaining a large kernel dictionary. This addresses the tension between giving each client flexible modeling choices and keeping distributed training practical.

The theoretical guarantee is personalized: each client has sublinear regret relative to the random-feature approximation of its own best kernel chosen in hindsight. Consequently, the average regret against that particular comparison target diminishes over time. The reference is the approximated kernel, and it can differ across clients. Experiments on real datasets report advantages over other online federated kernel-learning methods, supporting the framework's usefulness for heterogeneous distributed data.
summary.tldr: Random-feature approximations enable communication-efficient federated multi-kernel learning with a separate sublinear-regret guarantee for each client.

title: Personalized Online Federated Learning with Multiple Kernels

abstract: We study generalization properties of random features (RF) regression in high dimensions optimized by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) in under-/over-parameterized regime. In this work, we derive precise non-asymptotic error bounds of RF regression under both constant and polynomial-decay step-size SGD setting, and observe the double descent phenomenon both theoretically and empirically. Our analysis shows how to cope with multiple randomness sources of initialization, label noise, and data sampling (as well as stochastic gradients) with no closed-form solution, and also goes beyond the commonly-used Gaussian/spherical data assumption. Our theoretical results demonstrate that, with SGD training, RF regression still generalizes well for interpolation learning, and is able to characterize the double descent behavior by the unimodality of variance and monotonic decrease of bias. Besides, we also prove that the constant step-size SGD setting incurs no loss in convergence rate when compared to the exact minimum-norm interpolator, as a theoretical justification of using SGD in practice.

paragraphs: The paper studies how high-dimensional random-features regression generalizes when trained with stochastic gradient descent. It covers both underparameterized and overparameterized regimes and examines double descent, in which prediction error can improve, worsen, and improve again as model size changes. The aim is to explain this behavior for an iterative training procedure.

The authors derive precise non-asymptotic error bounds for both constant learning rates and polynomially decreasing learning rates. Their analysis handles randomness from initialization, noisy labels, sampled data, and stochastic gradients without relying on a closed-form trained solution. It also extends beyond the commonly used assumptions of Gaussian or spherical data.

The theory and experiments both exhibit double descent. The analysis characterizes it through variance that rises and falls around a single peak together with steadily decreasing bias, and shows good generalization can persist when training interpolates the data. The authors also prove that constant-step-size SGD loses no convergence rate relative to the exact minimum-norm interpolator in their setting, providing theoretical support for this practical optimization choice.
summary.tldr: The paper explains double descent in random-features regression trained with SGD through finite-sample bounds and a bias–variance analysis.

title: On the Double Descent of Random Features Models Trained with SGD

abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success in a variety of computer vision tasks, where massive labeled images are routinely required for model optimization. Yet, the data collected from the open world are unavoidably polluted by noise, which may significantly undermine the efficacy of the learned models. Various attempts have been made to reliably train DNNs under data noise, but they separately account for either the noise existing in the labels or that existing in the images. A naive combination of the two lines of works would suffer from the limitations in both sides, and miss the opportunities to handle the two kinds of noise in parallel. This works provides a first, unified framework for reliable learning under the joint (image, label)-noise. Technically, we develop a confidence-based sample filter to progressively filter out noisy data without the need of pre-specifying noise ratio. Then, we penalize the model uncertainty of the detected noisy data instead of letting the model continue over-fitting the misleading information in them. Experimental results on various challenging synthetic and real-world noisy datasets verify that the proposed method can outperform competing baselines in the aspect of classification performance.

paragraphs: Training images collected from the open world can contain two kinds of noise: corruption in the images themselves and mistakes in their labels. The paper argues that addressing these separately misses opportunities to handle their joint effects. It introduces a unified framework for training image classifiers when both forms of noise are present.

The method first uses a confidence-based filter to progressively identify noisy samples. It does not require the practitioner to specify the proportion of noisy data in advance. For samples detected as noisy, the training procedure penalizes model uncertainty, aiming to prevent continued overfitting to their misleading information.

This creates a coordinated approach to selecting and treating problematic training examples, rather than simply combining separate image-noise and label-noise methods. Experiments cover challenging synthetic and real-world noisy datasets. The reported results show that the framework can outperform competing baselines in classification performance. These findings support the usefulness of handling the two noise sources together and adapting sample filtering as training proceeds, without requiring a preset noise ratio.
summary.tldr: A unified training framework uses progressive confidence filtering and uncertainty penalties to improve classification with jointly noisy images and labels.

title: Confidence-based Reliable Learning under Dual Noises

abstract: We address a practical yet challenging problem of training robot agents to navigate in an environment following a path described by some language instructions. The instructions often contain descriptions of objects in the environment. To achieve accurate and efficient navigation, it is critical to build a map that accurately represents both spatial location and the semantic information of the environment objects. However, enabling a robot to build a map that well represents the environment is extremely challenging as the environment often involves diverse objects with various attributes. In this paper, we propose a multi-granularity map, which contains both object fine-grained details (\eg, color, texture) and semantic classes, to represent objects more comprehensively. Moreover, we propose a weakly-supervised auxiliary task, which requires the agent to localize instruction-relevant objects on the map. Through this task, the agent not only learns to localize the instruction-relevant objects for navigation but also is encouraged to learn a better map representation that reveals object information. We then feed the learned map and instruction to a waypoint predictor to determine the next navigation goal. Experimental results show our method outperforms the state-of-the-art by 4.0% and 4.6% w.r.t. success rate both in seen and unseen environments, respectively on VLN-CE dataset. The code is available at https://github.com/PeihaoChen/WS-MGMap.

paragraphs: A navigation instruction may identify a destination through both an object category and details such as color or texture. title: Weakly-Supervised Multi-Granularity Map Learning for Vision-and-Language Navigation

abstract: We present DreamWaltz, a novel framework for generating and animating complex 3D avatars given text guidance and parametric human body prior. While recent methods have shown encouraging results for text-to-3D generation of common objects, creating high-quality and animatable 3D avatars remains challenging. To create high-quality 3D avatars, DreamWaltz proposes 3D-consistent occlusion-aware Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) to optimize implicit neural representations with canonical poses. It provides view-aligned supervision via 3D-aware skeleton conditioning which enables complex avatar generation without artifacts and multiple faces. For animation, our method learns an animatable 3D avatar representation from abundant image priors of diffusion model conditioned on various poses, which could animate complex non-rigged avatars given arbitrary poses without retraining. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that DreamWaltz is an effective and robust approach for creating 3D avatars that can take on complex shapes and appearances as well as novel poses for animation. The proposed framework further enables the creation of complex scenes with diverse compositions, including avatar-avatar, avatar-object and avatar-scene interactions. See https://dreamwaltz3d.github.io/ for more vivid 3D avatar and animation results.

paragraphs: DreamWaltz tackles the combined challenge of generating a detailed three-dimensional avatar and making it move. Its inputs include text guidance and a parametric human-body prior. This body information gives the generation process a structural starting point, while the text specifies the avatar that the system should create.

For generation, the framework introduces an occlusion-aware, three-dimensionally consistent form of Score Distillation Sampling. It optimizes an implicit neural representation in a canonical pose and uses skeleton conditioning to align supervision with the current view. The authors present this alignment as a way to generate complex avatars while avoiding artifacts such as multiple faces.

For animation, DreamWaltz learns from diffusion-model image priors conditioned on different poses. The resulting representation can animate complex avatars without rigging or retraining for each requested pose. Evaluations support its effectiveness across varied shapes, appearances, and novel poses. The framework also supports more elaborate compositions involving interactions between avatars, objects, and scenes, extending its use beyond generating isolated characters.
summary.tldr: DreamWaltz combines text, body structure, and pose-conditioned diffusion guidance to create complex 3D avatars that can be animated without retraining.

title: DreamWaltz: Make a Scene with Complex 3D Animatable Avatars

abstract: Adapter-style efficient transfer learning (ETL) has shown excellent performance in the tuning of vision-language models (VLMs) under the low-data regime, where only a few additional parameters are introduced to excavate the task-specific knowledge based on the general and powerful representation of VLMs. However, most adapter-style works face two limitations: (i) modeling task-specific knowledge with a single modality only; and (ii) overlooking the exploitation of the inter-class relationships in downstream tasks, thereby leading to sub-optimal solutions. To mitigate that, we propose an effective adapter-style tuning strategy, dubbed GraphAdapter, which performs the textual adapter by explicitly modeling the dual-modality structure knowledge (i.e., the correlation of different semantics/classes in textual and visual modalities) with a dual knowledge graph. In particular, the dual knowledge graph is established with two sub-graphs, i.e., a textual knowledge sub-graph, and a visual knowledge sub-graph, where the nodes and edges represent the semantics/classes and their correlations in two modalities, respectively. This enables the textual feature of each prompt to leverage the task-specific structure knowledge from both textual and visual modalities, yielding a more effective classifier for downstream tasks. Extensive experimental results on 11 benchmark datasets reveal that our GraphAdapter significantly outperforms the previous adapter-based methods.

paragraphs: Adapter methods tune a vision-language model for a new task by adding relatively few parameters, which is useful when task-specific data are scarce. The paper identifies two shortcomings in many existing adapters: using only one modality to model task knowledge and overlooking relationships among the task’s classes. GraphAdapter addresses both through an explicit graph representation.

The method builds two connected sources of structural knowledge: a textual knowledge subgraph and a visual knowledge subgraph. In each, nodes represent classes or semantics, while edges represent correlations between them. A textual adapter uses this dual structure so that each prompt’s text features can incorporate class relationships from both language and images.

The resulting features form a more effective classifier for downstream tasks in the authors’ experiments. Across 11 benchmark datasets, GraphAdapter significantly outperforms the compared adapter-based approaches. The finding supports incorporating relationships between classes into efficient adaptation, with visual information contributing directly to the refinement of textual features rather than leaving the adapter’s task knowledge confined to one modality.
summary.tldr: GraphAdapter improves efficient vision-language adaptation by using both visual and textual class relationships to refine prompt features.

title: GraphAdapter: Tuning Vision-Language Models With Dual Knowledge Graph

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a promising distributed learning paradigm that enables multiple clients to learn a global model collaboratively without sharing their private data. However, the effectiveness of FL is highly dependent on the quality of the data that is being used for training. In particular, data heterogeneity issues, such as label distribution skew and feature skew, can significantly impact the performance of FL. Previous studies in FL have primarily focused on addressing label distribution skew data heterogeneity, while only a few recent works have made initial progress in tackling feature skew issues. Notably, these two forms of data heterogeneity have been studied separately and have not been well explored within a unified FL framework. To address this gap, we propose Fed-CO$_2$, a universal FL framework that handles both label distribution skew and feature skew within a Cooperation mechanism between the Online and Offline models. Specifically, the online model learns general knowledge that is shared among all clients, while the offline model is trained locally to learn the specialized knowledge of each individual client. To further enhance model cooperation in the presence of feature shifts, we design an intra-client knowledge transfer mechanism that reinforces mutual learning between the online and offline models, and an inter-client knowledge transfer mechanism to increase the models’ domain generalization ability. Extensive experiments show that our Fed-CO$_2$ outperforms a wide range of existing personalized federated learning algorithms in terms of handling label distribution skew and feature skew, both individually and collectively. The empirical results are supported by our convergence analyses in a simplified setting.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets clients train collaboratively without sharing their private training data, but their datasets can differ substantially. Clients may have different label frequencies, different input features, or both. Fed-CO2 addresses these two forms of heterogeneity within one framework, where earlier work often considered them separately.

Each client uses cooperating online and offline models. The online model learns general knowledge shared across clients, while the locally trained offline model learns knowledge specific to that client. An intra-client transfer mechanism supports mutual learning between the models, and an inter-client mechanism aims to improve generalization across feature domains.

Experiments show that Fed-CO2 outperforms a broad range of personalized federated learning methods when label skew and feature skew occur separately or together. Convergence analyses in a simplified setting support the empirical results. The approach matters because it gives shared and local knowledge explicit roles, then connects them through cooperation to address variation in both what clients observe and which labels they possess.
summary.tldr: Fed-CO2 combines shared and local models to improve federated learning under both label and feature distribution differences.

title: Fed-CO$_{2}$: Cooperation of Online and Offline Models for Severe Data Heterogeneity in Federated Learning

abstract: Recently, model-based reinforcement learning algorithms have demonstrated remarkable efficacy in visual input environments. These approaches begin by constructing a parameterized simulation world model of the real environment through self-supervised learning. By leveraging the imagination of the world model, the agent's policy is enhanced without the constraints of sampling from the real environment. The performance of these algorithms heavily relies on the sequence modeling and generation capabilities of the world model. However, constructing a perfectly accurate model of a complex unknown environment is nearly impossible. Discrepancies between the model and reality may cause the agent to pursue virtual goals, resulting in subpar performance in the real environment. Introducing random noise into model-based reinforcement learning has been proven beneficial.In this work, we introduce Stochastic Transformer-based wORld Model (STORM), an efficient world model architecture that combines the strong sequence modeling and generation capabilities of Transformers with the stochastic nature of variational autoencoders. STORM achieves a mean human performance of $126.7\%$ on the Atari $100$k benchmark, setting a new record among state-of-the-art methods that do not employ lookahead search techniques. Moreover, training an agent with $1.85$ hours of real-time interaction experience on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 graphics card requires only $4.3$ hours, showcasing improved efficiency compared to previous methodologies.

The paper motivates stochastic modeling as a useful ingredient when the learned environment cannot be perfectly accurate.

These results support both the agent's benchmark performance and the computational efficiency of the reported training setup.
summary.tldr: STORM combines Transformers and stochastic latent modeling to achieve strong Atari 100k performance with efficient single-GPU training.

title: STORM: Efficient Stochastic Transformer based World Models for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Offline reinforcement learning faces a significant challenge of value over-estimation due to the distributional drift between the dataset and the current learned policy, leading to learning failure in practice. The common approach is to incorporate a penalty term to reward or value estimation in the Bellman iterations. Meanwhile, to avoid extrapolation on out-of-distribution (OOD) states and actions, existing methods focus on conservative Q-function estimation. In this paper, we propose Conservative State Value Estimation (CSVE), a new approach that learns conservative V-function via directly imposing penalty on OOD states. Compared to prior work, CSVE allows more effective state value estimation with conservative guarantees and further better policy optimization. Further, we apply CSVE and develop a practical actor-critic algorithm in which the critic does the conservative value estimation by additionally sampling and penalizing the states around the dataset, and the actor applies advantage weighted updates extended with state exploration to improve the policy. We evaluate in classic continual control tasks of D4RL, showing that our method performs better than the conservative Q-function learning methods and is strongly competitive among recent SOTA methods.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning trains a policy from an existing dataset. As the policy changes, it can favor behavior unlike the data, causing overly optimistic value estimates and potentially learning failure. Conservative approaches address this problem by penalizing estimates involving unfamiliar states or actions. This paper shifts the focus to estimating the value of states directly.

Conservative State Value Estimation, or CSVE, imposes penalties on states outside the data distribution to learn a conservative V-function. The authors present conservative guarantees and use the approach in an actor-critic algorithm. Its critic samples and penalizes states around the dataset, while its actor combines advantage-weighted updates with state exploration to improve the policy.

This construction connects cautious state evaluation with the policy update itself: the critic shapes which states appear valuable, and the actor uses those evaluations when learning behavior. On D4RL continuous-control tasks, the method outperforms the conservative Q-function learning methods evaluated and remains strongly competitive with recent leading approaches. These findings support state-value conservatism as a useful offline learning strategy.
summary.tldr: CSVE penalizes unfamiliar states to learn conservative state values and improve offline policy learning.

title: Conservative State Value Estimation for Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Classical analysis of convex and non-convex optimization methods often requires the Lipschitz continuity of the gradient, which limits the analysis to functions bounded by quadratics. Recent work relaxed this requirement to a non-uniform smoothness condition with the Hessian norm bounded by an affine function of the gradient norm, and proved convergence in the non-convex setting via gradient clipping, assuming bounded noise. In this paper, we further generalize this non-uniform smoothness condition and develop a simple, yet powerful analysis technique that bounds the gradients along the trajectory, thereby leading to stronger results for both convex and non-convex optimization problems. In particular, we obtain the classical convergence rates for (stochastic) gradient descent and Nesterov's accelerated gradient method in the convex and/or non-convex setting under this general smoothness condition. The new analysis approach does not require gradient clipping and allows heavy-tailed noise with bounded variance in the stochastic setting.

paragraphs: Standard convergence analyses often assume that a function's gradient cannot change faster than a fixed global rate. This smoothness requirement restricts the functions covered by the theory. Earlier work relaxed it by allowing curvature to grow with gradient magnitude, but its nonconvex stochastic guarantees used gradient clipping and bounded noise.

This paper develops a broader smoothness condition and an analysis that controls gradients along the optimization trajectory. The focus is on bounding the gradients encountered as the algorithm proceeds. This technique yields stronger results for both convex and nonconvex problems under the generalized condition.

The authors recover classical convergence rates for gradient descent, stochastic gradient descent, and Nesterov's accelerated method in the settings covered by their results. Their approach does not require gradient clipping. In stochastic problems, it also permits heavy-tailed noise provided its variance is bounded. The contribution therefore broadens the theoretical conditions under which familiar optimization methods retain their established rates, including noise distributions excluded by a bounded-noise assumption.
summary.tldr: A generalized smoothness analysis recovers classical optimization rates without gradient clipping and permits stochastic noise with heavy tails and bounded variance.

title: Convex and Non-convex Optimization Under Generalized Smoothness

abstract: Standard diffusion models involve an image transform -- adding Gaussian noise -- and an image restoration operator that inverts this degradation. We observe that the generative behavior of diffusion models is not strongly dependent on the choice of image degradation, and in fact, an entire family of generative models can be constructed by varying this choice. Even when using completely deterministic degradations (e.g., blur, masking, and more), the training and test-time update rules that underlie diffusion models can be easily generalized to create generative models. The success of these fully deterministic models calls into question the community's understanding of diffusion models, which relies on noise in either gradient Langevin dynamics or variational inference and paves the way for generalized diffusion models that invert arbitrary processes.

paragraphs: Cold Diffusion investigates which parts of a diffusion model are responsible for its ability to generate images. Standard diffusion models degrade an image by adding Gaussian noise, then use a restoration operator to reverse that degradation. The paper asks how much the resulting generative behavior depends on choosing noise as the degradation process.

The authors vary the image transformation and generalize the training and generation update rules to accommodate other degradations. These include deterministic operations such as blurring and masking: transformations that do not themselves require random noise. This produces a family of generative models organized around different ways of degrading and restoring images.

The reported success of these deterministic models suggests that generative behavior is not strongly tied to the particular degradation chosen. That finding challenges explanations of diffusion models that place noise at the center through Langevin dynamics or variational inference. It supports exploring a broader framework for generation through reversing transformations, while the abstract presents inversion of arbitrary processes as a direction opened by the work rather than a demonstrated guarantee for every process.
summary.tldr: Cold Diffusion shows that diffusion-style generative models can use deterministic degradations such as blur and masking, challenging explanations centered on noise.

title: Cold Diffusion: Inverting Arbitrary Image Transforms Without Noise

abstract: Uncertainty estimation is an important research area to make deep neural networks (DNNs) more trustworthy. While extensive research on uncertainty estimation has been conducted with unimodal data, uncertainty estimation for multimodal data remains a challenge. Neural processes (NPs) have been demonstrated to be an effective uncertainty estimation method for unimodal data by providing the reliability of Gaussian processes with efficient and powerful DNNs. While NPs hold significant potential for multimodal uncertainty estimation, the adaptation of NPs for multimodal data has not been carefully studied. To bridge this gap, we propose Multimodal Neural Processes (MNPs) by generalising NPs for multimodal uncertainty estimation. Based on the framework of NPs, MNPs consist of several novel and principled mechanisms tailored to the characteristics of multimodal data. In extensive empirical evaluation, our method achieves state-of-the-art multimodal uncertainty estimation performance, showing its appealing robustness against noisy samples and reliability in out-of-distribution detection with faster computation time compared to the current state-of-the-art multimodal uncertainty estimation method.

paragraphs: A predictive model is more useful when it can indicate how much confidence its outputs deserve. Neural processes offer an approach to uncertainty estimation that combines qualities of Gaussian processes with the efficiency and expressive capacity of neural networks. Their adaptation to data containing multiple modalities, however, has received less careful study than their use with a single modality.

The paper introduces Multimodal Neural Processes, extending the neural-process framework with mechanisms designed for multimodal data. The central contribution is an uncertainty-estimation model that explicitly accounts for this setting. It addresses the challenge of assessing reliability when a prediction draws on several kinds of input.

Across extensive empirical evaluations, the method achieves reported state-of-the-art multimodal uncertainty performance. The experiments also show robustness to noisy samples, reliability in detecting inputs outside the training distribution, and faster computation than the compared leading method. These findings support its usefulness for assessing prediction reliability under the evaluated conditions, alongside its computational advantages.
summary.tldr: Multimodal Neural Processes extend neural-process uncertainty estimation to multiple modalities, with reported gains in robustness, detection reliability, and computation time.

title: Beyond Unimodal: Generalising Neural Processes for Multimodal Uncertainty Estimation

abstract: While recent advancements in vision-language models have had a transformative impact on multi-modal comprehension, the extent to which these models possess the ability to comprehend generated images remains uncertain. Synthetic images, in comparison to real data, encompass a higher level of diversity in terms of both content and style, thereby presenting significant challenges for the models to fully grasp. In light of this challenge, we introduce a comprehensive dataset, referred to as JourneyDB, that caters to the domain of generative images within the context of multi-modal visual understanding. Our meticulously curated dataset comprises 4 million distinct and high-quality generated images, each paired with the corresponding text prompts that were employed in their creation. Furthermore, we additionally introduce an external subset with results of another 22 text-to-image generative models, which makes JourneyDB a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating the comprehension of generated images. On our dataset, we have devised four benchmarks to assess the performance of generated image comprehension in relation to both content and style interpretation. These benchmarks encompass prompt inversion, style retrieval, image captioning, and visual question answering. Lastly, we evaluate the performance of state-of-the-art multi-modal models when applied to the JourneyDB dataset, providing a comprehensive analysis of their strengths and limitations in comprehending generated content. We anticipate that the proposed dataset and benchmarks will facilitate further research in the field of generative content understanding. The dataset is publicly available at https://journeydb.github.io.

paragraphs: Understanding generated images involves recognizing both their content and their style. The paper argues that synthetic images introduce substantial diversity along these dimensions, making it uncertain how well existing vision-language models understand them. JourneyDB provides a dedicated resource for examining that capability.

The dataset contains four million generated images paired with the text prompts used to create them. An additional external subset includes outputs from another 22 text-to-image models, broadening the benchmark’s coverage of image generators. These paired images and prompts provide a basis for evaluating different aspects of generated-image comprehension.

The contribution is a shared benchmark for studying generated-content understanding, alongside an initial assessment of existing models.
summary.tldr: JourneyDB pairs four million generated images with their prompts and introduces four benchmarks for understanding synthetic image content and style.

title: JourneyDB: A Benchmark for Generative Image Understanding

abstract: Diffusion probabilistic models (DPMs) have demonstrated a very promising ability in high-resolution image synthesis. However, sampling from a pre-trained DPM is time-consuming due to the multiple evaluations of the denoising network, making it more and more important to accelerate the sampling of DPMs. Despite recent progress in designing fast samplers, existing methods still cannot generate satisfying images in many applications where fewer steps (e.g., $<$10) are favored. In this paper, we develop a unified corrector (UniC) that can be applied after any existing DPM sampler to increase the order of accuracy without extra model evaluations, and derive a unified predictor (UniP) that supports arbitrary order as a byproduct. Combining UniP and UniC, we propose a unified predictor-corrector framework called UniPC for the fast sampling of DPMs, which has a unified analytical form for any order and can significantly improve the sampling quality over previous methods, especially in extremely few steps. We evaluate our methods through extensive experiments including both unconditional and conditional sampling using pixel-space and latent-space DPMs. Our UniPC can achieve 3.87 FID on CIFAR10 (unconditional) and 7.51 FID on ImageNet 256$\times$256 (conditional) with only 10 function evaluations. Code is available at https://github.com/wl-zhao/UniPC.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate images through repeated evaluations of a denoising network, making sampling expensive. Reducing the number of evaluations can compromise image quality, especially when very few steps are available. UniPC addresses this tradeoff through a predictor–corrector formulation for sampling.

The authors first derive UniC, a corrector that can follow any existing diffusion sampler and increase its order of accuracy without additional model evaluations. They also derive UniP, a predictor supporting arbitrary order. Combining them produces UniPC, whose analytical form applies across orders. summary.tldr: UniPC accelerates diffusion sampling with a unified predictor–corrector design whose corrector improves accuracy without extra model evaluations.

title: UniPC: A Unified Predictor-Corrector Framework for Fast Sampling of Diffusion Models

abstract: The popularity of bi-level optimization (BO) in deep learning has spurred a growing interest in studying gradient-based BO algorithms.However, existing algorithms involve two coupled learning rates that can be affected by approximation errors when computing hypergradients, making careful fine-tuning necessary to ensure fast convergence. To alleviate this issue, we investigate the use of recently proposed adaptive step-size methods, namely stochastic line search (SLS) and stochastic Polyak step size (SPS), for computing both the upper and lower-level learning rates. First, we revisit the use of SLS and SPS in single-level optimization without the additional interpolation condition that is typically assumed in prior works. For such settings, we investigate new variants of SLS and SPS that improve upon existing suggestions in the literature and are simpler to implement. Importantly, these two variants can be seen as special instances of general family of methods with an envelope-type step-size. This unified envelope strategy allows for the extension of the algorithms and their convergence guarantees to BO settings. Finally, our extensive experiments demonstrate that the new algorithms, which are available in both SGD and Adam versions, can find large learning rates with minimal tuning and converge faster than corresponding vanilla SGD or Adam BO algorithms that require fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Bi-level optimization couples an upper optimization problem to a lower one. Gradient-based methods must choose learning rates for both levels, and errors in estimating the upper-level gradient can make those choices delicate. This paper studies automatic step-size selection as a way to reduce tuning while retaining fast convergence.

The authors build on stochastic line search and stochastic Polyak step sizes. They first revisit these methods for single-level problems without the interpolation condition commonly assumed in earlier work. Their new variants are simpler to implement and fit within a shared family of envelope-type step-size rules. That common structure provides a route to extending both the algorithms and their convergence guarantees to bi-level problems.

Experiments evaluate versions based on SGD and Adam. The proposed methods find large learning rates with little tuning and converge faster than the corresponding conventional bi-level SGD or Adam methods requiring careful adjustment. The practical significance is coordinated adaptation of two interacting learning rates, supported by a framework that also connects the underlying single-level methods.
summary.tldr: BiSLS/SPS automatically adapts both learning rates in bi-level optimization, reducing tuning and improving convergence in experiments.

title: BiSLS/SPS: Auto-tune Step Sizes for Stable Bi-level Optimization

abstract: A diversity of tasks use language models trained on semantic similarity data. While there are a variety of datasets that capture semantic similarity, they are either constructed from modern web data or are relatively small datasets created in the past decade by human annotators. This study utilizes a novel source, newly digitized articles from off-copyright, local U.S. newspapers, to assemble a massive-scale semantic similarity dataset spanning 70 years from 1920 to 1989 and containing nearly 400M positive semantic similarity pairs. Historically, around half of articles in U.S. local newspapers came from newswires like the Associated Press. While local papers reproduced articles from the newswire, they wrote their own headlines, which form abstractive summaries of the associated articles. We associate articles and their headlines by exploiting document layouts and language understanding. We then use deep neural methods to detect which articles are from the same underlying source, in the presence of substantial noise and abridgement. The headlines of reproduced articles form positive semantic similarity pairs. The resulting publicly available HEADLINES dataset is significantly larger than most existing semantic similarity datasets and covers a much longer span of time. It will facilitate the application of contrastively trained semantic similarity models to a variety of tasks, including the study of semantic change across space and time.

paragraphs: HEADLINES turns historical newspaper publishing practices into a source of examples of similar meaning. Local U.S. newspapers often reproduced stories supplied by newswires while writing their own headlines. Different headlines attached to the same underlying story therefore provide naturally occurring pairs of short texts that summarize closely related content.

Building the dataset requires finding those connections in newly digitized newspapers. The researchers use page layout and language understanding to associate headlines with articles. They then apply deep neural methods to identify articles derived from the same source, despite substantial noise and shortened versions. The associated headlines become positive semantic similarity pairs.

The publicly available dataset contains nearly 400 million such pairs, covering 1920 through 1989. Its contribution combines scale with historical breadth, extending beyond datasets built mainly from contemporary web text or smaller annotation efforts. It is intended to support contrastively trained similarity models and research into how meaning varies across places and periods. The abstract presents these as uses the dataset enables.
summary.tldr: HEADLINES uses independently written headlines for reproduced newspaper stories to build nearly 400 million historical semantic similarity pairs.

title: A Massive Scale Semantic Similarity Dataset of Historical English

abstract: The adaptive leaky integrate-and-fire (ALIF) model is fundamental within computational neuroscience and has been instrumental in studying our brains $\textit{in silico}$. Due to the sequential nature of simulating these neural models, a commonly faced issue is the speed-accuracy trade-off: either accurately simulate a neuron using a small discretisation time-step (DT), which is slow, or more quickly simulate a neuron using a larger DT and incur a loss in simulation accuracy. Here we provide a solution to this dilemma, by algorithmically reinterpreting the ALIF model, reducing the sequential simulation complexity and permitting a more efficient parallelisation on GPUs. We computationally validate our implementation to obtain over a $50\times$ training speedup using small DTs on synthetic benchmarks. We also obtained a comparable performance to the standard ALIF implementation on different supervised classification tasks - yet in a fraction of the training time. Lastly, we showcase how our model makes it possible to quickly and accurately fit real electrophysiological recordings of cortical neurons, where very fine sub-millisecond DTs are crucial for capturing exact spike timing.

paragraphs: Simulating adaptive leaky integrate-and-fire neurons involves a familiar compromise. Small time steps capture neural activity more accurately but require many sequential computations. Larger steps reduce computation while sacrificing accuracy. The paper addresses this trade-off by changing how the neuron model is computed, particularly when fine timing resolution is needed.

The authors reinterpret the ALIF model algorithmically to reduce the sequential work involved in simulation. This makes the computation more amenable to parallel execution on GPUs. The goal is to retain small time steps while making training faster, so speed improvements do not have to come from using a coarser simulation.

On synthetic benchmarks, the implementation produces more than a 50-fold training speedup with small time steps. It also achieves performance comparable to standard ALIF implementations on several supervised classification tasks, with substantially shorter training times. Finally, the authors demonstrate fitting real recordings of cortical neurons quickly and accurately. That application highlights the value of retaining sub-millisecond resolution when precise spike timing is central to the task.
summary.tldr: An algorithmic reformulation makes adaptive spiking-neuron simulations more GPU-parallel, accelerating training while retaining fine time resolution.

title: Addressing the speed-accuracy simulation trade-off for adaptive spiking neurons

abstract: This paper deals with the problem of efficient sampling from a stochastic differential equation, given the drift function and the diffusion matrix. The proposed approach leverages a recent model for probabilities (Rudi and Ciliberto, 2021) (the positive semi-definite -- PSD model) from which it is possible to obtain independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) samples at precision $\varepsilon$ with a cost that is $m^2 d \log(1/\varepsilon)$ where $m$ is the dimension of the model, $d$ the dimension of the space. The proposed approach consists in: first, computing the PSD model that satisfies the Fokker-Planck equation (or its fractional variant) associated with the SDE, up to error $\varepsilon$, and then sampling from the resulting PSD model. Assuming some regularity of the Fokker-Planck solution (i.e. $\beta$-times differentiability plus some geometric condition on its zeros) We obtain an algorithm that: (a) in the preparatory phase obtains a PSD model with L2 distance $\varepsilon$ from the solution of the equation, with a model of dimension $m = \varepsilon^{-(d+1)/(\beta-2s)} (\log(1/\varepsilon))^{d+1}$ where $1/2\leq s\leq1$ is the fractional power to the Laplacian, and total computational complexity of $O(m^{3.5} \log(1/\varepsilon))$ and then (b) for Fokker-Planck equation, it is able to produce i.i.d.\ samples with error $\varepsilon$ in Wasserstein-1 distance, with a cost that is $O(d \varepsilon^{-2(d+1)/\beta-2} \log(1/\varepsilon)^{2d+3})$ per sample. This means that, if the probability associated with the SDE is somewhat regular, i.e. $\beta \geq 4d+2$, then the algorithm requires $O(\varepsilon^{-0.88} \log(1/\varepsilon)^{4.5d})$ in the preparatory phase, and $O(\varepsilon^{-1/2}\log(1/\varepsilon)^{2d+2})$ for each sample. Our results suggest that as the true solution gets smoother, we can circumvent the curse of dimensionality without requiring any sort of convexity.

Greater smoothness improves the computational bounds; the abstract gives a particularly favorable regime when differentiability is sufficiently high relative to dimension. This is a conditional benefit of regularity, not a claim about every stochastic differential equation.
summary.tldr: Approximating SDE distributions with positive semi-definite models enables efficient independent sampling under suitable smoothness and geometric conditions.

title: Efficient Sampling of Stochastic Differential Equations with Positive Semi-Definite Models

abstract: Supervised training of deep neural networks on pairs of clean image and noisy measurement achieves state-of-the-art performance for many image reconstruction tasks, but such training pairs are difficult to collect. Self-supervised methods enable training based on noisy measurements only, without clean images. In this work, we investigate the cost of self-supervised training in terms of sample complexity for a class of self-supervised methods that enable the computation of unbiased estimates of gradients of the supervised loss, including noise2noise methods. We analytically show that a model trained with such self-supervised training is as good as the same model trained in a supervised fashion, but self-supervised training requires more examples than supervised training. We then study self-supervised denoising and accelerated MRI empirically and characterize the cost of self-supervised training in terms of the number of additional samples required, and find that the performance gap between self-supervised and supervised training vanishes as a function of the training examples, at a problem-dependent rate, as predicted by our theory.

paragraphs: Training an image reconstruction model usually benefits from paired noisy measurements and clean images, but clean references can be difficult to collect. Self-supervised methods remove that requirement by learning from noisy measurements alone. This paper asks how much additional training data is needed to make up for the missing clean targets.

The analysis covers methods, including noise2noise, that can produce unbiased estimates of the supervised loss gradient. In this setting, the estimated training direction is correct on average. The authors show analytically that self-supervised training can make the same model as good as supervised training, although reaching that performance requires more examples.

Experiments on image denoising and accelerated MRI examine this additional sample requirement. They find that the performance gap shrinks away as the number of training examples grows, with the rate depending on the reconstruction problem. The result frames the tradeoff as a data requirement: for the analyzed class of methods, avoiding clean references need not impose a lasting performance disadvantage.
summary.tldr: For the analyzed self-supervised reconstruction methods, matching supervised performance requires more examples, with the gap closing at a problem-dependent rate.

title: Analyzing the Sample Complexity of Self-Supervised Image Reconstruction Methods

abstract: The advancement of continual reinforcement learning (RL) has been facing various obstacles, including standardized metrics and evaluation protocols, demanding computational requirements, and a lack of widely accepted standard benchmarks. In response to these challenges, we present COOM ($\textbf{C}$ontinual D$\textbf{OOM}$), a continual RL benchmark tailored for embodied pixel-based RL. COOM presents a meticulously crafted suite of task sequences set within visually distinct 3D environments, serving as a robust evaluation framework to assess crucial aspects of continual RL, such as catastrophic forgetting, knowledge transfer, and sample-efficient learning. Following an in-depth empirical evaluation of popular continual learning (CL) methods, we pinpoint their limitations, provide valuable insight into the benchmark and highlight unique algorithmic challenges. This makes our work the first to benchmark image-based CRL in 3D environments with embodied perception. The primary objective of the COOM benchmark is to offer the research community a valuable and cost-effective challenge. It seeks to deepen our comprehension of the capabilities and limitations of current and forthcoming CL methods in an RL setting. The code and environments are open-sourced and accessible on GitHub.

paragraphs: Continual reinforcement learning asks agents to learn across changing tasks while retaining useful earlier knowledge. Comparing methods is difficult when benchmarks, metrics, and evaluation procedures differ, and when experiments demand substantial computation. COOM, short for Continual DOOM, is introduced as a cost-effective benchmark addressing these evaluation challenges.

The benchmark contains carefully designed task sequences in visually distinct three-dimensional environments. Agents operate from pixel observations with embodied perception, making the setting relevant to learning through an agent's own visual experience. The task sequences support evaluation of catastrophic forgetting, transfer of knowledge between tasks, and sample efficiency. These dimensions examine different aspects of whether learning remains effective over a sequence.

The authors evaluate popular continual learning methods and identify limitations and algorithmic challenges in this setting. They describe COOM as the first benchmark for image-based continual reinforcement learning in three-dimensional environments with embodied perception. Its contribution is a shared experimental framework, with openly available code and environments, for investigating where existing and future methods succeed or struggle.
summary.tldr: COOM provides visual 3D task sequences for evaluating forgetting, knowledge transfer, and sample efficiency in continual reinforcement learning.

title: COOM: A Game Benchmark for Continual Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Learning fine-grained embeddings from coarse labels is a challenging task due to limited label granularity supervision, i.e., lacking the detailed distinctions required for fine-grained tasks. The task becomes even more demanding when attempting few-shot fine-grained recognition, which holds practical significance in various applications. To address these challenges, we propose a novel method that embeds visual embeddings into a hyperbolic space and enhances their discriminative ability with a hierarchical cosine margins manner. Specifically, the hyperbolic space offers distinct advantages, including the ability to capture hierarchical relationships and increased expressive power, which favors modeling fine-grained objects. Based on the hyperbolic space, we further enforce relatively large/small similarity margins between coarse/fine classes, respectively, yielding the so-called hierarchical cosine margins manner. While enforcing similarity margins in the regular Euclidean space has become popular for deep embedding learning, applying it to the hyperbolic space is non-trivial and validating the benefit for coarse-to-fine generalization is valuable. Extensive experiments conducted on five benchmark datasets showcase the effectiveness of our proposed method, yielding state-of-the-art results surpassing competing methods.

paragraphs: The paper tackles learning detailed visual distinctions when training labels describe only broad categories. This limited supervision makes fine-grained recognition difficult, particularly when only a few examples are available for the detailed recognition task. The authors seek representations that retain useful distinctions beyond the granularity explicitly provided by the labels.

Their method places visual embeddings in hyperbolic space, which supports hierarchical relationships and offers expressive capacity useful for modeling fine-grained objects. It then introduces hierarchical cosine margins: relatively large similarity margins between coarse classes and smaller margins between fine classes. These requirements adapt separation in the representation to the level of the hierarchy.

Applying similarity margins in hyperbolic space is a substantive part of the contribution, since familiar Euclidean-space margin methods do not transfer trivially. Experiments on five benchmark datasets report state-of-the-art performance over competing methods. The findings support combining hierarchical geometry with different margins at different levels to improve coarse-to-fine generalization, including the challenging setting of few-shot fine-grained recognition.
summary.tldr: Hyperbolic visual embeddings with hierarchical cosine margins improve fine-grained learning from coarse labels in the reported benchmarks.

title: Hyperbolic Space with Hierarchical Margin Boosts Fine-Grained Learning from Coarse Labels

abstract: This paper reveals a characteristic of DEtection Transformer (DETR) that negatively impacts its training efficacy, i.e., the cross-attention and self-attention layers in DETR decoder have contrary impacts on the object queries (though both impacts are important). Specifically, we observe the cross-attention tends to gather multiple queries around the same object, while the self-attention disperses these queries far away. To improve the training efficacy, we propose a Divide-And-Conquer DETR (DAC-DETR) that divides the cross-attention out from this contrary for better conquering. During training, DAC-DETR employs an auxiliary decoder that focuses on learning the cross-attention layers. The auxiliary decoder, while sharing all the other parameters, has NO self-attention layers and employs one-to-many label assignment to improve the gathering effect. Experiments show that DAC-DETR brings remarkable improvement over popular DETRs. For example, under the 12 epochs training scheme on MS-COCO, DAC-DETR improves Deformable DETR (ResNet-50) by +3.4 AP and achieves 50.9 (ResNet-50) / 58.1 AP (Swin-Large) based on some popular methods (i.e., DINO and an IoU-related loss). Our code will be made available at https://github.com/huzhengdongcs/DAC-DETR.

paragraphs: DETR detects objects using queries processed by attention layers. This paper identifies a tension inside its decoder: cross-attention tends to gather multiple queries around the same object, while self-attention pushes those queries apart. Both behaviors matter, but their opposing effects can make learning less effective when trained together.

DAC-DETR introduces an auxiliary decoder during training to give cross-attention a more focused learning path. This decoder removes self-attention while sharing all other parameters. It also assigns each object label to multiple queries, reinforcing the gathering behavior. The design therefore changes the training arrangement around the identified conflict rather than treating either attention mechanism as unnecessary.

Experiments show improvements over popular DETR variants. With 12 training epochs on MS-COCO, the method adds 3.4 AP to Deformable DETR with a ResNet-50 backbone. With other methods including DINO and an IoU-related loss, it reaches 50.9 AP with ResNet-50 and 58.1 AP with Swin-Large. These results support the value of giving the decoder's competing learning behaviors a more deliberate training structure.
summary.tldr: DAC-DETR improves detector training with an auxiliary decoder that strengthens cross-attention without competing self-attention.

title: DAC-DETR: Divide the Attention Layers and Conquer

abstract: Sequence prediction on temporal data requires the ability to understand compositional structures of multi-level semantics beyond individual and contextual properties of parts. The task of temporal action segmentation remains challenging for the reason, aiming at translating an untrimmed activity video into a sequence of action segments. This paper addresses the problem by introducing an effective activity grammar to guide neural predictions for temporal action segmentation. We propose a novel grammar induction algorithm, dubbed KARI, that extracts a powerful context-free grammar from action sequence data. We also develop an efficient generalized parser, dubbed BEP, that transforms frame-level probability distributions into a reliable sequence of actions according to the induced grammar with recursive rules. Our approach can be combined with any neural network for temporal action segmentation to enhance the sequence prediction and discover its compositional structure. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly improves temporal action segmentation in terms of both performance and interpretability on two standard benchmarks, Breakfast and 50 Salads.

paragraphs: Temporal action segmentation divides an untrimmed activity video into a sequence of labeled actions. Recognizing individual frames is only part of the problem: the predicted actions also need to fit together into a meaningful activity. This paper adds an explicit grammar to help neural predictions reflect that larger compositional structure.

The approach has two components. KARI learns a context-free grammar from action sequences, extracting rules that describe how actions can combine. BEP then uses that grammar to turn a network's frame-level probability predictions into an action sequence. Its support for recursive rules allows the parsing process to represent structure beyond isolated neighboring actions.

The grammar and parser can be combined with any neural network for temporal action segmentation, according to the authors. Experiments on Breakfast and 50 Salads show significant improvements in both segmentation performance and interpretability. The contribution is therefore not simply another frame classifier: it provides a way to organize predictions through learned activity rules and expose the compositional structure behind the resulting sequence.
summary.tldr: A learned activity grammar turns frame-level neural predictions into more accurate and interpretable action sequences.

title: Activity Grammars for Temporal Action Segmentation

abstract: Obtaining human-interpretable explanations of large, general-purpose language models is an urgent goal for AI safety. However, it is just as important that our interpretability methods are faithful to the causal dynamics underlying model behavior and able to robustly generalize to unseen inputs. Distributed Alignment Search (DAS) is a powerful gradient descent method grounded in a theory of causal abstraction that uncovered perfect alignments between interpretable symbolic algorithms and small deep learning models fine-tuned for specific tasks. In the present paper, we scale DAS significantly by replacing the remaining brute-force search steps with learned parameters -- an approach we call Boundless DAS. This enables us to efficiently search for interpretable causal structure in large language models while they follow instructions. We apply Boundless DAS to the Alpaca model (7B parameters), which, off the shelf, solves a simple numerical reasoning problem. With Boundless DAS, we discover that Alpaca does this by implementing a causal model with two interpretable boolean variables. Furthermore, we find that the alignment of neural representations with these variables is robust to changes in inputs and instructions. These findings mark a first step toward deeply understanding the inner-workings of our largest and most widely deployed language models.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether a large language model's internal computation can be explained through an interpretable causal model. The goal goes beyond finding a description that resembles the output: an explanation should reflect the mechanisms producing behavior and remain useful when inputs change. The authors build on Distributed Alignment Search, a gradient-based method grounded in causal abstraction.

Their extension, Boundless DAS, replaces the remaining brute-force search steps with learned parameters. This makes the search for interpretable causal structure practical at a larger scale. The authors find that Alpaca's neural representations align with this causal model and that the alignment remains robust across changes in inputs and instructions. This provides a concrete mechanism for the studied reasoning behavior. Its significance is a scalable demonstration of causal interpretability, with the reported explanation tied to the particular problem examined.
summary.tldr: Boundless DAS identifies a two-Boolean-variable causal mechanism underlying Alpaca's behavior on a simple numerical reasoning problem.

title: Interpretability at Scale: Identifying Causal Mechanisms in Alpaca

abstract: Identifying causal relations from purely observational data typically requires additional assumptions on relations and/or noise. Most current methods restrict their analysis to datasets that are assumed to have pure linear or nonlinear relations, which is often not reflective of real-world datasets that contain a combination of both. This paper presents CaPS, an ordering-based causal discovery algorithm that effectively handles linear and nonlinear relations. CaPS introduces a novel identification criterion for topological ordering and incorporates the concept of "parent score" during the post-processing optimization stage. These scores quantify the strength of the average causal effect, helping to accelerate the pruning process and correct inaccurate predictions in the pruning step. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed solutions outperform state-of-the-art baselines on synthetic data with varying ratios of linear and nonlinear relations. The results obtained from real-world data also support the competitiveness of CaPS. Code and datasets are available at https://github.com/E2real/CaPS.

paragraphs: Discovering causal relationships from observations generally requires assumptions about the relationships or their noise. Many existing methods focus on settings assumed to contain entirely linear or entirely nonlinear relationships. CaPS addresses datasets containing a mixture, making that combination central to the causal discovery procedure.

The algorithm first uses a new criterion to identify a topological ordering, an ordering compatible with the directions of the proposed causal relationships. During post-processing, it introduces parent scores that quantify the strength of average causal effects. These scores guide pruning, helping the algorithm remove proposed relationships more quickly and correct inaccurate predictions made during that step.

On synthetic datasets with different proportions of linear and nonlinear relationships, the proposed solutions outperform the state-of-the-art baselines evaluated. Results on real-world data also support CaPS’s competitiveness. The contribution combines an ordering criterion with effect-based guidance for refining the resulting graph. Its findings support handling mixed relationship types within one discovery approach, while the abstract retains the general need for assumptions when inferring causality from observations.
summary.tldr: CaPS combines a causal ordering criterion with parent scores to discover and refine mixed linear and nonlinear causal relationships.

title: Ordering-Based Causal Discovery for Linear and Nonlinear Relations

abstract: This paper proposes ProEdit - a simple yet effective framework for high-quality 3D scene editing guided by diffusion distillation in a novel progressive manner. Inspired by the crucial observation that multi-view inconsistency in scene editing is rooted in the diffusion model’s large feasible output space (FOS), our framework controls the size of FOS and reduces inconsistency by decomposing the overall editing task into several subtasks, which are then executed progressively on the scene. Within this framework, we design a difficulty-aware subtask decomposition scheduler and an adaptive 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) training strategy, ensuring high efficiency in performing each subtask. Extensive evaluation shows that our ProEdit achieves state-of-the-art results in various scenes and challenging editing tasks, all through a simple framework without any expensive or sophisticated add-ons like distillation losses, components, or training procedures. Notably, ProEdit also provides a new way to preview, control, and select the aggressivity of editing operation during the editing process.

paragraphs: Diffusion-guided three-dimensional editing can produce inconsistent views because the image generator has many possible outputs. ProEdit reduces that ambiguity by decomposing a requested edit into smaller changes and applying them progressively to the scene.

A difficulty-aware scheduler chooses the subtask decomposition, while an adaptive three-dimensional Gaussian-splatting training strategy carries out each step efficiently. The framework lets users preview intermediate results and choose how aggressively to apply the edit as it progresses.

Extensive evaluations across scenes and challenging edits report state-of-the-art results without expensive added components or elaborate auxiliary training procedures. The abstract does not supply quality scores, timings, or a formal consistency guarantee. Its contribution is the progressive editing strategy and supporting scheduler, with evidence that controlling the scope of each change can improve the final multiview result.
summary.tldr: ProEdit improves 3D editing consistency by breaking a large edit into progressive subtasks.

title: ProEdit: Simple Progression is All You Need for High-Quality 3D Scene Editing

abstract: The interaction between Fourier transform and deep learning opens new avenues for long-term time series forecasting (LTSF). We propose a new perspective to reconsider the Fourier transform from a basis functions perspective. Specifically, the real and imaginary parts of the frequency components can be viewed as the coefficients of cosine and sine basis functions at tiered frequency levels, respectively. We argue existing Fourier-based methods do not involve basis functions thus fail to interpret frequency coefficients precisely and consider the time-frequency relationship sufficiently, leading to inconsistent starting cycles and inconsistent series length issues. Accordingly, a novel Fourier basis mapping (FBM) method addresses these issues by mixing time and frequency domain features through Fourier basis expansion. Differing from existing approaches, FBM (i) embeds the discrete Fourier transform with basis functions, and then (ii) can enable plug-and-play in various types of neural networks for better performance. FBM extracts explicit frequency features while preserving temporal characteristics, enabling the mapping network to capture the time-frequency relationships. By incorporating our unique time-frequency features, the FBM variants can enhance any type of networks like linear, multilayer-perceptron-based, transformer-based, and Fourier-based networks, achieving state-of-the-art LTSF results on diverse real-world datasets with just one or three fully connected layers. The code is available at: https://github.com/runze1223/Fourier-Basis-Mapping.

The real and imaginary coefficients correspond to cosine and sine functions at different frequencies. Making that relationship explicit matters for interpreting where cycles begin and how representations relate to series length.

The authors introduce Fourier basis mapping, or FBM, which combines time-domain and frequency-domain features through Fourier basis expansion. It incorporates basis functions into the discrete Fourier transform so that explicit frequency information retains temporal characteristics. A mapping network can then learn relationships between timing and frequency instead of treating frequency coefficients without that explicit connection.

FBM is designed as a plug-in for several network families, including linear, multilayer-perceptron, transformer, and Fourier-based models. The authors report state-of-the-art long-term forecasting results on diverse real-world datasets using variants with only one or three fully connected layers. These findings suggest that a more explicit time–frequency representation can deliver strong forecasting performance without requiring a deep mapping network.
summary.tldr: Fourier basis mapping explicitly connects frequency coefficients with time, improving long-term forecasting across several neural network families.

title: Rethinking Fourier Transform from A Basis Functions Perspective for Long-term Time Series Forecasting

abstract: We address a generalization of the bandit with knapsacks problem, where a learner aims to maximize rewards while satisfying an arbitrary set of long-term constraints. Our goal is to design best-of-both-worlds algorithms that perform optimally under both stochastic and adversarial constraints. Previous works address this problem via primal-dual methods, and require some stringent assumptions, namely the Slater's condition, and in adversarial settings, they either assume knowledge of a lower bound on the Slater's parameter, or impose strong requirements on the primal and dual regret minimizers such as requiring weak adaptivity. We propose an alternative and more natural approach based on optimistic estimations of the constraints. Surprisingly, we show that estimating the constraints with an UCB-like approach guarantees optimal performances.Our algorithm consists of two main components: (i) a regret minimizer working on moving strategy sets and (ii) an estimate of the feasible set as an optimistic weighted empirical mean of previous samples. The key challenge in this approach is designing adaptive weights that meet the different requirements for stochastic and adversarial constraints. Our algorithm is significantly simpler than previous approaches, and has a cleaner analysis. Moreover, ours is the first best-of-both-worlds algorithm providing bounds logarithmic in the number of constraints. Additionally, in stochastic settings, it provides $\widetilde O(\sqrt{T})$ regret without Slater's condition.

Its goal is one algorithm with optimal performance whether those constraints arise stochastically or adversarially. Earlier approaches use primal-dual methods and can require demanding assumptions, including Slater's condition and additional knowledge or adaptivity requirements in adversarial settings.

In stochastic environments, it achieves square-root regret up to logarithmic factors without Slater's condition. Together with a simpler algorithm and analysis, these results make optimistic constraint estimation a substantive alternative to the established primal-dual approach.
summary.tldr: Optimistic constraint estimates yield a simpler best-of-both-worlds bandit algorithm with logarithmic dependence on the number of constraints.

title: Beyond Primal-Dual Methods in Bandits with Stochastic and Adversarial Constraints

abstract: The reliability of driving perception systems under unprecedented conditions is crucial for practical usage. Latest advancements have prompted increasing interest in multi-LiDAR perception. However, prevailing driving datasets predominantly utilize single-LiDAR systems and collect data devoid of adverse conditions, failing to capture the complexities of real-world environments accurately. Addressing these gaps, we proposed Place3D, a full-cycle pipeline that encompasses LiDAR placement optimization, data generation, and downstream evaluations. Our framework makes three appealing contributions. 1) To identify the most effective configurations for multi-LiDAR systems, we introduce the Surrogate Metric of the Semantic Occupancy Grids (M-SOG) to evaluate LiDAR placement quality. 2) Leveraging the M-SOG metric, we propose a novel optimization strategy to refine multi-LiDAR placements. 3) Centered around the theme of multi-condition multi-LiDAR perception, we collect a 280,000-frame dataset from both clean and adverse conditions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LiDAR placements optimized using our approach outperform various baselines. We showcase exceptional results in both LiDAR semantic segmentation and 3D object detection tasks, under diverse weather and sensor failure conditions.

paragraphs: A driving perception system's inputs depend on where its sensors are mounted, making placement part of the perception problem. Place3D studies this issue for multiple LiDAR sensors under varied operating conditions. It connects placement optimization, data generation, and downstream evaluation in one pipeline.

The authors introduce M-SOG, a surrogate measure based on semantic occupancy grids, to assess placement quality. They then use that measure to optimize multi-LiDAR configurations. This gives placement selection an explicit evaluation criterion linked to the scene representation, rather than treating sensor configuration as a fixed choice made before assessing perception performance.

The project also contributes a 280,000-frame dataset covering clean and adverse conditions. Experiments evaluate optimized placements through semantic segmentation and 3D object detection, including varied weather and sensor failures. The optimized configurations outperform several baselines in the reported comparisons. These results show why evaluating sensor placement together with downstream perception matters: the physical configuration can affect how effectively a system understands a scene under challenging conditions.
summary.tldr: Place3D optimizes multi-LiDAR placement and evaluates its perception benefits across clean conditions, adverse weather, and sensor failures.

title: Is Your LiDAR Placement Optimized for 3D Scene Understanding?

abstract: Surveys have recently gained popularity as a tool to study large language models. By comparing models’ survey responses to those of different human reference populations, researchers aim to infer the demographics, political opinions, or values best represented by current language models. In this work, we critically examine language models' survey responses on the basis of the well-established American Community Survey by the U.S. Census Bureau. Evaluating 43 different language models using de-facto standard prompting methodologies, we establish two dominant patterns. First, models' responses are governed by ordering and labeling biases, for example, towards survey responses labeled with the letter “A”. Second, when adjusting for these systematic biases through randomized answer ordering, models across the board trend towards uniformly random survey responses, irrespective of model size or training data. As a result, models consistently appear to better represent subgroups whose aggregate statistics are closest to uniform for the survey under consideration, leading to potentially misguided conclusions about model alignment.
