paragraphs: Researchers sometimes compare language models' survey answers with human populations to infer which demographics, opinions, or values the models represent. This paper tests the reliability of that interpretation using the American Community Survey. The authors evaluate 43 language models with prompting methods commonly used for this kind of analysis.

They find that answer order and labels strongly influence responses, including a preference for options labeled A. When the researchers randomize answer ordering to adjust for those biases, the models' responses trend toward a uniform distribution across options. This pattern appears across the evaluated models regardless of their size or training data.

That behavior can create misleading apparent similarities to human groups. A group whose aggregate survey statistics happen to be closer to uniform will appear better represented by the model. The findings therefore challenge interpreting survey-response similarity as straightforward evidence of model alignment: in this evaluation, response-format biases and near-uniform answering patterns can shape the apparent demographic match.
summary.tldr: Survey answers from 43 language models show formatting biases and near-uniform patterns that can mislead conclusions about demographic alignment.

title: Questioning the Survey Responses of Large Language Models

abstract: In this work, we introduce *Scribbles for All*, a label and training data generation algorithm for semantic segmentation trained on scribble labels. Training or fine-tuning semantic segmentation models with weak supervision has become an important topic recently and was subject to significant advances in model quality. In this setting, scribbles are a promising label type to achieve high quality segmentation results while requiring a much lower annotation effort than usual pixel-wise dense semantic segmentation annotations. The main limitation of scribbles as source for weak supervision is the lack of challenging datasets for scribble segmentation, which hinders the development of novel methods and conclusive evaluations. To overcome this limitation, *Scribbles for All* provides scribble labels for several popular segmentation datasets and provides an algorithm to automatically generate scribble labels for any dataset with dense annotations, paving the way for new insights and model advancements in the field of weakly supervised segmentation. In addition to providing datasets and algorithm, we evaluate state-of-the-art segmentation models on our datasets and show that models trained with our synthetic labels perform competitively with respect to models trained on manual labels. Thus, our datasets enable state-of-the-art research into methods for scribble-labeled semantic segmentation. The datasets, scribble generation algorithm, and baselines are publicly available at https://github.com/wbkit/Scribbles4All.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns categories to image pixels, but labeling every pixel is labor-intensive. Scribbles provide a lighter form of supervision by marking only parts of the image. Although this approach has produced promising models, a shortage of challenging scribble-labeled datasets makes it harder to develop methods and compare them convincingly.

Scribbles for All supplies an algorithm that automatically generates scribble labels from existing dense annotations. The authors use it to provide scribbles for several popular segmentation datasets. Because the procedure applies to datasets that already have dense labels, it creates a route for broadening scribble-supervision research using existing annotated resources.

The paper also evaluates state-of-the-art segmentation models on the resulting datasets. Models trained with synthetic scribbles perform competitively with models trained using manual scribble labels. This supports the generated annotations as useful research material for benchmarking weak supervision. The released datasets, generation algorithm, and baselines provide a shared basis for studying how segmentation models learn from sparse annotations.
summary.tldr: Scribbles for All converts dense segmentation labels into synthetic scribbles that support competitive training and broader benchmarking.

title: Scribbles for All: Benchmarking Scribble Supervised Segmentation Across Datasets

abstract: Semi-supervised graph domain adaptation, as a branch of graph transfer learning, aims to annotate unlabeled target graph nodes by utilizing transferable knowledge learned from a label-scarce source graph. However, most existing studies primarily concentrate on aligning feature distributions directly to extract domain-invariant features, while ignoring the utilization of the intrinsic structure information in graphs. Inspired by the significance of data structure information in enhancing models' generalization performance, this paper aims to investigate how to leverage the structure information to assist graph transfer learning. To this end, we propose an innovative framework called TFGDA. Specially, TFGDA employs a structure alignment strategy named STSA to encode graphs' topological structure information into the latent space, greatly facilitating the learning of transferable features. To achieve a stable alignment of feature distributions, we also introduce a SDA strategy to mitigate domain discrepancy on the sphere. Moreover, to address the overfitting issue caused by label scarcity, a simple but effective RNC strategy is devised to guide the discriminative clustering of unlabeled nodes. Experiments on various benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of TFGDA over SOTA methods.

paragraphs: TFGDA addresses transferring knowledge from a graph with few labels to unlabeled nodes in a target graph. Many approaches align feature distributions across domains, but the authors argue that this overlooks useful information in graph structure. Their framework combines structural alignment, feature alignment, and clustering to support transfer when labeled examples are scarce.

Its STSA component encodes topological information into a latent representation, helping the model learn transferable features from how graph elements are connected. The SDA component reduces differences between domains on a spherical representation space to stabilize feature alignment. A third component, RNC, guides discriminative clustering of unlabeled nodes to address overfitting associated with limited labels.

These components tackle complementary parts of the transfer problem: structural information, differences in feature distributions, and the shortage of direct supervision. Experiments on several benchmarks report better performance than state-of-the-art methods. The findings support incorporating graph topology into domain adaptation together with feature alignment and guidance from unlabeled-node clustering.
summary.tldr: TFGDA combines graph-structure alignment, spherical feature alignment, and unlabeled-node clustering to improve transfer between graphs with scarce labels.

title: TFGDA: Exploring Topology and Feature Alignment in Semi-supervised Graph Domain Adaptation through Robust Clustering

abstract: Mamba, a state-space model with selective mechanisms and hardware-aware architecture, has demonstrated outstanding performance in long sequence modeling tasks, particularly garnering widespread exploration and application in the field of computer vision. While existing works have mixed opinions of its application in visual tasks, the exploration of its internal workings and the optimization of its performance remain urgent and worthy research questions given its status as a novel model. Existing optimizations of the Mamba model, especially when applied in the visual domain, have primarily relied on predefined methods such as improving scanning mechanisms or integrating other architectures, often requiring strong priors and extensive trial and error. In contrast to these approaches, this paper proposes the Vision Mamba Mender, a systematic approach for understanding the workings of Mamba, identifying flaws within, and subsequently optimizing model performance. Specifically, we present methods for predictive correlation analysis of Mamba's hidden states from both internal and external perspectives, along with corresponding definitions of correlation scores, aimed at understanding the workings of Mamba in visual recognition tasks and identifying flaws therein. Additionally, tailored repair methods are proposed for identified external and internal state flaws to eliminate them and optimize model performance. Extensive experiments validate the efficacy of the proposed methods on prevalent Mamba architectures, significantly enhancing Mamba's performance.

The reported gains indicate that inspecting hidden-state behavior can provide a productive basis for improving the tested vision models.

title: Vision Mamba Mender

abstract: Many real-world graphs are large and have some characteristic subgraph patterns, such as triangles in social networks, cliques in web graphs, and cycles in molecular networks.Detecting such subgraph patterns is important in many applications; therefore, establishing graph neural networks (GNNs) that can detect such patterns and run fast on large graphs is demanding.In this study, we propose a new GNN layer, named \emph{graph homomorphism layer}.It enumerates local subgraph patterns that match the predefined set of patterns $\mathcal{P}^\bullet$, applies non-linear transformations to node features, and aggregates them along with the patterns. By stacking these layers, we obtain a deep GNN model called \emph{deep homomorphism network (DHN)}.The expressive power of the DHN is completely characterised by the set of patterns generated from $\mathcal{P}^\bullet$ by graph-theoretic operations;hence, it serves as a useful theoretical tool to analyse the expressive power of many GNN models.Furthermore, the model runs in the same time complexity as the graph homomorphisms, which is fast in many real-word graphs.Thus, it serves as a practical and lightweight model that solves difficult problems using domain knowledge.

paragraphs: Many graphs contain meaningful local structures, such as triangles in social networks, cliques in web graphs, or cycles in molecular networks. A graph neural network needs enough expressive power to recognize relevant structures while remaining practical on large graphs. This paper makes a chosen collection of structural patterns central to the network’s design.

Its graph homomorphism layer enumerates local matches to predefined patterns, transforms node features nonlinearly, and aggregates information along those patterns. Stacking the layers produces a deep homomorphism network. The initial pattern set supplies domain knowledge about the structures the model should use when processing the graph.

The authors completely characterize the network’s expressive power through patterns generated from that initial set by graph-theoretic operations. This makes the architecture a theoretical tool for analyzing other graph neural networks as well. Its runtime has the same complexity as the graph-homomorphism computations it uses, which the abstract describes as fast on many real-world graphs. The efficiency claim therefore accompanies an explicit connection between chosen patterns, representational power, and computational work.
summary.tldr: Deep homomorphism networks use predefined graph patterns to build expressive graph models with a precise theoretical characterization.

title: Deep Homomorphism Networks

abstract: Pre-trained language encoders---functions that represent text as vectors---are an integral component of many NLP tasks. We tackle a natural question in language encoder analysis: What does it mean for two encoders to be similar? We contend that a faithful measure of similarity needs to be \emph{intrinsic}, that is, task-independent, yet still be informative of \emph{extrinsic} similarity---the performance on downstream tasks. It is common to consider two encoders similar if they are \emph{homotopic}, i.e., if they can be aligned through some transformation. In this spirit, we study the properties of \emph{affine} alignment of language encoders and its implications on extrinsic similarity. We find that while affine alignment is fundamentally an asymmetric notion of similarity, it is still informative of extrinsic similarity. We confirm this on datasets of natural language representations. Beyond providing useful bounds on extrinsic similarity, affine intrinsic similarity also allows us to begin uncovering the structure of the space of pre-trained encoders by defining an order over them.

paragraphs: Language encoders turn text into vectors, but deciding whether two encoders are similar is not straightforward. This paper argues for a comparison that does not depend on a particular downstream task while still revealing something about downstream performance. It investigates whether aligning the vector representations through an affine transformation can provide that connection.

The authors find that affine alignment is fundamentally directional. Being able to align one encoder to another does not make similarity a symmetric relationship. Even so, the relationship remains informative about extrinsic similarity, meaning similarity in downstream-task performance. The paper develops useful bounds connecting this task-independent comparison to task-based behavior.

Experiments on datasets of natural-language representations support the connection. The authors also use affine similarity to define an order over pretrained encoders, beginning to describe how the broader space of encoders is structured. The significance is that representation comparison can reveal more than resemblance on a single benchmark: it can expose directional relationships with implications for downstream performance.
summary.tldr: Affine alignment provides a directional, task-independent comparison of language encoders that informs downstream-performance similarity.

title: On Affine Homotopy between Language Encoders

abstract: Diffusion models have emerged as effective distribution estimators in vision, language, and reinforcement learning, but their use as priors in downstream tasks poses an intractable posterior inference problem. This paper studies *amortized* sampling of the posterior over data, $\mathbf{x}\sim p^{\rm post}(\mathbf{x})\propto p(\mathbf{x})r(\mathbf{x})$, in a model that consists of a diffusion generative model prior $p(\mathbf{x})$ and a black-box constraint or likelihood function $r(\mathbf{x})$. We state and prove the asymptotic correctness of a data-free learning objective, *relative trajectory balance*, for training a diffusion model that samples from this posterior, a problem that existing methods solve only approximately or in restricted cases. Relative trajectory balance arises from the generative flow network perspective on diffusion models, which allows the use of deep reinforcement learning techniques to improve mode coverage. Experiments illustrate the broad potential of unbiased inference of arbitrary posteriors under diffusion priors: in vision (classifier guidance), language (infilling under a discrete diffusion LLM), and multimodal data (text-to-image generation). Beyond generative modeling, we apply relative trajectory balance to the problem of continuous control with a score-based behavior prior, achieving state-of-the-art results on benchmarks in offline reinforcement learning. Code is available at [this link](https://github.com/GFNOrg/diffusion-finetuning).

paragraphs: A diffusion model can describe plausible data, but using it to generate samples that also satisfy a separate constraint creates a difficult inference problem. The desired distribution combines the model’s prior with a black-box likelihood or constraint function. This paper studies how to train a sampler for that combined distribution, spreading the cost of inference across subsequent samples.

The proposed objective, relative trajectory balance, comes from viewing diffusion models through the framework of generative flow networks. It provides a data-free way to train a diffusion model toward the desired posterior. The authors prove asymptotic correctness: the guarantee concerns the limiting behavior of the method, rather than exact sampling after any finite amount of training. This perspective also enables reinforcement learning techniques intended to improve coverage of different modes.

Experiments cover classifier-guided images, language infilling, and text-to-image generation. The authors also apply the method to continuous control with a learned behavior prior, reporting state-of-the-art offline reinforcement learning results. Together, these findings support the approach’s potential across several forms of constrained generation and decision-making.
summary.tldr: Relative trajectory balance trains diffusion models to sample constrained posteriors with an asymptotic correctness guarantee and promising results across generation and control.

title: Amortizing intractable inference in diffusion models for vision, language, and control

abstract: Complex 3D scene understanding has gained increasing attention, with scene encoding strategies built on top of visual foundation models playing a crucial role in this success. However, the optimal scene encoding strategies for various scenarios remain unclear, particularly compared to their image-based counterparts. To address this issue, we present the first comprehensive study that probes various visual encoding models for 3D scene understanding, identifying the strengths and limitations of each model across different scenarios. Our evaluation spans seven vision foundation encoders, including image, video, and 3D foundation models. We evaluate these models in four tasks: Vision-Language Scene Reasoning, Visual Grounding, Segmentation, and Registration, each focusing on different aspects of scene understanding. Our evaluation yields key intriguing findings: Unsupervised image foundation models demonstrate superior overall performance, video models excel in object-level tasks, diffusion models benefit geometric tasks, language-pretrained models show unexpected limitations in language-related tasks, and the mixture-of-vision-expert (MoVE) strategy leads to consistent performance improvement. These insights challenge some conventional understandings, provide novel perspectives on leveraging visual foundation models, and highlight the need for more flexible encoder selection in future vision-language and scene understanding tasks.

paragraphs: Lexicon3D investigates which visual foundation encoders are useful for understanding complex three-dimensional scenes. Scene encoding determines the visual information available to later tasks, but the best choices across different scenarios remain unclear. The paper addresses this through a comparative study of seven encoders drawn from image, video, and 3D foundation models.

The evaluation covers vision-language scene reasoning, visual grounding, segmentation, and registration. These tasks test different aspects of scene understanding, allowing the authors to examine whether an encoder’s strengths carry across uses. They find that unsupervised image models perform best overall, video models excel at object-level tasks, and diffusion models are beneficial for geometric tasks.

The study also finds unexpected limitations for language-pretrained encoders on language-related tasks. Combining visual experts through the MoVE strategy produces consistent performance improvements in the evaluation. These findings support selecting encoders according to the demands of a scene-understanding task and exploring combinations of their strengths, rather than assuming that a model’s pretraining category alone predicts its suitability.
summary.tldr: Lexicon3D compares seven visual encoders across four 3D scene tasks, finding task-specific strengths and consistent gains from combining visual experts.

title: Lexicon3D: Probing Visual Foundation Models for Complex 3D Scene Understanding

abstract: We study the geometry of conditional optimal transport (COT) and prove a dynamic formulation which generalizes the Benamou-Brenier Theorem. Equipped with these tools, we propose a simulation-free flow-based method for conditional generative modeling. Our method couples an arbitrary source distribution to a specified target distribution through a triangular COT plan, and a conditional generative model is obtained by approximating the geodesic path of measures induced by this COT plan. Our theory and methods are applicable in infinite-dimensional settings, making them well suited for a wide class of Bayesian inverse problems. Empirically, we demonstrate that our method is competitive on several challenging conditional generation tasks, including an infinite-dimensional inverse problem.

paragraphs: Conditional generative modeling aims to produce samples that agree with specified conditioning information. This paper studies that task through conditional optimal transport, which describes how to couple source and target distributions while respecting the conditional structure. Its theoretical contribution is a dynamic formulation that extends the Benamou-Brenier theorem to this setting.

The formulation supports a simulation-free method based on flows. The method first connects an arbitrary source distribution to the specified target through a triangular conditional transport plan. It then learns to approximate the geodesic path of distributions induced by that plan. In this construction, the transport plan determines the route through distribution space that the conditional generator approximates.

Both the theory and the method apply in infinite-dimensional settings, making the approach relevant to a broad class of Bayesian inverse problems. The experiments include such an inverse problem alongside other challenging conditional generation tasks. The reported outcome is competitive performance, supporting the proposed connection between transport geometry and practical conditional generation without claiming universal superiority.
summary.tldr: A dynamic theory of conditional optimal transport yields a simulation-free generative method that also applies to infinite-dimensional inverse problems.

title: Dynamic Conditional Optimal Transport through Simulation-Free Flows

abstract: Transformer-based diffusion models have achieved significant advancements across a variety of generative tasks. However, producing high-quality outputs typically necessitates large transformer models, which result in substantial training and inference overhead. In this work, we investigate an alternative approach involving multiple experts for denoising, and introduce RemixDiT, a novel method designed to enhance output quality at a low cost. The goal of RemixDiT is to craft N diffusion experts for different denoising timesteps, yet without the need for expensive training of N independent models. To achieve this, RemixDiT employs K basis models (where K < N) and utilizes learnable mixing coefficients to adaptively craft expert models. This design offers two significant advantages: first, although the total model size is increased, the model produced by the mixing operation shares the same architecture as a plain model, making the overall model as efficient as a standard diffusion transformer. Second, the learnable mixing adaptively allocates model capacity across timesteps, thereby effectively improving generation quality. Experiments conducted on the ImageNet dataset demonstrate that RemixDiT achieves promising results compared to standard diffusion transformers and other multiple-expert methods.

RemixDiT explores whether different denoising timesteps can benefit from specialized experts without requiring a separately trained transformer for every expert. The method starts with K basis models and learns mixing coefficients that construct N experts, where K is smaller than N. These mixtures adapt model capacity to different denoising timesteps. Although storing the collection increases total model size, each constructed expert retains the architecture of a standard diffusion transformer. This preserves the computational form of the model used for denoising.

Experiments on ImageNet report promising results relative to standard diffusion transformers and other multiple-expert methods. The findings support learned model mixing as a way to obtain timestep-specific behavior without independently training every expert. The efficiency claim concerns the mixed model's standard architecture; the paper explicitly acknowledges that the overall collection of model parameters is larger.
summary.tldr: RemixDiT learns to mix a smaller set of basis models into timestep-specific diffusion experts, improving generation while retaining a standard expert architecture.

title: Remix-DiT: Mixing Diffusion Transformers for Multi-Expert Denoising

abstract: Molecular docking, a technique for predicting ligand binding poses, is crucial in structure-based drug design for understanding protein-ligand interactions. Recent advancements in docking methods, particularly those leveraging geometric deep learning (GDL), have demonstrated significant efficiency and accuracy advantages over traditional sampling methods. Despite these advancements, current methods are often tailored for specific docking settings, and limitations such as the neglect of protein side-chain structures, difficulties in handling large binding pockets, and challenges in predicting physically valid structures exist. To accommodate various docking settings and achieve accurate, efficient, and physically reliable docking, we propose a novel two-stage docking framework, DeltaDock, consisting of pocket prediction and site-specific docking. We innovatively reframe the pocket prediction task as a pocket-ligand alignment problem rather than direct prediction in the first stage. Then we follow a bi-level coarse-to-fine iterative refinement process to perform site-specific docking. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the superior performance of DeltaDock. Notably, in the blind docking setting, DeltaDock achieves a 31\% relative improvement over the docking success rate compared with the previous state-of-the-art GDL model DiffDock. With the consideration of physical validity, this improvement increases to about 300\%.

summary.tldr: DeltaDock combines pocket–ligand alignment with iterative pose refinement to improve docking accuracy and physical validity.

title: DeltaDock: A Unified Framework for Accurate, Efficient, and Physically Reliable Molecular Docking

abstract: We introduce $r$-loopy Weisfeiler-Leman ($r$-$\ell$WL), a novel hierarchy of graph isomorphism tests and a corresponding GNN framework, $r$-$\ell$MPNN, that can count cycles up to length $r{+}2$. Most notably, we show that $r$-$\ell$WL can count homomorphisms of cactus graphs. This extends 1-WL, which can only count homomorphisms of trees and, in fact, is incomparable to $k$-WL for any fixed $k$. We empirically validate the expressive and counting power of $r$-$\ell$MPNN on several synthetic datasets and demonstrate the scalability and strong performance on various real-world datasets, particularly on sparse graphs.

paragraphs: Graph-learning methods differ in which structural patterns they can distinguish and count. This paper introduces the r-loopy Weisfeiler-Leman hierarchy of graph isomorphism tests and a corresponding message-passing neural-network framework. The construction explicitly expands the treatment of loops, enabling the associated framework to count cycles of length up to r plus two.

A central theoretical result is the ability of r-loopy Weisfeiler-Leman to count homomorphisms of cactus graphs. This extends the tree-homomorphism counting capability of ordinary 1-WL. The proposed hierarchy is also incomparable to k-WL for any fixed k. That distinction matters because it places the contribution outside a simple claim of being uniformly stronger or weaker than one fixed level of the established hierarchy.

The authors test the corresponding neural networks on synthetic datasets to validate their expressive and counting capabilities. Experiments on real-world datasets also show scalability and strong performance, particularly for sparse graphs. The work connects a formal expansion in graph-pattern counting with a neural architecture whose practical behavior is evaluated on both controlled and real data.
summary.tldr: A loopy Weisfeiler-Leman hierarchy and matching graph networks extend structural counting to cycles and cactus-graph homomorphisms.

title: Weisfeiler and Leman Go Loopy: A New Hierarchy for Graph Representational Learning

abstract: The in-context learning (ICL) capability of pre-trained models based on the transformer architecture has received growing interest in recent years. While theoretical understanding has been obtained for ICL in reinforcement learning (RL), the previous results are largely confined to the single-agent setting. This work proposes to further explore the in-context learning capabilities of pre-trained transformer models in competitive multi-agent games, i.e., in-context game-playing (ICGP). Focusing on the classical two-player zero-sum games, theoretical guarantees are provided to demonstrate that pre-trained transformers can provably learn to approximate Nash equilibrium in an in-context manner for both decentralized and centralized learning settings. As a key part of the proof, constructional results are established to demonstrate that the transformer architecture is sufficiently rich to realize celebrated multi-agent game-playing algorithms, in particular, decentralized V-learning and centralized VI-ULCB.

This paper extends the analysis to competitive interaction, focusing on classical two-player zero-sum games.

The contribution is a theoretical demonstration of capability in the analyzed game settings, supporting a broader understanding of in-context learning when another strategic agent influences the problem.
summary.tldr: The paper proves that pretrained Transformers can learn approximate Nash equilibria in context for analyzed two-player zero-sum games.

title: Transformers as Game Players: Provable In-context Game-playing Capabilities of Pre-trained Models

abstract: Motivated by the recent discovery of a statistical and computational reduction from contextual bandits to offline regression \citep{simchi2020bypassing}, we address the general (stochastic) Contextual Markov Decision Process (CMDP) problem with horizon $H$ (as known as CMDP with $H$ layers). In this paper, we introduce a reduction from CMDPs to offline density estimation under the realizability assumption, i.e., a model class $\mathcal{M}$ containing the true underlying CMDP is provided in advance. We develop an efficient, statistically near-optimal algorithm requiring only $O(H \log T)$ calls to an offline density estimation algorithm (or oracle) across all $T$ rounds. This number can be further reduced to $O(H \log \log T)$ if $T$ is known in advance. Our results mark the first efficient and near-optimal reduction from CMDPs to offline density estimation without imposing any structural assumptions on the model class. A notable feature of our algorithm is the design of a layerwise exploration-exploitation tradeoff tailored to address the layerwise structure of CMDPs. Additionally, our algorithm is versatile and applicable to pure exploration tasks in reward-free reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Contextual Markov decision processes extend decision-making across multiple stages, so exploration must account for how actions affect later opportunities. This paper reduces learning in these processes to calls to an offline density-estimation procedure. Its central assumption is realizability: the supplied model class must contain the true underlying contextual decision process.

For a horizon of H stages and T rounds, the algorithm requires O(H log T) calls to the estimation oracle. If T is known beforehand, this falls to O(H log log T). The algorithm is described as efficient and statistically near-optimal, without additional structural assumptions on the model class beyond the stated realizability requirement.

A key design choice is to manage exploration and exploitation separately across the process’s layers, matching the algorithm to the staged structure of the problem. The approach also applies to pure exploration in reward-free reinforcement learning. The contribution is a reduction that combines strong statistical performance with relatively few oracle calls, making offline density estimation a reusable component for sequential learning.
summary.tldr: Under realizability, a layerwise exploration strategy reduces contextual MDP learning to few offline density-estimation calls with near-optimal statistical performance.

title: Offline Oracle-Efficient Learning for Contextual MDPs via Layerwise Exploration-Exploitation Tradeoff

abstract: Selecting appropriate hyperparameters is crucial for unlocking the full potential of advanced unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) methods in unlabeled target domains. Although this challenge remains under-explored, it has recently garnered increasing attention with the proposals of various model selection methods. Reliable model selection should maintain performance across diverse UDA methods and scenarios, especially avoiding highly risky worst-case selections—selecting the model or hyperparameter with the worst performance in the pool.\textit{Are existing model selection methods reliable and versatile enough for different UDA tasks?} In this paper, we provide a comprehensive empirical study involving 8 existing model selection approaches to answer this question. Our evaluation spans 12 UDA methods across 5 diverse UDA benchmarks and 5 popular UDA scenarios.Surprisingly, we find that none of these approaches can effectively avoid the worst-case selection. In contrast, a simple but overlooked ensemble-based selection approach, which we call EnsV, is both theoretically and empirically certified to avoid the worst-case selection, ensuring high reliability. Additionally, EnsV is versatile for various practical but challenging UDA scenarios, including validation of open-partial-set UDA and source-free UDA.Finally, we call for more attention to the reliability of model selection in UDA: avoiding the worst-case is as significant as achieving peak selection performance and should not be overlooked when developing new model selection methods. Code is available at https://github.com/LHXXHB/EnsV.

paragraphs: Unsupervised domain adaptation requires choosing models and hyperparameters without labeled examples from the target domain. A selection method therefore needs to do more than occasionally identify a strong candidate: it should also avoid selecting the worst-performing option in the available pool.

The paper evaluates eight existing selection approaches across 12 adaptation methods, five benchmarks, and five scenarios. None of those approaches effectively avoids worst-case selection in the study. This makes reliability a distinct concern alongside the usual goal of achieving high selected-model performance, especially when a selection rule must work across different adaptation methods and settings.

They also show its versatility in challenging settings, including open-partial-set and source-free adaptation. The contribution combines a broad evaluation of current practices with a certified baseline. Its central recommendation is to evaluate protection against disastrous choices alongside peak selection performance when developing future methods.
summary.tldr: A broad study exposes worst-case failures in domain-adaptation model selection and presents EnsV as a theoretically and empirically certified alternative.

title: Towards Reliable Model Selection for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation: An Empirical Study and A Certified Baseline

abstract: We present CrypticBio, the largest publicly available multimodal dataset of visually confusing species, specifically curated to support the development of AI models in the context of biodiversity applications. Visually confusing or cryptic species are groups of two or more taxa that are nearly indistinguishable based on visual characteristics alone. While much existing work addresses taxonomic identification in a broad sense, datasets that directly address the morphological confusion of cryptic species are small, manually curated, and target only a single taxon. Thus, the challenge of identifying such subtle differences in a wide range of taxa remains unaddressed. Curated from real-world trends in species misidentification among community annotators of iNaturalist, CrypticBio contains 52K unique cryptic groups spanning 67K species represented in 166 million images. Records in the dataset include research-grade image annotations—scientific, multicultural, and multilingual species terminology, hierarchical taxonomy, spatiotemporal context, and associated cryptic groups. To facilitate easy subset curation from CrypticBio, we provide an open-source pipeline, CrypticBio-Curate. The multimodal design of the dataset provides complementary cues such as spatiotemporal context that support the identification of cryptic species. To highlight the importance of the dataset, we benchmark a suite of state-of-the-art foundation models across CrypticBio subsets of common, unseen, endangered, and invasive species, and demonstrate the substantial impact of spatiotemporal context on vision-language zero-shot learning for cryptic species. By introducing CrypticBio, we aim to catalyze progress toward real-world-ready fine-grained species classification models for biodiversity monitoring capable of handling the nuanced challenges of species ambiguity. The data and the code are publicly available in the project website https://georgianagmanolache.github.io/crypticbio.

title: CrypticBio: A Large Multimodal Dataset for Visually Confusing Species

abstract: We introduce BikeBench, an engineering design benchmark for evaluating generative models on problems with multiple real-world objectives and constraints. As generative AI's reach continues to grow, evaluating its capability to understand physical laws, human guidelines, and hard constraints grows increasingly important. Engineering product design lies at the intersection of these difficult tasks, providing new challenges for AI capabilities. BikeBench evaluates AI models' capabilities to generate bicycle designs that not only resemble the dataset, but meet specific performance objectives and constraints. To do so, BikeBench quantifies a variety of human-centered and multiphysics performance characteristics, such as aerodynamics, ergonomics, structural mechanics, human-rated usability, and similarity to subjective text or image prompts. Supporting the benchmark are several datasets of simulation results, a dataset of 10,000 human-rated bicycle assessments, and a synthetically generated dataset of 1.6M designs, each with a parametric, CAD/XML, SVG, and PNG representation. BikeBench is uniquely configured to evaluate tabular generative models, large language models (LLMs), design optimization, and hybrid algorithms side-by-side. Our experiments indicate that LLMs and tabular generative models fall short of hybrid GenAI+optimization algorithms in design quality, constraint satisfaction, and similarity scores, suggesting significant room for improvement. We hope that BikeBench, a first-of-its-kind benchmark, will help catalyze progress in generative AI for constrained multi-objective engineering design problems. We provide code, data, an interactive leaderboard, and other resources at https://github.com/Lyleregenwetter/BikeBench.

It brings together requirements involving physical behavior, human use, and subjective preferences, making the task broader than reproducing the appearance or statistical patterns of existing designs.

Each synthetic design has parametric, CAD/XML, SVG, and PNG representations, supporting evaluation across different kinds of modeling systems.

In the reported experiments, combinations of generative AI and optimization outperform language models and tabular generators on design quality, constraint satisfaction, and similarity scores. The findings suggest that combining generation with optimization is valuable in these tested design tasks, while exposing substantial room for improvement in constrained engineering generation.
summary.tldr: BikeBench tests bicycle generation against engineering and human requirements, with hybrid generation-and-optimization methods leading the reported comparisons.

title: BikeBench: A Bicycle Design Benchmark for Generative Models with Objectives and Constraints

abstract: The estimation of optical flow and 6-DoF ego-motion—two fundamental tasks in 3-D vision—has typically been addressed independently. For neuromorphic vision (e.g., event cameras), however, the lack of robust data association makes solving the two problems separately an ill-posed challenge, especially in the absence of supervision via ground truth. Existing works mitigate this ill-posedness by either enforcing the smoothness of the flow field via an explicit variational regularizer or leveraging explicit structure-and-motion priors in the parametrization to improve event alignment. The former notably introduces bias in results and computational overhead, while the latter—which parametrizes the optical flow in terms of the scene depth and the camera motion—often converges to suboptimal local minima. To address these issues, we propose an unsupervised pipeline that jointly optimizes egomotion and flow via implicit spatial-temporal and geometric regularization. First, by modeling camera's egomotion as a continuous spline and optical flow as an implicit neural representation, our method inherently embeds spatial-temporal coherence through inductive biases. Second, we incorporate structure-and-motion priors through differential geometric constraints, bypassing explicit depth estimation while maintaining rigorous geometric consistency. As a result, our framework (called \textbf{E-MoFlow}) unifies egomotion and optical flow estimation via implicit regularization under a fully unsupervised paradigm. Experiments demonstrate its versatility to general 6-DoF motion scenarios, achieving state-of-the-art performance among unsupervised methods and competitive even with supervised approaches. Code will be released upon acceptance.

Experiments demonstrate its versatility to general 6-DoF motion scenarios, achieving state-of-the-art performance among unsupervised methods and competitive even with supervised approaches. Code will be released upon acceptance.

paragraphs: E-MoFlow jointly estimates camera motion and optical flow from event-camera data without ground-truth supervision. Optical flow describes apparent image motion, while egomotion describes the camera’s own movement. The paper argues that solving these separately is particularly difficult when reliable associations between events are unavailable.

The method builds coherence into its representations. Camera motion follows a continuous spline, and optical flow is represented by a neural function, giving both estimates spatial or temporal structure through their modeling choices. It also applies differential geometric constraints that connect scene structure and motion. These constraints maintain geometric consistency without requiring explicit depth estimation.

This combination addresses weaknesses identified in earlier approaches: explicit flow-smoothing penalties can introduce bias and computation, while directly expressing flow through depth and camera motion can become trapped in suboptimal solutions. Experiments cover general motion with six degrees of freedom. E-MoFlow achieves the strongest reported performance among unsupervised methods in those experiments and remains competitive with supervised approaches, supporting joint estimation through implicit regularization.
summary.tldr: E-MoFlow jointly learns camera motion and optical flow from event data using structured representations and geometric constraints without supervision.

title: E-MoFlow: Learning Egomotion and Optical Flow from Event Data via Implicit Regularization

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) has demonstrated a promising future in privacy-friendly collaboration but it faces the data heterogeneity problem. Knowledge Distillation (KD) can serve as an effective method to address this issue. However, challenges arise from the unreliability of existing distillation methods in multi-domain scenarios. Prevalent distillation solutions primarily aim to fit the distributions of the global model directly by minimizing forward Kullback-Leibler divergence (KLD). This results in significant bias when the outputs of the global model are multi-peaked, which indicates the unreliability of the distillation pathway. Meanwhile, cross-domain update conflicts can notably reduce the accuracy of the global model (teacher model) in certain domains, reflecting the unreliability of the teacher model in these domains. In this work, we propose DKDR (Dynamic Knowledge Distillation for Reliability in Federated Learning), which dynamically assigns weights to forward and reverse KLD based on knowledge discrepancies. This enables clients to fit the outputs from the teacher precisely. Moreover, we use knowledge decoupling to identify domain experts, thus clients can acquire reliable domain knowledge from experts. Empirical results from single-domain and multi-domain image classification tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method and the efficiency of its key modules. The code is available at https://github.com/YueyangYuan/DKDR.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets clients collaborate, but differences between their data can make shared knowledge unreliable. This paper identifies two problems with using knowledge distillation to address those differences. Directly matching a global model through forward Kullback–Leibler divergence can introduce substantial bias when its outputs have multiple peaks. Meanwhile, conflicting updates from different domains can make the global teacher inaccurate in particular domains.

DKDR addresses the matching problem by dynamically balancing forward and reverse Kullback–Leibler divergence according to discrepancies in knowledge. This changes how clients fit the teacher’s outputs instead of relying on one fixed direction of comparison. To address the teacher’s reliability, the framework also decouples knowledge to identify domain experts from which clients can obtain more reliable domain-specific information.

The two components target different weaknesses: the route by which knowledge is transferred and the source supplying that knowledge. Experiments on single-domain and multi-domain image classification support the effectiveness of DKDR and the efficiency of its key modules. The findings connect reliable distillation with both adaptive output matching and domain-sensitive teacher selection.
summary.tldr: DKDR improves federated distillation by adapting its distribution-matching objective and drawing domain knowledge from identified experts.

title: DKDR: Dynamic Knowledge Distillation for Reliability in Federated Learning

abstract: Unsupervised and open-vocabulary 3D object detection has recently gained attention, particularly in autonomous driving, where reducing annotation costs and recognizing unseen objects are critical for both safety and scalability. However, most existing approaches uniformly annotate 3D bounding boxes, ignore objects’ physical states, and require multiple self-training iterations for annotation refinement, resulting in suboptimal quality and substantial computational overhead. To address these challenges, we propose OpenBox, a two-stage automatic annotation pipeline that leverages a 2D vision foundation model. In the first stage, OpenBox associates instance-level cues from 2D images processed by a vision foundation model with the corresponding 3D point clouds via context-aware refinement. In the second stage, it categorizes instances by rigidity and motion state, then generates adaptive bounding boxes with class-specific size statistics. As a result, OpenBox produces high-quality 3D bounding box annotations without requiring self-training. Experiments on the Waymo Open Dataset (WOD), the Lyft Level 5 Perception dataset, and the nuScenes dataset demonstrate improved accuracy and efficiency over baselines.

paragraphs: Automatically creating three-dimensional bounding boxes can reduce annotation costs in autonomous driving and support recognition of previously unseen objects. Existing approaches often treat objects uniformly and refine annotations through repeated self-training. OpenBox addresses these issues with a two-stage pipeline that uses a two-dimensional vision foundation model and accounts for objects’ physical states.

The first stage associates instance-level cues extracted from images with corresponding three-dimensional point clouds. Context-aware refinement improves this association between image evidence and spatial data. The second stage categorizes instances according to rigidity and motion state, then generates adaptive bounding boxes using class-specific size statistics. These distinctions let the annotation process respond to differences between the objects it encounters.

OpenBox produces its annotations without self-training, removing the need for repeated annotation-refinement cycles of that kind. Experiments on the Waymo Open Dataset, Lyft Level 5 Perception, and nuScenes report improvements in accuracy and efficiency over baselines. The results support combining foundation-model image cues with physical-state-aware box generation for automatic 3D annotation.
summary.tldr: OpenBox creates 3D bounding-box annotations by connecting image cues to point clouds and adapting boxes to object rigidity and motion.

title: OpenBox: Annotate Any Bounding Boxes in 3D

abstract: Despite the rapid advancement of LLM-based agents, the reliable evaluation of their safety and security remains a significant challenge. Existing rule-based or LLM-based evaluators often miss dangers in agents' step-by-step actions, overlook subtle meanings, fail to see how small issues compound, and get confused by unclear safety or security rules. To overcome this evaluation crisis, we introduce AgentAuditor, a universal, training-free, memory-augmented reasoning framework that empowers LLM evaluators to emulate human expert evaluators. AgentAuditor constructs an experiential memory by having an LLM adaptively extract structured semantic features (e.g., scenario, risk, behavior) and generate associated chain-of-thought reasoning traces for past interactions. A multi-stage, context-aware retrieval-augmented generation process then dynamically retrieves the most relevant reasoning experiences to guide the LLM evaluator's assessment of new cases. Moreover, we developed ASSEBench, the first benchmark designed to check how well LLM-based evaluators can spot both safety risks and security threats. ASSEBench comprises 2293 meticulously annotated interaction records, covering 15 risk types across 29 application scenarios. A key feature of ASSEBench is its nuanced approach to ambiguous risk situations, employing "Strict" and "Lenient" judgment standards. Experiments demonstrate that AgentAuditor not only consistently improves the evaluation performance of LLMs across all benchmarks but also sets a new state-of-the-art in LLM-as-a-judge for agent safety and security, achieving human-level accuracy. Our work is openly accessible at https://github.com/Astarojth/AgentAuditor.

paragraphs: Evaluating an agent requires understanding how its actions unfold, including subtle risks and problems that accumulate across steps. AgentAuditor tackles weaknesses in automated evaluators by giving a language model access to structured experience from previous interactions. The framework requires no training and aims to make judgments more like those of human experts.

To construct its memory, an LLM extracts features such as the scenario, risk, and behavior, alongside reasoning traces associated with past cases. A multistage retrieval process then selects relevant experiences for a new interaction. This makes earlier assessments available as context for evaluating the current case, with retrieval guided by the situation being assessed.

The paper also introduces ASSEBench, containing 2,293 annotated interactions spanning 15 risk types and 29 application scenarios. Its strict and lenient standards explicitly address ambiguous cases. Experiments report improved evaluation performance across all tested benchmarks and human-level accuracy. These findings concern the quality of the evaluator's judgments; the framework's contribution is better assessment of agent safety and security.
summary.tldr: AgentAuditor uses retrieved reasoning experiences to improve agent safety and security evaluations, achieving reported human-level accuracy.

title: AgentAuditor: Human-level Safety and Security Evaluation for LLM Agents

abstract: World models have become indispensable tools for embodied intelligence, serving as powerful simulators capable of generating realistic robotic videos while addressing critical data scarcity challenges. However, current embodied world models exhibit limited physical awareness, particularly in modeling 3D geometry and motion dynamics, resulting in unrealistic video generation for contact-rich robotic scenarios. In this paper, we present RoboScape, a unified physics-informed world model that jointly learns RGB video generation and physics knowledge within an integrated framework. We introduce two key physics-informed joint training tasks: temporal depth prediction that enhances 3D geometric consistency in video rendering, and keypoint dynamics learning that implicitly encodes physical properties (e.g., object shape and material characteristics) while improving complex motion modeling. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RoboScape generates videos with superior visual fidelity and physical plausibility across diverse robotic scenarios. We further validate its practical utility through downstream applications including robotic policy training with generated data and policy evaluation. Our work provides new insights for building efficient physics-informed world models to advance embodied intelligence research. Our code and demos are available at: https://github.com/tsinghua-fib-lab/RoboScape.

paragraphs: Robotic world models can generate videos that help address limited training data, but visually plausible scenes can still represent geometry or motion poorly. This is particularly problematic when robots make contact with objects. RoboScape combines video generation with learning signals intended to improve the model’s physical awareness.

The framework jointly trains RGB video generation with two additional tasks. Temporal depth prediction encourages geometric consistency as a scene changes over time. Keypoint dynamics learning improves motion modeling and implicitly encodes physical properties, including information associated with object shape and material characteristics. Both tasks are integrated into the same training framework as video generation.

Experiments report better visual fidelity and physical plausibility across diverse robotic scenarios. The authors also evaluate generated data for robot-policy training and use the world model for policy evaluation, demonstrating practical applications beyond judging videos by appearance. The findings support incorporating geometry and dynamics into world-model training so that generated robotic interactions can be more useful as well as more convincing.
summary.tldr: RoboScape jointly learns robotic video generation, temporal depth, and keypoint dynamics to improve visual quality and physical plausibility.

title: RoboScape: Physics-informed Embodied World Model

abstract: Traffic flow data are of great value in smart city applications. However, limited by data collection costs and privacy sensitivity, it is rather difficult to obtain large-scale traffic flow data. Therefore, various data generation methods have been proposed in the literature. Nevertheless, these methods often require data from a specific city for training and are difficult to directly apply to new cities lacking data. To address this problem, this paper proposes a retrieval-augmented diffusion generation model with representation alignment. We use data from multiple source cities for training, extract consistent representations across multiple cities, and leverage retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) technology to incorporate historical data from source cities under similar conditions into the condition, aiming to improve the accuracy of data generation in the target city. Experiments on four real-world datasets demonstrate that, compared with existing deep learning methods, our method achieves better cross-city transfer performance.

paragraphs: Traffic-flow data support smart-city applications, but collecting them at scale can be expensive and privacy-sensitive. Generating synthetic traffic data offers an alternative, yet methods trained for one city often struggle when applied to another city with little available data. This paper targets that transfer problem rather than treating each city as an independent training task.

The proposed model combines diffusion-based generation, representation alignment, and retrieval of historical examples. Training on multiple source cities helps it extract representations that are consistent across cities. During generation, it also retrieves source-city traffic records from similar conditions and incorporates them into the conditioning information used to generate data for the target city.

These components give the generator both shared patterns learned across cities and relevant historical examples for the current conditions. Experiments on four real-world datasets show better cross-city transfer than the existing deep-learning methods used in the comparisons. The reported finding supports combining aligned representations with retrieval as a way to improve traffic generation when city-specific data are limited.
summary.tldr: A diffusion model combines shared cross-city representations with retrieved traffic histories to improve generation for data-scarce cities.

title: Cross City Traffic Flow Generation via Retrieval Augmented Diffusion Model

abstract: Low-rank structure is a common implicit assumption in many modern reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms. For instance, reward-free and goal-conditioned RL methods often presume that the successor measure admits a low-rank representation. In this work, we challenge this assumption by first remarking that the successor measure itself is not approximately low-rank. Instead, we demonstrate that a low-rank structure naturally emerges in the shifted successor measure, which captures the system dynamics after bypassing a few initial transitions. We provide finite-sample performance guarantees for the entry-wise estimation of a low-rank approximation of the shifted successor measure from sampled entries. Our analysis reveals that both the approximation and estimation errors are primarily governed by a newly introduced quantitity: the spectral recoverability of the corresponding matrix. To bound this parameter, we derive a new class of functional inequalities for Markov chains that we call Type II Poincaré inequalities and from which we can quantify the amount of shift needed for effective low-rank approximation and estimation. This analysis shows in particular that the required shift depends on decay of the high-order singular values of the shifted successor measure and is hence typically small in practice. Additionally, we establish a connection between the necessary shift and the local mixing properties of the underlying dynamical system, which provides a natural way of selecting the shift. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings with experiments, and demonstrate that shifting the successor measure indeed leads to improved performance in goal-conditioned RL.

paragraphs: Many reinforcement-learning methods assume that a successor measure, which represents future system behavior, has a compact low-rank structure. This paper challenges that assumption for the measure itself. It shows that a low-rank structure instead emerges after shifting the measure to bypass a few initial transitions, changing what should be represented compactly.

The authors provide finite-sample guarantees for estimating entries of a low-rank approximation from sampled entries. Both approximation and estimation errors are governed mainly by a quantity they introduce as spectral recoverability. A further connection to local mixing properties provides a natural basis for choosing it. Experiments support the theory and show improved goal-conditioned reinforcement-learning performance. The contribution is therefore both a correction to a common representation assumption and a principled way to obtain a more suitable target.
summary.tldr: Bypassing initial transitions reveals a low-rank successor representation with estimation guarantees and demonstrated benefits for goal-conditioned reinforcement learning.

title: Shift Before You Learn: Enabling Low-Rank Representations in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In recent times, the standard practice for developing MLLMs is to feed features from vision encoder(s) into the LLM and train with natural language supervision. This approach often causes models to lean towards language comprehension and undermine the rich visual perception signals present in the data, which are critical for tasks involving spatial reasoning in the domain of embodied AI and robotics. Is it possible to optimize both at the same time? In this work, we propose VisPer-LM, the first approach that infuses visual perception knowledge from expert vision encoders into the LLM's (of an MLLM) hidden representations. We start by investigating MLLMs trained solely with natural language supervision and identify a positive correlation between the quality of visual representations within these models and their downstream performance. Given this insight, we formulate the objective during the pretraining stage in MLLMs as a coupled optimization of predictive visual embedding and next (text) token prediction. Moreover, through extensive probing, we observe improved visual representation quality due to embedding optimization, underscoring the effectiveness of our probing setup. We demonstrate that our VisPer-LM outperforms the single and multi-encoder baselines, proving our approach's superiority over explicitly feeding the corresponding features to the LLM. In particular, VisPer-LM boosts performance by an average margin of up to 2.5% on various benchmarks, with a notable improvement of 8.7% on the Depth task in CV-Bench.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models commonly receive visual features but learn mainly through text supervision. The authors argue that this can favor language understanding while underusing visual information needed for spatial reasoning. They first examine existing models and find a positive association between the quality of their internal visual representations and their downstream performance.

VisPer-LM responds by teaching the language model’s hidden representations to capture knowledge from expert vision encoders. During pretraining, the model learns both to predict visual embeddings and to predict the next text token. This makes visual representation quality an explicit training objective, giving perception a direct learning signal alongside the usual language objective.

Probing shows improved visual representations after embedding optimization. In the reported evaluations, VisPer-LM outperforms baselines using either one vision encoder or multiple encoders, including approaches that directly supply the corresponding features. The paper reports average improvements of up to 2.5% across benchmarks and an 8.7% improvement on CV-Bench’s Depth task. These results support explicitly training the internal representation of visual information.
summary.tldr: VisPer-LM jointly trains visual embedding prediction and text prediction to strengthen visual representations inside multimodal language models.

title: Elevating Visual Perception in Multimodal LLMs with Visual Embedding Distillation

abstract: Deep model merging represents an emerging research direction that combines multiple fine-tuned models to harness their specialized capabilities across different tasks and domains. Current model merging techniques focus on merging all available models simultaneously, with weight interpolation-based methods being the predominant approach. However, these conventional approaches are not well-suited for scenarios where models become available sequentially, and they often suffer from high memory requirements and potential interference between tasks. In this study, we propose a training-free projection-based continual merging method that processes models sequentially through orthogonal projections of weight matrices and adaptive scaling mechanisms. Our method operates by projecting new parameter updates onto subspaces orthogonal to existing merged parameter updates while using an adaptive scaling mechanism to maintain stable parameter distances, enabling efficient sequential integration of task-specific knowledge. Our approach maintains constant memory complexity to the number of models, minimizes interference between tasks through orthogonal projections, and retains the performance of previously merged models through adaptive task vector scaling. Extensive experiments on CLIP-ViT models demonstrate that our method achieves a 5-8% average accuracy improvement while maintaining robust performance in different task orderings. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/tanganke/opcm .

paragraphs: Model merging combines separately fine-tuned models so that one model can draw on several specializations. Many methods assume all models are available together, which is awkward when new ones arrive over time. This paper proposes a training-free method that incorporates models sequentially while addressing memory growth and interference between tasks.

The method projects a new model’s parameter updates onto subspaces orthogonal to updates already incorporated into the merged model. This is intended to reduce conflict between new and existing task information. Adaptive scaling then controls parameter distances, helping preserve previously integrated capabilities as further models arrive. Projection and scaling therefore address different parts of the continual integration problem.

Memory complexity remains constant with respect to the number of merged models, making the approach suitable for a growing sequence. Experiments on CLIP-ViT models report a 5–8% improvement in average accuracy and robust performance under different task orderings. These findings support sequential merging as a practical alternative when specialized models become available incrementally and retraining is undesirable.
summary.tldr: Orthogonal projections and adaptive scaling merge models sequentially without retraining or memory growth proportional to the number of models.

title: Merging on the Fly Without Retraining: A Sequential Approach to Scalable Continual Model Merging

abstract: Linear TD($\lambda$) is one of the most fundamental reinforcement learning algorithms for policy evaluation. Previously, convergence rates are typically established under the assumption of linearly independent features, which does not hold in many practical scenarios. This paper instead establishes the first $L^2$ convergence rates for linear TD($\lambda$) operating under arbitrary features, without making any algorithmic modification or additional assumptions. Our results apply to both the discounted and average-reward settings. To address the potential non-uniqueness of solutions resulting from arbitrary features, we develop a novel stochastic approximation result featuring convergence rates to the solution set instead of a single point.

paragraphs: Linear temporal-difference learning evaluates a policy using a value estimate built from features. Existing convergence-rate analyses typically require those features to be linearly independent. That requirement excludes many practical representations in which some features overlap or can be expressed through combinations of others.

This paper establishes mean-square convergence rates for linear TD(lambda) with arbitrary features. It obtains these results without modifying the algorithm or adding assumptions to replace feature independence. The guarantees cover both discounted evaluation and the average-reward setting, extending the theoretical treatment across two formulations of policy evaluation.

The central mathematical challenge is that arbitrary features can produce multiple solutions. Instead of requiring convergence toward one particular parameter vector, the authors develop a stochastic-approximation result that measures convergence toward the solution set. This makes the target compatible with non-unique representations. The contribution is therefore a finite-sample account of the existing algorithm's behavior when redundant features prevent the usual single-solution analysis from applying.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes mean-square convergence rates for unmodified linear TD(lambda) with arbitrary, potentially redundant features.

title: Finite Sample Analysis of Linear Temporal Difference Learning with Arbitrary Features

abstract: While existing research on Multilingual CLIP (MCLIP) has prioritized model architecture design, our work uncovers a critical challenge in practical adaptation: fine-tuning MCLIP through a single source language risks diminishing its multilingual capabilities in downstream tasks due to cross-linguistic disparities. To bridge this gap, we systematically investigate the role of token similarity in cross-lingual transferability for image-text retrieval, establishing it as a key factor governing fine-tuning efficacy. Building on this insight, we propose two novel strategies to enhance efficiency while preserving multilinguality: 1) TaPCL dynamically optimizes training by prioritizing linguistically distant language pairs during corpus sampling, reducing redundant computation, and 2) CiPCL enriches the source corpus with multilingual key terms, enabling targeted knowledge transfer without reliance on exhaustive parallel data. By strategically balancing token similarity and domain-critical information, our methods significantly lower computational costs and mitigate over-dependence on parallel corpora. Experimental evaluations across diverse datasets validate the effectiveness and scalability of our framework, demonstrating robust multilingual retention across languages. This work provides a principled pathway for adapting MCLIP to real-world scenarios, where computational efficiency and cross-lingual robustness are paramount. Our codes are available at https://github.com/tiggers23/TaPCL-CiPCL.

Experimental evaluations across diverse datasets validate the effectiveness and scalability of our framework, demonstrating robust multilingual retention across languages. This work provides a principled pathway for adapting MCLIP to real-world scenarios, where computational efficiency and cross-lingual robustness are paramount. Our codes are available at https://github.com/tiggers23/TaPCL-CiPCL.

paragraphs: Adapting Multilingual CLIP for image-text retrieval using one source language can weaken its ability to work across other languages. This paper investigates that practical adaptation problem and identifies token similarity as a key factor in how effectively fine-tuning transfers across languages. The approach uses that relationship to guide where training effort should go.

The first strategy, TaPCL, changes corpus sampling to prioritize linguistically distant language pairs. Its purpose is to reduce redundant computation while emphasizing pairs that need more cross-language transfer. The second, CiPCL, adds multilingual key terms to the source corpus. This provides targeted information across languages without requiring exhaustive collections of parallel text.

Together, the strategies balance language similarity with information important to the downstream domain. Evaluations across diverse datasets report reduced computational costs, less dependence on parallel corpora, and robust retention of multilingual capability. The contribution is an adaptation strategy that treats language coverage as something to actively preserve during specialization, with evidence that this can be done efficiently.
summary.tldr: TaPCL and CiPCL use language-aware sampling and multilingual key terms to adapt MCLIP efficiently while preserving multilingual retrieval capabilities.

title: Efficiently Maintaining the Multilingual Capacity of MCLIP in Downstream Cross-Modal Retrieval Tasks

abstract: Multimodal language analysis is a rapidly evolving field that leverages multiple modalities to enhance the understanding of high-level semantics underlying human conversational utterances. Despite its significance, little research has investigated the capability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to comprehend cognitive-level semantics. In this paper, we introduce MMLA, a comprehensive benchmark specifically designed to address this gap. MMLA comprises over 61K multimodal utterances drawn from both staged and real-world scenarios, covering six core dimensions of multimodal semantics: intent, emotion, dialogue act, sentiment, speaking style, and communication behavior. We evaluate eight mainstream branches of LLMs and MLLMs using three methods: zero-shot inference, supervised fine-tuning, and instruction tuning. Extensive experiments reveal that even fine-tuned models achieve only about 60~70% accuracy, underscoring the limitations of current MLLMs in understanding complex human language. We believe that MMLA will serve as a solid foundation for exploring the potential of large language models in multimodal language analysis and provide valuable resources to advance this field. The datasets and code are open-sourced at https://github.com/thuiar/MMLA.

paragraphs: Understanding a conversation involves more than recognizing its words. A system may need to identify a speaker’s intention, emotional state, or communicative behavior from multiple kinds of information. MMLA is a benchmark designed to test whether language models and multimodal language models can interpret these higher-level meanings in conversational utterances.

The dataset contains more than 61,000 multimodal utterances from staged and real-world situations. It covers six dimensions: intent, emotion, dialogue act, sentiment, speaking style, and communication behavior. The authors evaluate eight mainstream model branches using zero-shot inference, supervised fine-tuning, and instruction tuning. These settings examine both existing model capabilities and what task-oriented training can add.

Even the fine-tuned models reach only about 60–70% accuracy in the reported experiments. That result indicates substantial remaining difficulty in the tested forms of conversational understanding, rather than establishing a universal ceiling for multimodal models. By releasing the data and code, the authors provide a shared basis for investigating these capabilities more systematically.
summary.tldr: MMLA tests six dimensions of conversational meaning across more than 61,000 multimodal utterances, with evaluated fine-tuned models reaching about 60–70% accuracy.

title: Can Large Language Models Help Multimodal Language Analysis? MMLA: A Comprehensive Benchmark

abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) exhibit exceptional energy efficiency on neuromorphic hardware due to their sparse activation patterns. However, conventional training methods based on surrogate gradients and Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT) not only lag behind Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) in performance, but also incur significant computational and memory overheads that grow linearly with the temporal dimension. To enable high-performance SNN training under limited computational resources, we propose an enhanced self-distillation framework, jointly optimized with rate-based backpropagation. Specifically, the firing rates of intermediate SNN layers are projected onto lightweight ANN branches, and high-quality knowledge generated by the model itself is used to optimize substructures through the ANN pathways. Unlike traditional self-distillation paradigms, we observe that low-quality self-generated knowledge may hinder convergence. To address this, we decouple the teacher signal into reliable and unreliable components, ensuring that only reliable knowledge is used to guide the optimization of the model. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, CIFAR10-DVS, and ImageNet demonstrate that our method reduces training complexity while achieving high-performance SNN training. Our code is available at https://github.com/Intelli-Chip-Lab/enhanced-self-distillation-framework-for-snn.
