paragraphs: Spiking neural networks can use energy efficiently on neuromorphic hardware because their activations are sparse. Training them remains expensive: conventional surrogate-gradient training with backpropagation through time incurs computation and memory costs that grow linearly with the temporal dimension. This paper seeks strong performance when training resources are limited.

The proposed framework combines self-distillation with rate-based backpropagation. It projects firing rates from intermediate spiking layers into lightweight artificial neural network branches. Knowledge produced by the model then guides its own substructures through those branches, providing an additional pathway for optimization within the training framework.

A key observation is that the model's own teaching signals are not uniformly useful: low-quality signals can hinder convergence. The authors separate reliable and unreliable components and use only the reliable portion to guide learning. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, CIFAR10-DVS, and ImageNet demonstrate reduced training complexity alongside high performance. The contribution ties efficiency to selective self-teaching, rather than assuming every self-generated prediction is a helpful training target.
summary.tldr: The framework trains spiking networks efficiently by combining rate-based backpropagation with reliable self-distillation signals routed through lightweight ANN branches.

title: Enhanced Self-Distillation Framework for Efficient Spiking Neural Network Training

abstract: Label shift adaptation aims to recover target class priors when the labelled source distribution $P$ and the unlabelled target distribution $Q$ share $P(X \mid Y) = Q(X \mid Y)$ but $P(Y) \neq Q(Y)$. Classical black‑box shift estimators invert an empirical confusion matrix of a frozen classifier, producing a brittle point estimate that ignores sampling noise and similarity among classes. We present Graph‑Smoothed Bayesian BBSE (GS‑B$^3$SE), a fully probabilistic alternative that places Laplacian–Gaussian priors on both target log‑priors and confusion‑matrix columns, tying them together on a label‑similarity graph. The resulting posterior is tractable with HMC or a fast block Newton–CG scheme. We prove identifiability, $N^{-1/2}$ contraction, variance bounds that shrink with the graph’s algebraic connectivity, and robustness to Laplacian misspecification. We also reinterpret GS‑B$^3$SE through information geometry, showing that it generalizes existing shift estimators.

paragraphs: Label shift means class frequencies change between source and target data while the distribution of inputs within each class stays the same. Estimating the new frequencies is difficult when target labels are unavailable. Classical black-box estimators invert an empirical confusion matrix from a frozen classifier, producing a point estimate that overlooks sampling uncertainty and relationships among classes.

The proposed Bayesian estimator models uncertainty in both target class proportions and the confusion matrix. It places Laplacian–Gaussian priors on target log-proportions and confusion-matrix columns, using a label-similarity graph to connect related quantities. The resulting posterior can be handled with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo or a faster block Newton–CG procedure.

The paper proves identifiability, contraction at an N-to-the-minus-one-half rate, and variance bounds that become smaller with greater algebraic connectivity of the graph. It also establishes robustness to Laplacian misspecification. An information-geometric interpretation shows how the method generalizes existing shift estimators. These guarantees give a theoretical account of uncertainty and graph-based smoothing within the stated label-shift setting.
summary.tldr: A graph-smoothed Bayesian label-shift estimator jointly models class proportions and classifier uncertainty, with theoretical estimation guarantees.

title: Graph–Smoothed Bayesian Black-Box Shift Estimator and Its Information Geometry

abstract: A key question in sequence modeling with neural networks is how to represent and learn highly nonlinear and probabilistic state dynamics. Operator theory views such dynamics as linear maps on Hilbert spaces containing mean embedding vectors of distributions, offering an appealing but currently overlooked perspective. We propose a new approach to sequence modeling based on an operator-theoretic view of a hidden Markov model (HMM). Instead of materializing stochastic recurrence, we embed the full sequence distribution as a tensor in the product Hilbert space. A generative process is then defined as maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) gradient flow in the space of sequences. To overcome challenges with large tensors and slow sampling convergence, we introduce spectral mean flows, a novel tractable algorithm integrating two core concepts. First, we propose a new neural architecture by leveraging spectral decomposition of linear operators to derive a scalable tensor network decomposition of sequence mean embeddings. Second, we extend MMD gradient flows to time-dependent Hilbert spaces and connect them to flow matching via the continuity equation, enabling simulation-free learning and faster sampling. We demonstrate competitive results on a range of time-series modeling datasets.

paragraphs: Spectral mean flows approach sequence modeling through representations of probability distributions. Operator theory describes nonlinear probabilistic dynamics using linear maps in a suitable Hilbert space. Building on this perspective for hidden Markov models, the paper embeds an entire sequence distribution as a tensor instead of explicitly constructing stochastic recurrence.

Generation is formulated as a maximum mean discrepancy gradient flow over sequences. Two computational problems then arise: the distribution tensors can become large, and sampling can converge slowly. The proposed algorithm addresses the first through spectral decomposition of linear operators, producing a scalable tensor-network representation of sequence mean embeddings.

For the second problem, the authors extend these gradient flows to time-dependent Hilbert spaces and connect them to flow matching through the continuity equation. This enables simulation-free learning and faster sampling. Experiments report competitive results across time-series modeling datasets. The contribution connects a distribution-level view of sequence dynamics with a tractable neural architecture and a more efficient generative procedure, making the operator-theoretic formulation usable for sequence modeling.
summary.tldr: Spectral mean flows combine operator-based sequence representations, tensor networks, and flow matching for tractable time-series generation.

title: Sequence Modeling with Spectral Mean Flows

abstract: Riemannian symmetric spaces (RSS) such as hyperbolic spaces and symmetric positive definite (SPD) manifolds have become popular spaces for representation learning. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for building discriminative neural networks on Siegel spaces, a family of RSS that is largely unexplored in machine learning tasks. For classification applications, one focus of recent works is the construction of multiclass logistic regression (MLR) and fully-connected (FC) layers for hyperbolic and SPD neural networks. Here we show how to build such layers for Siegel neural networks. Our approach relies on the quotient structure of those spaces and the notation of vector-valued distance on RSS. We demonstrate the relevance of our approach on two applications, i.e., radar signal classification and node classification. Our results successfully demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across all datasets.

paragraphs: Representation learning can place data in geometric spaces with structures different from ordinary Euclidean space. Hyperbolic spaces and manifolds of symmetric positive definite matrices are established examples. This paper develops discriminative neural networks on Siegel spaces, a family of Riemannian symmetric spaces that has received relatively little attention in machine learning.

The main construction supplies multiclass logistic regression and fully connected layers for these networks. Those layers provide core components for classification directly within the chosen geometry. The approach uses the quotient structure of Siegel spaces and vector-valued distance on Riemannian symmetric spaces, making the geometry part of how the network layers are defined.

The authors evaluate the resulting networks on radar signal classification and node classification. They report state-of-the-art performance across all datasets in their evaluation. These findings demonstrate the relevance of the proposed constructions in two application areas. The contribution is both mathematical and practical: it develops classification machinery for an underexplored geometric family and tests that machinery on classification tasks.
summary.tldr: The paper constructs classification layers for Siegel-space neural networks and reports state-of-the-art results on evaluated radar and node-classification datasets.

title: Siegel Neural Networks

abstract: Current text-to-image (T2I) generation models struggle to align spatial composition with the input text, especially in complex scenes. Even layout-based approaches yield suboptimal spatial control, as their generation process is decoupled from layout planning, making it difficult to refine the layout during synthesis. We present CoT-Diff, a framework that brings step-by-step CoT-style reasoning into T2I generation by tightly integrating Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM)-driven 3D layout planning with the diffusion process. CoT-Diff enables layout-aware reasoning inline within a single diffusion round: at each denoising step, the MLLM evaluates intermediate predictions, dynamically updates the 3D scene layout, and continuously guides the generation process. The updated layout is converted into semantic conditions and depth maps, which are fused into the diffusion model via a condition-aware attention mechanism, enabling precise spatial control and semantic injection. Experiments on 3D Scene benchmarks show that CoT-Diff significantly improves spatial alignment and compositional fidelity, and outperforms the state-of-the-art method by 34.7% in complex scene spatial accuracy, thereby validating the effectiveness of this entangled generation paradigm.

We present CoT-Diff, a framework that brings step-by-step CoT-style reasoning into T2I generation by tightly integrating Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM)-driven 3D layout planning with the diffusion process. paragraphs: Text-to-image models can struggle to place objects according to a prompt, especially in complicated scenes. Providing a layout helps, but planning that layout separately from image synthesis makes it difficult to revise the arrangement as the image develops. CoT-Diff connects those two processes throughout generation.

At each denoising step, a multimodal large language model examines intermediate image predictions and updates a three-dimensional scene layout. The revised layout becomes semantic conditions and depth maps, which enter the diffusion model through a condition-aware attention mechanism. This gives subsequent generation steps both information about scene content and guidance about spatial structure.

The step-by-step reasoning therefore takes place inside a single diffusion round, allowing planning to respond to the developing image. On 3D Scene benchmarks, the authors report improved spatial alignment and compositional fidelity, including a 34.7% improvement over the state-of-the-art method in complex-scene spatial accuracy. These results support tightly coupling layout refinement with synthesis for the evaluated spatial composition tasks.
summary.tldr: CoT-Diff repeatedly revises a 3D scene layout during diffusion to improve how faithfully generated images follow spatial instructions.

title: CoT-lized Diffusion: Let's Reinforce T2I Generation Step-by-step

abstract: Agricultural parcels serve as basic units for conducting agricultural practices and applications, which is vital for land ownership registration, food security assessment, soil erosion monitoring, etc. However, existing agriculture parcel extraction studies only focus on mid-resolution mapping or regular plain farmlands while lacking representation of complex terraced terrains due to the demands of precision agriculture. In this paper, we introduce a more fine-grained terraced parcel dataset named GTPBD (Global Terraced Parcel and Boundary Dataset), which is the first fine-grained dataset covering major worldwide terraced regions with more than 200,000 complex terraced parcels with manually annotation. GTPBD comprises 47,537 high-resolution images with three-level labels, including pixel-level boundary labels, mask labels, and parcel labels. It covers seven major geographic zones in China and transcontinental climatic regions around the world. Compared to the existing datasets, the GTPBD dataset brings considerable challenges due to the: (1) terrain diversity; (2) complex and irregular parcel objects; and (3) multiple domain styles. Our proposed GTPBD dataset is suitable for four different tasks, including semantic segmentation, edge detection, terraced parcel extraction and unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) tasks. Accordingly, we benchmark the GTPBD dataset on eight semantic segmentation methods, four edge extraction methods, three parcel extraction methods and five UDA methods, along with a multi-dimensional evaluation framework integrating pixel-level and object-level metrics. GTPBD fills a critical gap in terraced remote sensing research, providing a basic infrastructure for fine-grained agricultural terrain analysis and cross-scenario knowledge transfer. The code and data are available at https://github.com/Z-ZW-WXQ/GTPBD/.

title: GTPBD: A Fine-Grained Global Terraced Parcel and Boundary Dataset

abstract: We study offline imitation learning (IL) in cooperative multi-agent settings, where demonstrations have unlabeled mixed quality - containing both expert and suboptimal trajectories. Our proposed solution is structured in two stages: trajectory labeling and multi-agent imitation learning, designed jointly to enable effective learning from heterogeneous, unlabeled data. In the first stage, we combine advances in large language models and preference-based reinforcement learning to construct a progressive labeling pipeline that distinguishes expert-quality trajectories. In the second stage, we introduce MisoDICE, a novel multi-agent IL algorithm that leverages these labels to learn robust policies while addressing the computational complexity of large joint state-action spaces. By extending the popular single-agent DICE framework to multi-agent settings with a new value decomposition and mixing architecture, our method yields a convex policy optimization objective and ensures consistency between global and local policies. We evaluate MisoDICE on multiple standard multi-agent RL benchmarks and demonstrate superior performance, especially when expert data is scarce.

paragraphs: Cooperative agents learning from demonstrations may receive a mixture of expert and suboptimal behavior without quality labels. Treating all demonstrations equally can obscure which behavior is worth imitating. This paper develops a two-stage approach that jointly addresses the identification of expert-quality trajectories and the learning of coordinated policies from the resulting labels.

The first stage combines large language models with preference-based reinforcement learning in a progressive labeling pipeline. The second stage uses MisoDICE, a multi-agent imitation algorithm built to handle the large joint state-action spaces that arise when several agents act together. It extends the single-agent DICE framework through a new value-decomposition and mixing architecture.

The formulation yields a convex policy-optimization objective and ensures consistency between global and local policies. That connection matters because the agents' individual policies must agree with the collective behavior being learned. Evaluations on standard multi-agent reinforcement-learning benchmarks report superior performance, particularly when expert demonstrations are scarce, supporting the combined labeling and imitation approach for mixed-quality offline data.
summary.tldr: MisoDICE combines trajectory-quality labeling with coordinated imitation learning to use mixed-quality demonstrations effectively.

title: MisoDICE: Multi-Agent Imitation from Mixed-Quality Demonstrations

abstract: An effective approach to structure learning and parameter estimation for Gaussian graphical models is to impose a sparsity prior, such as a Laplace prior, on the entries of the precision matrix. Such an approach involves a hyperparameter that must be tuned to control the amount of sparsity. In this paper, we introduce a parameter-free method for estimating a precision matrix with sparsity that adapts to the data automatically. We achieve this by formulating a hierarchical Bayesian model of the precision matrix with a non-informative Jeffreys’ hyperprior. We also naturally enforce the symmetry and positive-definiteness constraints on the precision matrix by parameterizing it with the Cholesky decomposition. Experiments on simulated and real (cell signaling) data demonstrate that the proposed approach not only automatically adapts the sparsity of the model, but it also results in improved estimates of the precision matrix compared to the Laplace prior model with sparsity parameter chosen by cross-validation.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate a Gaussian graphical model while deciding how sparse its precision matrix should be. A common approach places a sparsity-promoting prior, such as a Laplace prior, on matrix entries. That approach requires choosing a hyperparameter that controls the amount of sparsity, making this choice part of the estimation problem.

The proposed method makes sparsity adapt automatically to the data through a hierarchical Bayesian model. It uses a non-informative Jeffreys’ hyperprior to avoid a separately tuned sparsity parameter. The precision matrix is represented through a Cholesky decomposition, which naturally enforces the symmetry and positive-definiteness constraints that a valid precision matrix must satisfy.

Experiments use both simulated data and real cell-signaling data. The method automatically adjusts sparsity and produces better precision-matrix estimates than the compared Laplace-prior model, whose sparsity parameter is selected by cross-validation. The findings therefore support both parts of the proposal: removing manual sparsity tuning and improving estimation in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical Bayesian model automatically adapts precision-matrix sparsity and improves estimates in simulated and cell-signaling experiments.

title: Adaptive Sparsity in Gaussian Graphical Models

abstract: Scaling up deep learning algorithms has been shown to lead to increased performance in benchmark tasks and to enable discovery of complex high-level features. Recent efforts to train extremely large networks (with over 1 billion parameters) have relied on cloud-like computing infrastructure and thousands of CPU cores. In this paper, we present technical details and results from our own system based on Commodity Off-The-Shelf High Performance Computing (COTS HPC) technology: a cluster of GPU servers with Infiniband interconnects and MPI. Our system is able to train 1 billion parameter networks on just 3 machines in a couple of days, and we show that it can scale to networks with over 11 billion parameters using just 16 machines. As this infrastructure is much more easily marshaled by others, the approach enables much wider-spread research with extremely large neural networks.

paragraphs: Training extremely large neural networks creates an infrastructure challenge as well as a learning challenge. The paper starts from evidence that scaling deep learning can improve benchmark performance and reveal complex features. Earlier billion-parameter training efforts had used cloud-like infrastructure with thousands of CPU cores, making comparable research difficult to organize.

The authors present a system built from commercially available high-performance computing components. It combines GPU servers, Infiniband connections, and MPI communication. The contribution includes technical details and training results, showing how this combination supports very large networks using a relatively small number of machines.

The system trains networks with one billion parameters on three machines in a couple of days and scales beyond eleven billion parameters on sixteen machines. These are concrete demonstrations of training capacity. Their significance is that researchers can potentially assemble the necessary infrastructure more readily, broadening access to experiments with extremely large networks. The reported achievement concerns the feasibility and scale of training on this hardware configuration.
summary.tldr: A cluster of commodity GPU servers trains billion-parameter networks with far fewer machines than the large CPU-based infrastructure described.

title: Deep learning with COTS HPC systems

abstract: As the central notion in semi-supervised learning, smoothness is often realized on a graph representation of the data. In this paper, we study two complementary dimensions of smoothness: its pointwise nature and probabilistic modeling. While no existing graph-based work exploits them in conjunction, we encompass both in a novel framework of Probabilistic Graph-based Pointwise Smoothness (PGP), building upon two foundational models of data closeness and label coupling. This new form of smoothness axiomatizes a set of probability constraints, which ultimately enables class prediction. Theoretically, we provide an error and robustness analysis of PGP. Empirically, we conduct extensive experiments to show the advantages of PGP.

paragraphs: Graph-based semi-supervised learning uses relationships among data points to help predict classes when labels are only partially available. Smoothness expresses how predictions should relate across that graph. This paper focuses on combining two aspects of smoothness: its behavior at individual points and an explicit probabilistic formulation.

The authors introduce Probabilistic Graph-based Pointwise Smoothness, abbreviated PGP. Its construction starts from models of data closeness and label coupling. These address related but distinct questions: how data points are connected, and how their labels are linked. The framework combines them into probability constraints that support class prediction.

The contribution is a joint treatment of pointwise smoothness and probabilistic modeling, which the authors identify as absent from existing graph-based work. They provide theoretical analyses of prediction error and robustness, alongside extensive experiments reporting advantages for PGP. This gives the framework both an analytical treatment and empirical support. Its significance is to make the local meaning of smoothness part of the probability model used for prediction.
summary.tldr: PGP combines pointwise smoothness and probability constraints to support graph-based semi-supervised classification.

title: Graph-based Semi-supervised Learning: Realizing Pointwise Smoothness Probabilistically

abstract: We formalize and illustrate the general concept of algorithmic anti-differentiation: given an algorithmic procedure, e.g., an approximation algorithm for which worst-case approximation guarantees are available or a heuristic that has been engineered to be practically-useful but for which a precise theoretical understanding is lacking, an algorithmic anti-derivative is a precise statement of an optimization problem that is exactly solved by that procedure. We explore this concept with a case study of approximation algorithms for finding locally-biased partitions in data graphs, demonstrating connections between min-cut objectives, a personalized version of the popular PageRank vector, and the highly effective "push" procedure for computing an approximation to personalized PageRank. We show, for example, that this latter algorithm solves (exactly, but implicitly) an l1-regularized l2-regression problem, a fact that helps to explain its excellent performance in practice. We expect that, when available, these implicit optimization problems will be critical for rationalizing and predicting the performance of many approximation algorithms on realistic data.

paragraphs: The paper asks a reverse question about algorithms: given a procedure, what optimization problem does it solve exactly? The authors call this algorithmic anti-differentiation. It can apply both to approximation algorithms with known worst-case guarantees and to practical heuristics whose behavior lacks a precise theoretical explanation.

The case study concerns locally biased partitions of graphs. The authors connect minimum-cut objectives, personalized PageRank, and the push procedure used to approximate personalized PageRank. Their key example shows that push implicitly solves an l1-regularized l2-regression problem exactly. Thus, a procedure understood as an approximation to one target can also be understood as an exact solution to a different objective.

Identifying this implicit objective helps explain the procedure's strong practical performance by exposing the optimization problem behind its operations. The broader proposed value is explanatory and predictive: when such objectives can be found, they may help researchers reason about approximation algorithms on realistic data. That broader promise is presented as an expectation.
summary.tldr: Algorithmic anti-differentiation reveals exact objectives behind approximation procedures, including an implicit regularized regression problem solved by PageRank push.

title: Anti-differentiating approximation algorithms:A case study with min-cuts, spectral, and flow

abstract: We introduce BilBOWA (Bilingual Bag-of-Words without Alignments), a simple and computationally-efficient model for learning bilingual distributed representations of words which can scale to large monolingual datasets and does not require word-aligned parallel training data. Instead it trains directly on monolingual data and extracts a bilingual signal from a smaller set of raw-text sentence-aligned data. This is achieved using a novel sampled bag-of-words cross-lingual objective, which is used to regularize two noise-contrastive language models for efficient cross-lingual feature learning. We show that bilingual embeddings learned using the proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art methods on a cross-lingual document classification task as well as a lexical translation task on the WMT11 data.

paragraphs: BilBOWA learns word vectors for two languages using large monolingual text collections alongside a smaller bilingual resource. Its training does not require individual words to be matched across languages. It does require sentence-aligned text, which supplies the connection between the two languages without specifying exactly which words translate one another.

The model combines two noise-contrastive language models with a sampled cross-language bag-of-words objective. The language models learn from monolingual data, while the additional objective regularizes them using the bilingual signal. In this way, sentence-level correspondence helps shape word representations across languages while the larger monolingual collections contribute information within each language.

The authors emphasize computational efficiency and the ability to scale to large monolingual datasets. They evaluate the resulting embeddings on cross-language document classification and lexical translation using WMT11 data, reporting improvements over state-of-the-art methods. These results show that the coarser sentence-alignment signal can support useful bilingual word representations in the tested tasks, without the word-level alignment requirement that the method was designed to remove.
summary.tldr: BilBOWA efficiently learns bilingual word vectors from monolingual text and sentence-aligned data without requiring word alignments.

title: BilBOWA: Fast Bilingual Distributed Representations without Word Alignments

abstract: Subspace clustering groups data into several lowrank subspaces. In this paper, we propose a theoretical framework to analyze a popular optimization-based algorithm, Sparse Subspace Clustering (SSC), when the data dimension is compressed via some random projection algorithms. We show SSC provably succeeds if the random projection is a subspace embedding, which includes random Gaussian projection, uniform row sampling, FJLT, sketching, etc. Our analysis applies to the most general deterministic setting and is able to handle both adversarial and stochastic noise. It also results in the first algorithm for privacy-preserved subspace clustering.

paragraphs: Subspace clustering groups observations according to the low-dimensional spaces they occupy. This paper asks when Sparse Subspace Clustering, an optimization-based method for this task, continues to work after the observations are compressed into fewer dimensions. The question connects the computational appeal of compression with the need to preserve the structure that determines the clusters.

The authors develop a theoretical framework in which a subspace embedding provides the key condition for success. Such a projection preserves the relevant subspace geometry. The analysis covers several projection approaches, including Gaussian projections, uniform row sampling, fast Johnson–Lindenstrauss transforms, and sketching. The guarantee is conditional on the embedding property, rather than a claim that arbitrary compression preserves clustering.

The framework treats the data in a deterministic setting and accommodates both adversarial and stochastic noise. This makes its scope broader than an analysis tied only to randomly generated data or one noise model. The authors also report that their analysis yields the first algorithm for subspace clustering with privacy preservation.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes conditions under which sparse subspace clustering succeeds on compressed, noisy data and derives a privacy-preserving algorithm.

title: A Deterministic Analysis of Noisy Sparse Subspace Clustering for Dimensionality-reduced Data

abstract: We develop a family of accelerated stochastic algorithms that optimize sums of convex functions. Our algorithms improve upon the fastest running time for empirical risk minimization (ERM), and in particular linear least-squares regression, across a wide range of problem settings. To achieve this, we establish a framework, based on the classical proximal point algorithm, useful for accelerating recent fast stochastic algorithms in a black-box fashion. Empirically, we demonstrate that the resulting algorithms exhibit notions of stability that are advantageous in practice. Both in theory and in practice, the provided algorithms reap the computational benefits of adding a large strongly convex regularization term, without incurring a corresponding bias to the original ERM problem.

paragraphs: Empirical risk minimization fits a model by minimizing an objective assembled from losses on training examples. This paper considers objectives that are sums of convex functions and develops accelerated stochastic algorithms for solving them. The reported running-time improvements apply across a broad range of settings, including the important case of linear least-squares regression.

The central idea is to use the classical proximal point approach as an acceleration framework around existing fast stochastic algorithms. Treating those algorithms as black boxes makes the framework a way to improve existing optimization methods without requiring a separate redesign of their internal workings. Approximate proximal computations provide the organizing principle for this family of algorithms.

A key result is that the methods obtain the computational advantages of adding a large strongly convex regularization term without introducing the corresponding bias into the original learning problem. This separates an optimization aid from a permanent change in what is being optimized. The authors support this benefit theoretically and practically, and their experiments also identify forms of stability that are advantageous in use.
summary.tldr: A proximal point framework accelerates stochastic convex optimization while gaining regularization’s computational benefits without its corresponding bias.

title: Un-regularizing: approximate proximal point and faster stochastic algorithms for empirical risk minimization

abstract: We develop Square Root Graphical Models (SQR), a novel class of parametric graphical models that provides multivariate generalizations of univariate exponential family distributions. Previous multivariate graphical models [Yang et al. 2015] did not allow positive dependencies for the exponential and Poisson generalizations. However, in many real-world datasets, variables clearly have positive dependencies. For example, the airport delay time in New York—modeled as an exponential distribution—is positively related to the delay time in Boston. With this motivation, we give an example of our model class derived from the univariate exponential distribution that allows for almost arbitrary positive and negative dependencies with only a mild condition on the parameter matrix—a condition akin to the positive definiteness of the Gaussian covariance matrix. Our Poisson generalization allows for both positive and negative dependencies without any constraints on the parameter values. We also develop parameter estimation methods using node-wise regressions with \ell_1 regularization and likelihood approximation methods using sampling. Finally, we demonstrate our exponential generalization on a synthetic dataset and a real-world dataset of airport delay times.

paragraphs: Square Root Graphical Models extend single-variable exponential-family distributions into models of several interacting variables. The motivation is a restriction in earlier exponential and Poisson graphical models: they could not represent positive dependencies. Such dependencies matter in applications, including the tendency for airport delays in different cities to increase together.

The proposed exponential generalization supports almost arbitrary positive and negative dependencies, subject to a mild condition on its parameter matrix resembling the positive-definiteness condition for a Gaussian covariance matrix. The Poisson generalization permits both dependency signs without constraints on parameter values. These are distinct results, with a matrix condition retained for the exponential case.

The authors develop parameter estimation through node-wise regressions with l1 regularization and approximate likelihood calculations using sampling. They demonstrate the exponential model on synthetic data and real airport delay data. The contribution expands the dependency patterns available to these distribution families and supplies estimation tools, making the additional modeling flexibility usable in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Square Root Graphical Models allow positive and negative dependencies in exponential and Poisson generalizations, with corresponding estimation methods.

title: Square Root Graphical Models: Multivariate Generalizations of Univariate Exponential Families that Permit Positive Dependencies

abstract: We consider the minimization of non-convex functions that typically arise in machine learning. Specifically, we focus our attention on a variant of trust region methods known as cubic regularization. This approach is particularly attractive because it escapes strict saddle points and it provides stronger convergence guarantees than first- and second-order as well as classical trust region methods. However, it suffers from a high computational complexity that makes it impractical for large-scale learning. Here, we propose a novel method that uses sub-sampling to lower this computational cost. By the use of concentration inequalities we provide a sampling scheme that gives sufficiently accurate gradient and Hessian approximations to retain the strong global and local convergence guarantees of cubically regularized methods. To the best of our knowledge this is the first work that gives global convergence guarantees for a sub-sampled variant of cubic regularization on non-convex functions. Furthermore, we provide experimental results supporting our theory.

paragraphs: Cubic regularization is an approach to non-convex optimization with attractive convergence properties, including the ability to escape strict saddle points. Its computational cost can nevertheless make it impractical for large learning problems. This paper develops a subsampled version intended to retain those theoretical advantages while reducing the work needed for each optimization step.

The method approximates gradients and Hessians using samples. The key question is how accurate these approximations must be to preserve the behavior of cubic regularization. The authors use concentration inequalities to design a sampling scheme that provides sufficient accuracy, connecting reduced computation to the requirements of the convergence analysis.

They establish that the scheme retains strong global and local convergence guarantees of cubically regularized methods. Here, global convergence describes the optimization guarantee; it is not a claim of finding a global minimum of every non-convex function. Experiments support the theory. The contribution shows how carefully controlled subsampling can reduce the cost of curvature-based optimization without giving up the stated convergence properties.
summary.tldr: A controlled subsampling scheme reduces cubic regularization's computational cost while preserving its stated global and local convergence guarantees.

title: Sub-sampled Cubic Regularization for Non-convex Optimization

abstract: As a step towards developing zero-shot task generalization capabilities in reinforcement learning (RL), we introduce a new RL problem where the agent should learn to execute sequences of instructions after learning useful skills that solve subtasks. In this problem, we consider two types of generalizations: to previously unseen instructions and to longer sequences of instructions. For generalization over unseen instructions, we propose a new objective which encourages learning correspondences between similar subtasks by making analogies. For generalization over sequential instructions, we present a hierarchical architecture where a meta controller learns to use the acquired skills for executing the instructions. To deal with delayed reward, we propose a new neural architecture in the meta controller that learns when to update the subtask, which makes learning more efficient. Experimental results on a stochastic 3D domain show that the proposed ideas are crucial for generalization to longer instructions as well as unseen instructions.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a reinforcement learning problem in which an agent first acquires skills for subtasks and then uses them to execute instruction sequences. It distinguishes generalizing to previously unseen instructions from generalizing to longer instruction sequences. These require both recognizing relationships among tasks and organizing skills across time.

For unseen instructions, the authors propose an objective that encourages analogies between similar subtasks. For sequences, they introduce a hierarchical architecture whose meta controller learns to use acquired skills to follow instructions. A further neural component learns when to update the active subtask, improving learning efficiency in the presence of delayed rewards.

Experiments in a stochastic three-dimensional domain show that these proposed ideas are crucial to generalization to both unseen and longer instructions. The contribution brings together learning correspondences, composing skills, and deciding when to move between subtasks. It is presented as a step toward zero-shot task generalization, with the reported evidence tied to the instruction-following problem and domain studied.
summary.tldr: Analogy-based learning and hierarchical skill control help a reinforcement learning agent generalize to unseen instructions and longer instruction sequences.

title: Zero-Shot Task Generalization with Multi-Task Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Many real-world tasks involve multiple agents with partial observability and limited communication. Learning is challenging in these settings due to local viewpoints of agents, which perceive the world as non-stationary due to concurrently-exploring teammates. Approaches that learn specialized policies for individual tasks face problems when applied to the real world: not only do agents have to learn and store distinct policies for each task, but in practice identities of tasks are often non-observable, making these approaches inapplicable. This paper formalizes and addresses the problem of multi-task multi-agent reinforcement learning under partial observability. We introduce a decentralized single-task learning approach that is robust to concurrent interactions of teammates, and present an approach for distilling single-task policies into a unified policy that performs well across multiple related tasks, without explicit provision of task identity.

This paper formalizes and addresses the problem of multi-task multi-agent reinforcement learning under partial observability. We introduce a decentralized single-task learning approach that is robust to concurrent interactions of teammates, and present an approach for distilling single-task policies into a unified policy that performs well across multiple related tasks, without explicit provision of task identity.

paragraphs: When several agents learn together, each may observe only part of the environment and have limited communication with teammates. Because those teammates are also exploring, an agent's local experience can appear to come from a changing environment. This paper formalizes the additional challenge of learning across multiple tasks under these conditions.

Maintaining a separate policy for every task creates two problems: agents must learn and store multiple policies, and choosing among them requires knowing which task is active. The paper specifically addresses settings where task identity is not directly observable. It first introduces a decentralized approach for learning a single task that is robust to teammates' concurrent interactions.

The next step distills the single-task policies into one policy that performs well across related tasks without receiving an explicit task identity. This links learning under interacting teammates with learning behavior shared across tasks. The resulting formulation makes hidden task identity part of the problem itself, rather than assuming an external label will select the appropriate specialized policy.
summary.tldr: Decentralized learning and policy distillation produce a unified multi-agent policy for related tasks without explicit task identities.

title: Deep Decentralized Multi-task Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning under Partial Observability

abstract: We address the statistical and optimization impacts of using classical sketch versus Hessian sketch to solve approximately the Matrix Ridge Regression (MRR) problem. Prior research has considered the effects of classical sketch on least squares regression (LSR), a strictly simpler problem. We establish that classical sketch has a similar effect upon the optimization properties of MRR as it does on those of LSR—namely, it recovers nearly optimal solutions. In contrast, Hessian sketch does not have this guarantee; instead, the approximation error is governed by a subtle interplay between the “mass” in the responses and the optimal objective value. For both types of approximations, the regularization in the sketched MRR problem gives it significantly different statistical properties from the sketched LSR problem. In particular, there is a bias-variance trade-off in sketched MRR that is not present in sketched LSR. We provide upper and lower bounds on the biases and variances of sketched MRR; these establish that the variance is significantly increased when classical sketches are used, while the bias is significantly increased when using Hessian sketches. Empirically, sketched MRR solutions can have risks that are higher by an order-of-magnitude than those of the optimal MRR solutions. We establish theoretically and empirically that model averaging greatly decreases this gap. Thus, in the distributed setting, sketching combined with model averaging is a powerful technique that quickly obtains near-optimal solutions to the MRR problem while greatly mitigating the statistical risks incurred by sketching.

paragraphs: Sketching reduces the computational size of a regression problem, but a good approximation to its optimization objective need not preserve its statistical behavior. This paper examines that distinction for matrix ridge regression, comparing classical sketching with Hessian sketching. Regularization makes the statistical effects different from those previously studied for ordinary least squares.

Classical sketching recovers nearly optimal objective values, whereas Hessian sketching lacks that guarantee; its approximation error depends on the response mass and optimal objective value. Statistical bounds reveal another contrast: classical sketches substantially increase variance, while Hessian sketches substantially increase bias. Ridge regression therefore introduces a bias-variance tradeoff absent from the sketched least-squares setting discussed.

Experiments show that sketched solutions can have statistical risks an order of magnitude above those of optimal ridge solutions. The authors establish theoretically and empirically that averaging models greatly reduces this gap. In distributed settings, sketching with model averaging thus offers a way to obtain near-optimal solutions quickly while mitigating the statistical costs of sketching.
summary.tldr: Sketching can increase ridge regression's bias or variance, while model averaging substantially reduces the resulting statistical risk.

title: Sketched Ridge Regression: Optimization Perspective, Statistical Perspective, and Model Averaging

abstract: Direct policy gradient methods for reinforcement learning and continuous control problems are a popular approach for a variety of reasons: 1) they are easy to implement without explicit knowledge of the underlying model, 2) they are an “end-to-end” approach, directly optimizing the performance metric of interest, 3) they inherently allow for richly parameterized policies. A notable drawback is that even in the most basic continuous control problem (that of linear quadratic regulators), these methods must solve a non-convex optimization problem, where little is understood about their efficiency from both computational and statistical perspectives. In contrast, system identification and model based planning in optimal control theory have a much more solid theoretical footing, where much is known with regards to their computational and statistical properties. This work bridges this gap showing that (model free) policy gradient methods globally converge to the optimal solution and are efficient (polynomially so in relevant problem dependent quantities) with regards to their sample and computational complexities.

A notable drawback is that even in the most basic continuous control problem (that of linear quadratic regulators), these methods must solve a non-convex optimization problem, where little is understood about their efficiency from both computational and statistical perspectives. paragraphs: Policy-gradient methods directly optimize a policy's performance and can operate without explicit knowledge of the underlying system. These features make them appealing for continuous control. However, even the linear quadratic regulator leads to a nonconvex optimization problem when approached through policy gradients, raising questions about whether optimization can reliably find the best policy.

This paper establishes global convergence to the optimal solution for model-free policy-gradient methods in the linear quadratic regulator setting. It also shows that the methods have polynomial sample and computational complexity in relevant problem-dependent quantities. The analysis therefore addresses both the quality of the eventual solution and the resources needed to obtain it.

The result gives direct policy optimization a firmer theoretical basis in this control problem, helping close a gap with system identification and model-based planning. Its significance is that nonconvexity does not prevent the analyzed methods from reaching the optimum efficiently in this setting. The stated guarantee concerns the linear quadratic regulator rather than arbitrary reinforcement learning problems.
summary.tldr: Model-free policy-gradient methods can solve the linear quadratic regulator globally with polynomial sample and computational complexity.

title: Global Convergence of Policy Gradient Methods for the Linear Quadratic Regulator

abstract: We propose a bandit algorithm that explores by randomizing its history of rewards. Specifically, it pulls the arm with the highest mean reward in a non-parametric bootstrap sample of its history with pseudo rewards. We design the pseudo rewards such that the bootstrap mean is optimistic with a sufficiently high probability. We call our algorithm Giro, which stands for garbage in, reward out. We analyze Giro in a Bernoulli bandit and derive a $O(K \Delta^{-1} \log n)$ bound on its $n$-round regret, where $\Delta$ is the difference in the expected rewards of the optimal and the best suboptimal arms, and $K$ is the number of arms. The main advantage of our exploration design is that it easily generalizes to structured problems. To show this, we propose contextual Giro with an arbitrary reward generalization model. We evaluate Giro and its contextual variant on multiple synthetic and real-world problems, and observe that it performs well.

Specifically, it pulls the arm with the highest mean reward in a non-parametric bootstrap sample of its history with pseudo rewards. We design the pseudo rewards such that the bootstrap mean is optimistic with a sufficiently high probability. We call our algorithm Giro, which stands for garbage in, reward out. We analyze Giro in a Bernoulli bandit and derive a $O(K \Delta^{-1} \log n)$ bound on its $n$-round regret, where $\Delta$ is the difference in the expected rewards of the optimal and the best suboptimal arms, and $K$ is the number of arms. The main advantage of our exploration design is that it easily generalizes to structured problems. To show this, we propose contextual Giro with an arbitrary reward generalization model. We evaluate Giro and its contextual variant on multiple synthetic and real-world problems, and observe that it performs well.

paragraphs: Giro addresses exploration in multi-armed bandits, where a learner repeatedly chooses among actions with uncertain rewards. The algorithm randomizes the reward history using non-parametric bootstrap samples and selects the arm with the highest sampled mean. It adds artificial rewards to the history so that the bootstrap estimate has a sufficiently high probability of being optimistic.

Those pseudo rewards are the mechanism that encourages exploration. Randomized histories can make an action look attractive enough to try, allowing the learner to gather further evidence about its reward. For Bernoulli bandits, the authors prove an n-round regret bound of O(K log(n)/Delta), where K is the number of arms and Delta separates the optimal arm from the best suboptimal arm.

The authors also introduce contextual Giro, which can use an arbitrary reward generalization model. This illustrates the intended flexibility of the exploration design for structured problems. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world problems find that both Giro and its contextual version perform well, complementing the theoretical result for the Bernoulli setting.
summary.tldr: Giro explores by bootstrapping reward histories augmented with pseudo rewards, with a Bernoulli-bandit regret bound and a flexible contextual extension.

title: Garbage In, Reward Out: Bootstrapping Exploration in Multi-Armed Bandits

abstract: Neural networks with a large number of parameters admit a mean-field description, which has recently served as a theoretical explanation for the favorable training properties of models with a large number of parameters. In this regime, gradient descent obeys a deterministic partial differential equation (PDE) that converges to a globally optimal solution for networks with a single hidden layer under appropriate assumptions. In this work, we propose a non-local mass transport dynamics that leads to a modified PDE with the same minimizer. We implement this non-local dynamics as a stochastic neuronal birth/death process and we prove that it accelerates the rate of convergence in the mean-field limit. We subsequently realize this PDE with two classes of numerical schemes that converge to the mean-field equation, each of which can easily be implemented for neural networks with finite numbers of parameters. We illustrate our algorithms with two models to provide intuition for the mechanism through which convergence is accelerated.

paragraphs: For networks with many parameters, a mean-field description represents training through a partial differential equation. Under appropriate assumptions, the gradient-descent equation for a single-hidden-layer network converges to a global optimum. This paper asks whether changing the dynamics can accelerate that convergence while preserving the same minimizer.

The proposed change adds non-local mass transport, implemented as a stochastic process in which neurons undergo birth and death. The authors prove faster convergence in the mean-field limit for the modified dynamics. This is a statement about the limiting equation, and the mean-field setting is central to the claimed acceleration guarantee.

To connect the theory to computation, the paper develops two classes of numerical schemes that converge to the mean-field equation and can be implemented with finitely many network parameters. Two models illustrate how the acceleration mechanism works. The contribution therefore links a modified theoretical training process to implementable algorithms, while distinguishing the proved limiting behavior from the finite-network realizations used to demonstrate the idea.
summary.tldr: Stochastic neuron birth and death implements modified training dynamics with provably faster convergence in the mean-field limit.

title: Neuron birth-death dynamics accelerates gradient descent and converges asymptotically

abstract: Real-world machine learning applications often have complex test metrics, and may have training and test data that are not identically distributed. Motivated by known connections between complex test metrics and cost-weighted learning, we propose addressing these issues by using a weighted loss function with a standard loss, where the weights on the training examples are learned to optimize the test metric on a validation set. These metric-optimized example weights can be learned for any test metric, including black box and customized ones for specific applications. We illustrate the performance of the proposed method on diverse public benchmark datasets and real-world applications. We also provide a generalization bound for the method.

Motivated by known connections between complex test metrics and cost-weighted learning, we propose addressing these issues by using a weighted loss function with a standard loss, where the weights on the training examples are learned to optimize the test metric on a validation set. These metric-optimized example weights can be learned for any test metric, including black box and customized ones for specific applications. We illustrate the performance of the proposed method on diverse public benchmark datasets and real-world applications. We also provide a generalization bound for the method.

paragraphs: The metric used to judge a deployed model can be more complicated than the loss used to train it. Training and test data may also follow different distributions. This paper addresses these issues by learning how much weight to place on individual training examples, using validation performance to guide those choices.

The model is trained with a standard loss multiplied by learned example weights. Those weights are optimized for the desired test metric on a validation set. The approach builds on connections between complex evaluation metrics and cost-weighted learning, allowing the evaluation objective to influence training through the importance assigned to examples.

The authors state that the weights can be learned for any test metric, including black-box metrics and application-specific measures. They illustrate the method on public benchmarks and real applications and provide a generalization bound. The contribution is a flexible interface between an ordinary training loss and a potentially complicated evaluation criterion. It places the adaptation in the example weights, so the chosen metric can shape learning without requiring the standard loss itself to become that metric.
summary.tldr: Learning training-example weights against a validation metric lets standard losses target complex or black-box evaluation objectives.

title: Metric-Optimized Example Weights

abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have shown much empirical success in solving perceptual tasks across various cognitive modalities. While they are only loosely inspired by the biological brain, recent studies report considerable similarities between representations extracted from task-optimized DNNs and neural populations in the brain. DNNs have subsequently become a popular model class to infer computational principles underlying complex cognitive functions, and in turn, they have also emerged as a natural testbed for applying methods originally developed to probe information in neural populations. In this work, we utilize mean-field theoretic manifold analysis, a recent technique from computational neuroscience that connects geometry of feature representations with linear separability of classes, to analyze language representations from large-scale contextual embedding models. We explore representations from different model families (BERT, RoBERTa, GPT, etc.) and find evidence for emergence of linguistic manifolds across layer depth (e.g., manifolds for part-of-speech tags), especially in ambiguous data (i.e, words with multiple part-of-speech tags, or part-of-speech classes including many words). In addition, we find that the emergence of linear separability in these manifolds is driven by a combined reduction of manifolds’ radius, dimensionality and inter-manifold correlations.

In addition, we find that the emergence of linear separability in these manifolds is driven by a combined reduction of manifolds’ radius, dimensionality and inter-manifold correlations.

paragraphs: This paper studies how linguistic information becomes organized inside large contextual language models. It applies mean-field theoretic manifold analysis, a technique from computational neuroscience that relates the geometry of feature representations to how easily a linear boundary can separate classes. Here, the classes include linguistic categories such as part-of-speech tags.

The authors examine representations across layers in several model families, including BERT, RoBERTa, and GPT. They find evidence that linguistic manifolds emerge with depth. The effect is especially apparent in ambiguous data, including words that can have multiple part-of-speech tags and part-of-speech categories containing many different words.

The analysis attributes emerging linear separability to a combination of smaller manifold radii, lower dimensionality, and reduced correlations between manifolds. These findings give a geometric account of how linguistic categories become easier to distinguish within the studied models. They also demonstrate how a tool developed for studying neural populations can help characterize the internal representations of language networks.
summary.tldr: Language-model layers show increasingly separable linguistic representations associated with reductions in manifold size, dimensionality, and inter-manifold correlations.

title: Emergence of Separable Manifolds in Deep Language Representations

abstract: Most recommender systems (RS) research assumes that a user’s utility can be maximized independently of the utility of the other agents (e.g., other users, content providers). In realistic settings, this is often not true – the dynamics of an RS ecosystem couple the long-term utility of all agents. In this work, we explore settings in which content providers cannot remain viable unless they receive a certain level of user engagement. We formulate this problem as one of equilibrium selection in the induced dynamical system, and show that it can be solved as an optimal constrained matching problem. Our model ensures the system reaches an equilibrium with maximal social welfare supported by a sufficiently diverse set of viable providers. We demonstrate that even in a simple, stylized dynamical RS model, the standard myopic approach to recommendation - always matching a user to the best provider - performs poorly. We develop several scalable techniques to solve the matching problem, and also draw connections to various notions of user regret and fairness, arguing that these outcomes are fairer in a utilitarian sense.

In this work, we explore settings in which content providers cannot remain viable unless they receive a certain level of user engagement. We formulate this problem as one of equilibrium selection in the induced dynamical system, and show that it can be solved as an optimal constrained matching problem. Our model ensures the system reaches an equilibrium with maximal social welfare supported by a sufficiently diverse set of viable providers. We demonstrate that even in a simple, stylized dynamical RS model, the standard myopic approach to recommendation - always matching a user to the best provider - performs poorly. We develop several scalable techniques to solve the matching problem, and also draw connections to various notions of user regret and fairness, arguing that these outcomes are fairer in a utilitarian sense.

paragraphs: A recommendation affects more than the user receiving it. When content providers need a minimum level of engagement to remain viable, today’s recommendations influence which providers will be available later. This paper studies that coupling between users and providers, treating long-term utility as a property of the recommendation ecosystem.

The authors formulate the task as selecting an equilibrium of a dynamical system and show that it can be solved through optimal constrained matching. Within their model, the selected equilibrium maximizes social welfare while supporting a sufficiently diverse collection of viable providers. The matching constraints make provider survival part of the recommendation objective.

Even in a simple, stylized model, always matching each user to their currently best provider performs poorly. The paper develops scalable techniques for solving the constrained matching problem and connects the outcomes to user regret and fairness. Its fairness argument is utilitarian: it concerns aggregate welfare. The results show why immediate individual utility can be an inadequate guide to long-term recommendation quality.
summary.tldr: Constrained matching accounts for provider viability to maximize long-term social welfare in the paper’s recommendation-system model.

title: Optimizing Long-term Social Welfare in Recommender Systems: A Constrained Matching Approach

abstract: It is well known that the standard greedy algorithm guarantees a worst-case approximation factor of $1-1/e$ when maximizing a monotone submodular function under a cardinality constraint. However, empirical studies show that its performance is substantially better in practice. This raises a natural question of explaining this improved performance of the greedy algorithm. In this work, we define sharpness for submodular functions as a candidate explanation for this phenomenon. We show that the greedy algorithm provably performs better as the sharpness of the submodular function increases. This improvement ties in closely with the faster convergence rates of first order methods for sharp functions in convex optimization.
originalAbstract: It is well known that the standard greedy algorithm guarantees a worst-case approximation factor of $1-1/e$ when maximizing a monotone submodular function under a cardinality constraint. However, empirical studies show that its performance is substantially better in practice. This raises a natural question of explaining this improved performance of the greedy algorithm. In this work, we define sharpness for submodular functions as a candidate explanation for this phenomenon. We show that the greedy algorithm provably performs better as the sharpness of the submodular function increases. This improvement ties in closely with the faster convergence rates of first order methods for sharp functions in convex optimization.

paragraphs: For monotone submodular maximization with a limit on the number of selected items, the standard greedy algorithm guarantees a worst-case approximation factor of 1−1/e. Such problems have diminishing returns: an item's extra value can shrink as more items are selected. Yet empirical performance often substantially exceeds the worst-case guarantee.

This paper introduces sharpness for submodular functions as a candidate explanation for that gap. The authors prove that the greedy algorithm's performance improves as the function's sharpness increases. This gives a way to express stronger guarantees using additional structure in the objective, rather than evaluating every problem solely through the same worst-case factor.

The result also connects greedy selection to convex optimization, where sharpness is associated with faster convergence of first-order methods. That relationship places improved greedy behavior within a broader mathematical pattern. Sharpness is presented as a candidate explanation for observed effectiveness, and the theorem establishes a specific link between that property and improved guarantees under the stated submodular, monotone, cardinality-constrained setting.
summary.tldr: A sharpness property yields stronger guarantees for greedy submodular maximization and offers a candidate explanation for its strong practical performance.

title: On the Unreasonable Effectiveness of the Greedy Algorithm: Greedy Adapts to Sharpness

abstract: Balancing performance and safety is crucial to deploying autonomous vehicles in multi-agent environments. In particular, autonomous racing is a domain that penalizes safe but conservative policies, highlighting the need for robust, adaptive strategies. Current approaches either make simplifying assumptions about other agents or lack robust mechanisms for online adaptation. This work makes algorithmic contributions to both challenges. First, to generate a realistic, diverse set of opponents, we develop a novel method for self-play based on replica-exchange Markov chain Monte Carlo. Second, we propose a distributionally robust bandit optimization procedure that adaptively adjusts risk aversion relative to uncertainty in beliefs about opponents’ behaviors. We rigorously quantify the tradeoffs in performance and robustness when approximating these computations in real-time motion-planning, and we demonstrate our methods experimentally on autonomous vehicles that achieve scaled speeds comparable to Formula One racecars.

paragraphs: Autonomous racing makes the tension between safety and performance especially visible: excessive caution can undermine competitive performance, while other vehicles introduce uncertainty. FormulaZero addresses this setting through both preparation before deployment and adaptation during operation. The aim is to provide realistic behavioral variety among opponents and a robust way to respond when their behavior remains uncertain.

For preparation, the authors develop a self-play method based on replica-exchange Markov chain Monte Carlo. It generates a diverse, realistic population of opponents. For online adaptation, they introduce a distributionally robust bandit optimization procedure. This procedure adjusts risk aversion in relation to uncertainty in the system's beliefs about opponent behavior, connecting the treatment of risk to the information currently available.

The paper also rigorously quantifies performance and robustness tradeoffs when these computations are approximated for real-time motion planning. That analysis connects the proposed optimization methods to the need to make decisions quickly. Experiments demonstrate the approach on autonomous vehicles reaching scaled speeds comparable to Formula One racecars. These demonstrations support its use in demanding racing conditions without establishing universal safety.
summary.tldr: FormulaZero combines diverse self-play opponents with uncertainty-sensitive risk adaptation for autonomous racing.

title: FormulaZero: Distributionally Robust Online Adaptation via Offline Population Synthesis

abstract: We develop a functional encoder-decoder approach to supervised meta-learning, where labeled data is encoded into an infinite-dimensional functional representation rather than a finite-dimensional one. Furthermore, rather than directly producing the representation, we learn a neural update rule resembling functional gradient descent which iteratively improves the representation. The final representation is used to condition the decoder to make predictions on unlabeled data. Our approach is the first to demonstrates the success of encoder-decoder style meta-learning methods like conditional neural processes on large-scale few-shot classification benchmarks such as miniImageNet and tieredImageNet, where it achieves state-of-the-art performance.

Furthermore, rather than directly producing the representation, we learn a neural update rule resembling functional gradient descent which iteratively improves the representation. The final representation is used to condition the decoder to make predictions on unlabeled data. Our approach is the first to demonstrates the success of encoder-decoder style meta-learning methods like conditional neural processes on large-scale few-shot classification benchmarks such as miniImageNet and tieredImageNet, where it achieves state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: MetaFun addresses supervised meta-learning with an encoder-decoder architecture. The encoder turns labeled examples into a representation that the decoder uses to predict labels for new inputs. Its distinctive choice is to represent the labeled data as a function in an infinite-dimensional space, rather than compressing it into a finite-dimensional representation.

The method also changes how this representation is constructed. A learned neural update rule repeatedly improves the function, in a process resembling gradient descent over functions. The final function conditions the decoder’s predictions on unlabeled data. This makes iterative refinement part of the learned encoding procedure, rather than asking the encoder to produce its final representation in a single step.

The abstract reports state-of-the-art results on the large-scale few-shot classification benchmarks miniImageNet and tieredImageNet. It presents these results as evidence that encoder-decoder meta-learning approaches, including the style associated with conditional neural processes, can succeed in this setting. The contribution combines a different representation space with learned updates that adapt that representation to the available labeled examples.
summary.tldr: MetaFun iteratively updates a functional representation of labeled examples and reports state-of-the-art few-shot classification performance.

title: MetaFun: Meta-Learning with Iterative Functional Updates

abstract: The lack of anisotropic kernels in graph neural networks (GNNs) strongly limits their expressiveness, contributing to well-known issues such as over-smoothing. To overcome this limitation, we propose the first globally consistent anisotropic kernels for GNNs, allowing for graph convolutions that are defined according to topologicaly-derived directional flows. First, by defining a vector field in the graph, we develop a method of applying directional derivatives and smoothing by projecting node-specific messages into the field. Then, we propose the use of the Laplacian eigenvectors as such vector field. We show that the method generalizes CNNs on an $n$-dimensional grid and is provably more discriminative than standard GNNs regarding the Weisfeiler-Lehman 1-WL test. We evaluate our method on different standard benchmarks and see a relative error reduction of 8% on the CIFAR10 graph dataset and 11% to 32% on the molecular ZINC dataset, and a relative increase in precision of 1.6% on the MolPCBA dataset. An important outcome of this work is that it enables graph networks to embed directions in an unsupervised way, thus allowing a better representation of the anisotropic features in different physical or biological problems.

paragraphs: Graph networks can struggle to distinguish information arriving from different directions. The paper connects this lack of direction-sensitive kernels to limited expressiveness and problems such as over-smoothing. It introduces kernels whose directional interpretation is globally consistent across a graph, with directions derived from the graph’s own topology.

The method first defines a vector field over the graph and projects messages associated with individual nodes into that field. This supports directional derivatives and directional smoothing. The authors then use eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian to supply the field, enabling directions to be embedded without supervision. They show that the construction generalizes convolutional networks on n-dimensional grids and has greater discriminative power than standard GNNs relative to 1-WL.

Reported results include relative error reductions of 8% on CIFAR10 graphs and 11% to 32% on ZINC, plus a 1.6% relative precision increase on MolPCBA. These findings support the usefulness of representing directional features, including those relevant to physical and biological problems.
summary.tldr: Directional Graph Networks derive consistent directions from graph structure to improve expressive power and benchmark performance.

title: Directional Graph Networks

abstract: We propose a method for learning de-identified prosody representations from raw audio using a contrastive self-supervised signal. Whereas prior work has relied on conditioning models with bottlenecks, we introduce a set of inductive biases that exploit the natural structure of prosody to minimize timbral information and decouple prosody from speaker representations. Despite aggressive downsampling of the input and having no access to linguistic information, our model performs comparably to state-of-the-art speech representations on DAMMP, a new benchmark we introduce for spoken language understanding. We use minimum description length probing to show that our representations have selectively learned the subcomponents of non-timbral prosody, and that the product quantizer naturally disentangles them without using bottlenecks. We derive an information-theoretic definition of speech de-identifiability and use it to demonstrate that our prosody representations are less identifiable than the other speech representations.

Despite aggressive downsampling of the input and having no access to linguistic information, our model performs comparably to state-of-the-art speech representations on DAMMP, a new benchmark we introduce for spoken language understanding. paragraphs: Speech carries information about delivery as well as speaker identity. This paper learns prosody representations directly from audio while seeking to reduce identifying timbral information. It uses a contrastive self-supervised signal and inductive biases based on the natural structure of prosody to separate prosodic information from representations of the speaker.

The authors introduce DAMMP, a spoken-language-understanding benchmark. Despite strong input downsampling and no access to linguistic information, their model performs comparably to state-of-the-art speech representations on this benchmark. This provides evidence that the retained prosodic information can remain useful even as the representation reduces other information available in the audio.

Minimum description length probing indicates that the representations selectively capture components of non-timbral prosody. The authors also find that their product quantizer separates these components without bottlenecks. Finally, they formulate speech de-identifiability in information-theoretic terms and use it to show lower identifiability than other speech representations. The stated result is a comparative reduction in identifiability, rather than a claim that identity information is entirely absent.
summary.tldr: A contrastive audio model learns useful prosody representations that retain less speaker-identifying information than other speech representations.

title: Learning de-identified representations of prosody from raw audio

abstract: We study the problem of Gaussian bandits with general side information, as first introduced by Wu, Szepesvári, and György. In this setting, the play of an arm reveals information about other arms, according to an arbitrary a priori known side information matrix: each element of this matrix encodes the fidelity of the information that the “row" arm reveals about the “column" arm. In the case of Gaussian noise, this model subsumes standard bandits, full-feedback, and graph-structured feedback as special cases. In this work, we first construct an LP-based asymptotic instance-dependent lower bound on the regret. The LP optimizes the cost (regret) required to reliably estimate the suboptimality gap of each arm. This LP lower bound motivates our main contribution: the first known asymptotically optimal algorithm for this general setting.

In this setting, the play of an arm reveals information about other arms, according to an arbitrary a priori known side information matrix: each element of this matrix encodes the fidelity of the information that the “row" arm reveals about the “column" arm. In the case of Gaussian noise, this model subsumes standard bandits, full-feedback, and graph-structured feedback as special cases.
