paragraphs: In this bandit problem, choosing an action can reveal information about other actions as well as the chosen one. A known matrix describes how informative each action is about every other action. With Gaussian observation noise, this formulation includes ordinary bandits, full feedback, and feedback organized by a graph within one general setting.

The central challenge is deciding which observations are worth the reward sacrificed to obtain them. The authors express that tradeoff through a linear program. It finds the regret cost required to estimate reliably how far each action falls below the best one. This produces an asymptotic lower bound that depends on the particular problem instance and its information structure.

The lower bound then guides an algorithm whose regret matches it asymptotically. The paper presents this as the first known asymptotically optimal algorithm for the general setting. The result explains how to exploit unequal information quality when planning exploration: a choice can be valuable because it helps assess other choices. The optimality claim concerns long-run behavior under the stated Gaussian model.
summary.tldr: The paper derives an instance-dependent exploration lower bound and an asymptotically matching algorithm for Gaussian bandits with general side observations.

title: Asymptotically-Optimal Gaussian Bandits with Side Observations

abstract: Detecting change points in time series, i.e., points in time at which some observed process suddenly changes, is a fundamental task that arises in many real-world applications, with consequences for safety and reliability. In this work, we propose ADAGA, a novel Gaussian process-based solution to this problem, that leverages a powerful heuristics we developed based on statistical hypothesis testing. In contrast to prior approaches, ADAGA adapts to changes both in mean and covariance structure of the temporal process. In extensive experiments, we show its versatility and applicability to different classes of change points, demonstrating that it is significantly more accurate than current state-of-the-art alternatives.
originalAbstract: Detecting change points in time series, i.e., points in time at which some observed process suddenly changes, is a fundamental task that arises in many real-world applications, with consequences for safety and reliability. In this work, we propose ADAGA, a novel Gaussian process-based solution to this problem, that leverages a powerful heuristics we developed based on statistical hypothesis testing. In contrast to prior approaches, ADAGA adapts to changes both in mean and covariance structure of the temporal process. In extensive experiments, we show its versatility and applicability to different classes of change points, demonstrating that it is significantly more accurate than current state-of-the-art alternatives.

paragraphs: A change point is a moment when the behavior of an observed time series suddenly shifts. Detecting such moments matters for monitoring processes whose reliability or safety depends on recognizing changing conditions. The paper introduces ADAGA, a Gaussian-process approach intended to recognize different kinds of these changes.

Its central feature is adaptation to both the mean and the covariance structure of the process. A mean change concerns the level around which observations vary. A covariance change concerns how those variations relate across time. Accounting for both lets the method address changes that cannot be described solely as a rise or fall in the average signal.

ADAGA uses a heuristic developed from statistical hypothesis testing to support this detection process. The authors report extensive experiments spanning different classes of change points, finding significantly greater accuracy than the state-of-the-art alternatives they evaluate. These findings support the method’s versatility across the tested changes. The contribution combines a broader view of what can change in a temporal process with an empirically effective detection approach.
summary.tldr: ADAGA detects changes in both time-series averages and covariance structure, improving accuracy over evaluated alternatives.

title: Adaptive Gaussian Process Change Point Detection

abstract: Nearest prototype classifiers (NPCs) assign to each input point the label of the nearest prototype with respect to a chosen distance metric. A direct advantage of NPCs is that the decisions are interpretable. Previous work could provide lower bounds on the minimal adversarial perturbation in the $\ell_p$-threat model when using the same $\ell_p$-distance for the NPCs. In this paper we provide a complete discussion on the complexity when using $\ell_p$-distances for decision and $\ell_q$-threat models for certification for $p,q \in \{1,2,\infty\}$. In particular we provide scalable algorithms for the exact computation of the minimal adversarial perturbation when using $\ell_2$-distance and improved lower bounds in other cases. Using efficient improved lower bounds we train our \textbf{P}rovably adversarially robust \textbf{NPC} (PNPC), for MNIST which have better $\ell_2$-robustness guarantees than neural networks. Additionally, we show up to our knowledge the first certification results w.r.t. to the LPIPS perceptual metric which has been argued to be a more realistic threat model for image classification than $\ell_p$-balls. Our PNPC has on CIFAR10 higher certified robust accuracy than the empirical robust accuracy reported in \cite{laidlaw2021perceptual}. The code is available in our \href{https://github.com/vvoracek/Provably-Adversarially-Robust-Nearest-Prototype-Classifiers}{repository}.

paragraphs: Nearest-prototype classifiers label an input according to its closest representative example, making their decisions interpretable. Robustness certification asks how much an adversary must change an input to alter that label. This paper examines cases where the distance used for classification differs from the distance used to measure an adversarial change.

The authors analyze combinations of the 1, 2, and infinity norms. For classifiers using Euclidean distance, they provide scalable algorithms that compute the minimum adversarial perturbation exactly; other cases receive improved lower bounds. They then use efficient lower bounds to train robust prototype classifiers, obtaining stronger Euclidean robustness guarantees than neural networks on MNIST.

The paper also reports what the authors believe are the first certification results for the LPIPS perceptual metric. On CIFAR10, their classifier’s certified robust accuracy exceeds the empirical robust accuracy reported in the cited comparison. These are distinct forms of evidence: certification establishes a guarantee, whereas empirical robustness describes measured performance under evaluation.
summary.tldr: New exact computations and lower bounds strengthen robustness certification and training for interpretable nearest-prototype classifiers.

title: Provably Adversarially Robust Nearest Prototype Classifiers

abstract: Latent variable models are powerful tools for modeling complex phenomena involving in particular partially observed data, unobserved variables or underlying complex unknown structures. Inference is often difficult due to the latent structure of the model. To deal with parameter estimation in the presence of latent variables, well-known efficient methods exist, such as gradient-based and EM-type algorithms, but with practical and theoretical limitations. In this paper, we propose as an alternative for parameter estimation an efficient preconditioned stochastic gradient algorithm. Our method includes a preconditioning step based on a positive definite Fisher information matrix estimate. We prove convergence results for the proposed algorithm under mild assumptions for very general latent variables models. We illustrate through relevant simulations the performance of the proposed methodology in a nonlinear mixed effects model and in a stochastic block model.

paragraphs: Latent-variable models describe partially observed data and hidden structure, but those hidden quantities make parameter estimation difficult. Gradient methods and expectation-maximization methods offer established solutions with practical and theoretical limitations. This paper proposes a preconditioned stochastic-gradient alternative for a broad family of latent-variable models.

The algorithm estimates a positive-definite Fisher information matrix and uses it to precondition gradient updates. This changes how updates are scaled and oriented according to the model’s information geometry. The authors establish convergence under mild assumptions for very general latent-variable settings, connecting the proposed update rule to a formal optimization guarantee.

Simulations examine a nonlinear mixed-effects model and a stochastic block model, illustrating the method in two distinct types of latent structure. The contribution is an estimation procedure with convergence analysis and application evidence. The abstract does not provide numerical speedups or claim that it uniformly dominates expectation-maximization across all latent-variable problems.
summary.tldr: Fisher-information preconditioning yields a stochastic-gradient estimator with convergence guarantees for general latent-variable models.

title: Efficient preconditioned stochastic gradient descent for estimation in latent variable models

abstract: Recent large-scale generative models learned on big data are capable of synthesizing incredible images yet suffer from limited controllability. This work offers a new generation paradigm that allows flexible control of the output image, such as spatial layout and palette, while maintaining the synthesis quality and model creativity. With compositionality as the core idea, we first decompose an image into representative factors, and then train a diffusion model with all these factors as the conditions to recompose the input. At the inference stage, the rich intermediate representations work as composable elements, leading to a huge design space (i.e., exponentially proportional to the number of decomposed factors) for customizable content creation. It is noteworthy that our approach, which we call Composer, supports various levels of conditions, such as text description as the global information, depth map and sketch as the local guidance, color histogram for low-level details, etc. Besides improving controllability, we confirm that Composer serves as a general framework and facilitates a wide range of classical generative tasks without retraining. Code and models will be made available.

paragraphs: Composer addresses the difficulty of controlling particular aspects of images produced by large generative models. The goal is to give users flexible influence over properties such as spatial layout and color palette while preserving image quality and creative possibilities. Its central idea is to make different image properties available as conditions that can be combined.

During training, an image is decomposed into representative factors, and a diffusion model learns to reconstruct it using those factors as guidance. The conditions operate at different levels: text provides global information, depth maps and sketches supply local guidance, and color histograms describe lower-level appearance. At generation time, these representations become elements that can be composed to specify desired content.

The authors describe a design space that grows exponentially with the number of decomposed factors. They also report that the same framework supports a range of established image-generation tasks without retraining. The approach matters because it connects varied forms of user control through a shared generation model, allowing combinations of guidance within the learned framework.
summary.tldr: Composer trains a diffusion model to combine image factors such as text, depth, sketches, and color for flexible control without task-specific retraining.

title: Composer: Creative and Controllable Image Synthesis with Composable Conditions

abstract: We investigate the challenge of parametrizing policies for reinforcement learning (RL) in high-dimensional continuous action spaces. Our objective is to develop a multimodal policy that overcomes limitations inherent in the commonly-used Gaussian parameterization. To achieve this, we propose a principled framework that models the continuous RL policy as a generative model of optimal trajectories. By conditioning the policy on a latent variable, we derive a novel variational bound as the optimization objective, which promotes exploration of the environment. We then present a practical model-based RL method, called Reparameterized Policy Gradient (RPG), which leverages the multimodal policy parameterization and learned world model to achieve strong exploration capabilities and high data efficiency. Empirical results demonstrate that our method can help agents evade local optima in tasks with dense rewards and solve challenging sparse-reward environments by incorporating an object-centric intrinsic reward. Our method consistently outperforms previous approaches across a range of tasks. Code and supplementary materials are available on the project page https://haosulab.github.io/RPG/

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning in high-dimensional continuous action spaces requires a policy capable of representing useful choices. This paper targets limitations of the commonly used Gaussian parameterization by developing a multimodal policy. Such a policy can represent distinct possibilities within the agent’s behavior rather than relying on a single Gaussian form.

The framework treats the policy as a generative model of optimal trajectories and conditions it on a latent variable. From this construction, the authors derive a variational optimization objective that promotes exploration. Their practical algorithm, Reparameterized Policy Gradient, combines this policy parameterization with a learned world model to support exploration and data-efficient learning.

Experiments show that the approach can help agents escape local optima in tasks with dense rewards. For difficult sparse-reward environments, the reported success includes an object-centric intrinsic reward, so that component is part of the stated result. The method consistently outperforms previous approaches across the tested tasks. Together, these findings support the combination of multimodal policies and model-based learning as a useful approach to exploring different possible trajectories.
summary.tldr: Reparameterized Policy Gradient combines latent-conditioned multimodal policies with a learned world model to improve exploration and data efficiency.

title: Reparameterized Policy Learning for Multimodal Trajectory Optimization

abstract: We introduce a randomized topological augmentor based on Schur complements for Graph Contrastive Learning (GCL). Given a graph laplacian matrix, the technique generates unbiased approximations of its Schur complements and treats the corresponding graphs as augmented views. We discuss the benefits of our approach, provide theoretical justifications and present connections with graph diffusion. Unlike previous efforts, we study the empirical effectiveness of the augmentor in a controlled fashion by varying the design choices for subsequent GCL phases, such as encoding and contrasting. Extensive experiments on node and graph classification benchmarks demonstrate that our technique consistently outperforms pre-defined and adaptive augmentation approaches to achieve state-of-the-art results.

paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning uses different views of a graph to learn useful representations. How those views are constructed can therefore influence what the model learns. This paper introduces a randomized method for generating structural views using Schur complements of the graph’s Laplacian matrix, a mathematical representation of its connectivity.

The method produces unbiased approximations of those Schur complements and interprets the resulting matrices as augmented graphs. The authors provide theoretical justification for this construction and describe its connections to graph diffusion. This gives the augmentation a specific mathematical foundation. The unbiasedness claim applies to the Schur-complement approximations, rather than automatically establishing that every later prediction is unbiased.

The experimental study varies choices in later contrastive-learning stages, including encoding and contrasting, to examine the augmentor in a controlled way. Across node-classification and graph-classification benchmarks, the authors report consistent improvements over predefined and adaptive augmentation approaches, reaching state-of-the-art results. The findings support this structural augmentation across the tested downstream configurations, rather than only as part of one fixed learning pipeline.
summary.tldr: Randomized Schur-complement graph views improve contrastive learning across tested encoding and contrasting choices, with leading classification results.

title: Randomized Schur Complement Views for Graph Contrastive Learning

abstract: We attack the state-of-the-art Go-playing AI system KataGo by training adversarial policies against it, achieving a $>$97% win rate against KataGo running at superhuman settings. Our adversaries do not win by playing Go well. Instead, they trick KataGo into making serious blunders. Our attack transfers zero-shot to other superhuman Go-playing AIs, and is comprehensible to the extent that human experts can implement it without algorithmic assistance to consistently beat superhuman AIs. The core vulnerability uncovered by our attack persists even in KataGo agents adversarially trained to defend against our attack. Our results demonstrate that even superhuman AI systems may harbor surprising failure modes. Example games are available https://goattack.far.ai/.

paragraphs: A Go system can outperform human players yet still make severe mistakes against a deliberately chosen opponent. This paper trains adversarial policies against KataGo to uncover such weaknesses. The resulting opponents achieve a win rate above 97% against KataGo operating at settings described as superhuman.

The adversaries succeed by provoking serious blunders rather than through generally strong Go play. Their attack also transfers to other superhuman Go systems without additional training against those systems. Human experts can understand the strategy well enough to implement it without algorithmic assistance and consistently defeat superhuman opponents. This makes the discovered weakness accessible through a human-executable strategy as well as a trained policy.

The authors further report that the core vulnerability remains in KataGo agents adversarially trained to resist the attack. These results establish a concrete separation between exceptional playing strength and resistance to targeted exploitation. They show that superhuman performance can coexist with surprising failure modes, including one that the reported defensive training does not eliminate.
summary.tldr: Trained adversarial opponents beat superhuman KataGo by provoking blunders, with attacks that transfer to other Go AIs and can be executed by human experts.

title: Adversarial Policies Beat Superhuman Go AIs

abstract: Accelerated magnetic resonance (MR) imaging attempts to reduce acquisition time by collecting data below the Nyquist rate. As an ill-posed inverse problem, many plausible solutions exist, yet the majority of deep learning approaches generate only a single solution. We instead focus on sampling from the posterior distribution, which provides more comprehensive information for downstream inference tasks. To do this, we design a novel conditional normalizing flow (CNF) that infers the signal component in the measurement operator’s nullspace, which is later combined with measured data to form complete images. Using fastMRI brain and knee data, we demonstrate fast inference and accuracy that surpasses recent posterior sampling techniques for MRI. Code is available at https://github.com/jwen307/mri_cnf

paragraphs: Accelerated MR imaging collects fewer measurements to shorten acquisition time. The resulting reconstruction problem can admit many plausible images, so producing a single image leaves part of that ambiguity unexplored. This paper instead learns to sample from the posterior distribution: a distribution of possible images conditioned on the available measurements.

The proposed conditional normalizing flow targets the signal component in the measurement operator’s nullspace. This is the part of the signal that the measurements do not determine. The model infers that missing component and then combines it with measured data to construct complete images. This design ties the generative task directly to the structure of the reconstruction problem.

Experiments using fastMRI brain and knee data report fast inference and better accuracy than recent MRI posterior sampling techniques. The contribution therefore concerns both reconstruction performance and the ability to produce multiple plausible solutions. Such samples can provide downstream inference tasks with more comprehensive information than a single reconstruction, while the reported comparisons establish the method’s effectiveness on the evaluated data.
summary.tldr: A conditional normalizing flow reconstructs accelerated MRI by sampling unmeasured signal components, producing plausible images with strong reported accuracy and fast inference.

title: A Conditional Normalizing Flow for Accelerated Multi-Coil MR Imaging

abstract: In reinforcement learning, unsupervised skill discovery aims to learn diverse skills without extrinsic rewards. Previous methods discover skills by maximizing the mutual information (MI) between states and skills. However, such an MI objective tends to learn simple and static skills and may hinder exploration. In this paper, we propose a novel unsupervised skill discovery method through contrastive learning among behaviors, which makes the agent produce similar behaviors for the same skill and diverse behaviors for different skills. Under mild assumptions, our objective maximizes the MI between different behaviors based on the same skill, which serves as an upper bound of the previous MI objective. Meanwhile, our method implicitly increases the state entropy to obtain better state coverage. We evaluate our method on challenging mazes and continuous control tasks. The results show that our method generates diverse and far-reaching skills, and also obtains competitive performance in downstream tasks compared to the state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Unsupervised skill discovery seeks to give a reinforcement learning agent diverse behaviors without supplying external rewards. Earlier approaches often maximize mutual information between states and skills, encouraging states to reveal which skill is active. The authors argue that this objective can favor simple, static skills and restrict exploration.

Their alternative contrasts behaviors directly. It encourages behaviors produced by the same skill to resemble one another while making behaviors from different skills distinct. Under mild assumptions, the objective maximizes mutual information between different behaviors associated with the same skill. That quantity upper-bounds the earlier state-and-skill mutual-information objective.

The method also implicitly increases state entropy, supporting broader coverage of the environment. In challenging mazes and continuous control tasks, it produces diverse skills that reach farther through the environment and delivers competitive downstream performance against state-of-the-art methods. Together, the theoretical relationship and experiments support using behavioral diversity to learn skills that do more than remain distinguishable at isolated states.
summary.tldr: Contrasting behaviors helps agents discover diverse, far-reaching skills without external rewards.

title: Behavior Contrastive Learning for Unsupervised Skill Discovery

abstract: Learning decompositions of expensive-to-evaluate black-box functions promises to scale Bayesian optimisation (BO) to high-dimensional problems. However, the success of these techniques depends on finding proper decompositions that accurately represent the black-box. While previous works learn those decompositions based on data, we investigate data-independent decomposition sampling rules in this paper. We find that data-driven learners of decompositions can be easily misled towards local decompositions that do not hold globally across the search space. Then, we formally show that a random tree-based decomposition sampler exhibits favourable theoretical guarantees that effectively trade off maximal information gain and functional mismatch between the actual black-box and its surrogate as provided by the decomposition. Those results motivate the development of the random decomposition upper-confidence bound algorithm (RDUCB) that is straightforward to implement - (almost) plug-and-play - and, surprisingly, yields significant empirical gains compared to the previous state-of-the-art on a comprehensive set of benchmarks. We also confirm the plug-and-play nature of our modelling component by integrating our method with HEBO, showing improved practical gains in the highest dimensional tasks from Bayesmark problem suite.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimisation searches for good inputs to a function that is expensive to evaluate. In high dimensions, splitting the function into smaller components can make this search more manageable. The difficulty is choosing a decomposition that represents the function across the search space. This paper shows that learning decompositions from observed data can favor patterns that work locally but fail more broadly.

The authors instead study decomposition sampling rules that do not depend on the observations. They establish theoretical guarantees for a random tree-based sampler that balances two considerations: how much information the search can gain and how much the decomposed model differs from the true function. This analysis motivates the random decomposition upper-confidence bound algorithm, RDUCB.

RDUCB achieves substantial empirical improvements over previous leading methods across the reported benchmarks. Integrating its modelling component into HEBO also improves results on the highest-dimensional Bayesmark tasks. These findings support random decomposition as a useful, easily integrated alternative, without establishing that it is sufficient for every high-dimensional optimisation problem.
summary.tldr: Random tree-based decompositions provide theoretical guarantees and strong empirical results for high-dimensional Bayesian optimisation.

title: Are Random Decompositions all we need in High Dimensional Bayesian Optimisation?

abstract: When users stand to gain from certain predictive outcomes, they are prone to act strategically to obtain predictions that are favorable. Most current works consider strategic behavior that manifests as users modifying their features; instead, we study a novel setting in which users decide whether to even participate (or not), this in response to the learned classifier. Considering learning approaches of increasing strategic awareness, we investigate the effects of user self-selection on learning, and the implications of learning on the composition of the self-selected population. Building on this, we propose a differentiable framework for learning under self-selective behavior, which can be optimized effectively. We conclude with experiments on real data and simulated behavior that complement our analysis and demonstrate the utility of our approach.

paragraphs: A classifier can influence who chooses to be evaluated by it. If people benefit from receiving a favorable prediction, they may decide whether to participate based on the classifier they expect to face. This paper studies that form of strategic behavior, making participation itself part of the learning problem.

The authors examine learning approaches with increasing awareness of this self-selection. Their analysis follows both directions of the interaction: users’ participation decisions affect learning, and the learned classifier affects the composition of the participating population. This matters because the population a model encounters can depend on the model’s own decision rule, rather than remaining fixed throughout the process.

Building on this analysis, the paper introduces a differentiable framework that incorporates self-selective behavior and can be optimized effectively. Experiments combine real data with simulated user behavior and demonstrate the approach’s utility. The findings support accounting for strategic participation when designing classifiers, with the experimental evidence specifically reflecting the simulated behavioral responses used in the study.
summary.tldr: A differentiable learning framework accounts for users strategically deciding whether to participate in response to a classifier.

title: Classification Under Strategic Self-Selection

abstract: Discovering features with synergistic interactions in multi-view data, that provide more information gain when considered together than when considered separately, is particularly valuable. This fosters a more comprehensive understanding of the target outcome from diverse perspectives (views). However, despite the increasing opportunities presented by multi-view data, surprisingly little attention has been paid to uncovering these crucial interactions. To address this gap, we formally define the problem of selecting synergistic and non-synergistic feature subsets in multi-view data, leveraging an information-theoretic concept known as interaction information. To this end, we introduce a novel deep learning-based feature selection method that identifies different interactions across multiple views, employing a Bernoulli relaxation technique to solve this intractable subset searching problem. Experiments on synthetic, semi-synthetic, and real-world multi-view datasets demonstrate that our model discovers relevant feature subsets with synergistic and non-synergistic interactions, achieving remarkable similarity to the ground truth. Furthermore, we corroborate the discovered features with supporting medical and scientific literature, underscoring its utility in elucidating complex dependencies and interactions in multi-view data.

paragraphs: When data describes an outcome from several perspectives, useful information can lie in combinations of features. A synergistic interaction occurs when features provide more information together than separately. This paper focuses on identifying such combinations across multiple views, alongside feature subsets whose interactions are non-synergistic.

The authors formalize this selection problem using interaction information, an information-theoretic concept for describing relationships among variables. They introduce a deep learning method that searches for feature subsets with different interaction types. Because direct subset search is intractable, the method employs a Bernoulli relaxation to make the selection problem amenable to its learning procedure.

Experiments on synthetic, semi-synthetic, and real-world datasets show that the method discovers relevant feature subsets and closely matches ground truth in the reported evaluations. The authors also corroborate discovered features using medical and scientific literature. This provides support for the interpretive usefulness of the selected combinations: the method aims to reveal dependencies across views, rather than merely rank individual features by how informative they appear alone.
summary.tldr: An information-theoretic feature-selection method identifies combinations across multiple data views that become especially informative when considered together.

title: Discovering Features with Synergistic Interactions in Multiple Views

abstract: The computational efficiency of many neural operators, widely used for learning solutions of PDEs, relies on the fast Fourier transform (FFT) for performing spectral computations. As the FFT is limited to equispaced (rectangular) grids, this limits the efficiency of such neural operators when applied to problems where the input and output functions need to be processed on general non-equispaced point distributions. Leveraging the observation that a limited set of Fourier (Spectral) modes suffice to provide the required expressivity of a neural operator, we propose a simple method, based on the efficient direct evaluation of the underlying spectral transformation, to extend neural operators to arbitrary domains. An efficient implementation of such direct spectral evaluations is coupled with existing neural operator models to allow the processing of data on arbitrary non-equispaced distributions of points. With extensive empirical evaluation, we demonstrate that the proposed method allows us to extend neural operators to arbitrary point distributions with significant gains in training speed over baselines, while retaining or improving the accuracy of Fourier neural operators (FNOs) and related neural operators.

paragraphs: Neural operators learn relationships between functions, including mappings used to predict solutions of partial differential equations. Many gain computational efficiency from the fast Fourier transform. Its reliance on evenly spaced rectangular grids becomes restrictive when the available measurements or desired outputs lie on irregularly distributed points.

The paper proposes evaluating the underlying spectral transformation directly. Its central observation is that a limited number of Fourier modes can provide the expressivity a neural operator needs. Working with this smaller collection makes direct spectral evaluation a practical route to handling arbitrary point distributions. The authors integrate an efficient implementation with existing neural operator models.

Extensive empirical evaluation reports substantial training-speed improvements over baselines while preserving or improving the accuracy of Fourier neural operators and related models. The contribution connects the representation a model actually uses to the computation it requires: if only a limited set of modes is needed, processing irregular points need not depend on the regular-grid machinery that originally made these models efficient.
summary.tldr: Directly evaluating a limited set of Fourier modes extends neural operators to irregular point distributions with reported gains in training speed.

title: Beyond Regular Grids: Fourier-Based Neural Operators on Arbitrary Domains

abstract: In offline reinforcement learning, the challenge of out-of-distribution (OOD) is pronounced. To address this, existing methods often constrain the learned policy through policy regularization. However, these methods often suffer from the issue of unnecessary conservativeness, hampering policy improvement. This occurs due to the indiscriminate use of all actions from the behavior policy that generates the offline dataset as constraints. The problem becomes particularly noticeable when the quality of the dataset is suboptimal. Thus, we propose Adaptive Advantage-guided Policy Regularization (A2PR), obtaining high-advantage actions from an augmented behavior policy combined with VAE to guide the learned policy. A2PR can select high-advantage actions that differ from those present in the dataset, while still effectively maintaining conservatism from OOD actions. This is achieved by harnessing the VAE capacity to generate samples matching the distribution of the data points. We theoretically prove that the improvement of the behavior policy is guaranteed. Besides, it effectively mitigates value overestimation with a bounded performance gap. Empirically, we conduct a series of experiments on the D4RL benchmark, where A2PR demonstrates state-of-the-art performance. Furthermore, experimental results on additional suboptimal mixed datasets reveal that A2PR exhibits superior performance. Code is available at https://github.com/ltlhuuu/A2PR.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns decisions from an existing dataset. Keeping a learned policy close to the behavior that generated those data can protect against unreliable estimates for unfamiliar actions. However, treating every recorded action as equally worth following can also preserve poor decisions, especially when the dataset contains suboptimal behavior.

Adaptive Advantage-guided Policy Regularization, or A2PR, makes this constraint more selective. It uses an augmented behavior policy together with a variational autoencoder to obtain actions with high advantage: actions estimated to be better than the policy's usual choices. The autoencoder can propose actions beyond the exact recorded examples while generating samples consistent with the data distribution.

This creates room for improvement while retaining caution around actions outside the supported distribution. The paper provides a theoretical guarantee of behavior-policy improvement and results on reducing value overestimation with a bounded performance gap. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on D4RL and superior results on additional suboptimal mixed datasets, supporting the usefulness of selective regularization.
summary.tldr: A2PR guides offline policy learning toward high-advantage actions while retaining distribution-based caution.

title: Adaptive Advantage-Guided Policy Regularization for Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Existing work in scientific machine learning (SciML) has shown that data-driven learning of solution operators can provide a fast approximate alternative to classical numerical partial differential equation (PDE) solvers. Of these, Neural Operators (NOs) have emerged as particularly promising. We observe that several uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods for NOs fail for test inputs that are even moderately out-of-domain (OOD), even when the model approximates the solution well for in-domain tasks. To address this limitation, we show that ensembling several NOs can identify high-error regions and provide good uncertainty estimates that are well-correlated with prediction errors. Based on this, we propose a cost-effective alternative, DiverseNO, that mimics the properties of the ensemble by encouraging diverse predictions from its multiple heads in the last feed-forward layer. We then introduce Operator-ProbConserv, a method that uses these well-calibrated UQ estimates within the ProbConserv framework to update the model. Our empirical results show that Operator-ProbConserv enhances OOD model performance for a variety of challenging PDE problems and satisfies physical constraints such as conservation laws.

title: Using Uncertainty Quantification to Characterize and Improve Out-of-Domain Learning for PDEs

abstract: Graph neural network architectures aligned with the $k$-dimensional Weisfeiler–Leman ($k$-WL) hierarchy offer theoretically well-understood expressive power. However, these architectures often fail to deliver state-of-the-art predictive performance on real-world graphs, limiting their practical utility. While recent works aligning graph transformer architectures with the $k$-WL hierarchy have shown promising empirical results, employing transformers for higher orders of $k$ remains challenging due to a prohibitive runtime and memory complexity of self-attention as well as impractical architectural assumptions, such as an infeasible number of attention heads. Here, we advance the alignment of transformers with the $k$-WL hierarchy, showing stronger expressivity results for each $k$, making them more feasible in practice. In addition, we develop a theoretical framework that allows the study of established positional encodings such as Laplacian PEs and SPE. We evaluate our transformers on the large-scale PCQM4Mv2 dataset, showing competitive predictive performance with the state-of-the-art and demonstrating strong downstream performance when fine-tuning them on small-scale molecular datasets.

Applying transformers at higher orders also introduces substantial runtime and memory demands.

This paper strengthens the connection between transformers and the hierarchy, establishing stronger expressivity results for each order while making the constructions more feasible in practice. The motivation includes avoiding impractical architectural requirements in earlier approaches, such as infeasible numbers of attention heads. The authors also develop a framework for analyzing established positional encodings, including Laplacian encodings and SPE.

Experiments on PCQM4Mv2 show predictive performance competitive with the state of the art. Fine-tuning on smaller molecular datasets also produces strong downstream results. Together, the theory and experiments connect formal graph-discrimination capabilities with practical prediction, without claiming that greater expressivity alone guarantees better performance on every graph task.
summary.tldr: The paper strengthens transformers’ alignment with the Weisfeiler–Leman hierarchy and demonstrates competitive molecular prediction performance.

title: Aligning Transformers with Weisfeiler-Leman

abstract: Randomized Smoothing (RS) is currently a scalable certified defense method providing robustness certification against adversarial examples. Although significant progress has been achieved in providing defenses against $\ell_p$ adversaries, the interaction between the smoothing distribution and the robustness certification still remains vague. In this work, we comprehensively study the effect of two families of distributions, named Exponential Standard Gaussian (ESG) and Exponential General Gaussian (EGG) distributions, on Randomized Smoothing and Double Sampling Randomized Smoothing (DSRS). We derive an analytic formula for ESG’s certified radius, which converges to the origin formula of RS as the dimension $d$ increases. Additionally, we prove that EGG can provide tighter constant factors than DSRS in providing $\Omega(\sqrt{d})$ lower bounds of $\ell_2$ certified radius, and thus further addresses the curse of dimensionality in RS. Our experiments on real-world datasets confirm our theoretical analysis of the ESG distributions, that they provide almost the same certification under different exponents $\eta$ for both RS and DSRS. In addition, EGG brings a significant improvement to the DSRS certification, but the mechanism can be different when the classifier properties are different. Compared to the primitive DSRS, the increase in certified accuracy provided by EGG is prominent, up to 6.4% on ImageNet.

paragraphs: Randomized smoothing certifies robustness by averaging a classifier under input noise, so the noise distribution affects the guarantee. This paper studies two distribution families, Exponential Standard Gaussian and Exponential General Gaussian, for ordinary and double-sampling randomized smoothing. The goal is to understand which changes genuinely improve certification.

For the standard family, the authors derive an analytic certified-radius formula that approaches the original smoothing formula as dimension increases. For the generalized family, they prove tighter constants in an Ω(√d) lower bound on the ℓ₂ certified radius. The analysis distinguishes improvements in constants from changes in the dimensional scaling itself.

Experiments confirm that changing exponents in the standard family yields nearly identical certification, while the generalized family improves double-sampling certification. The reported certified-accuracy gain reaches 6.4% on ImageNet. The mechanism can depend on classifier properties, so the result supports a distribution-sensitive approach rather than one universal explanation for all smoothed models.
summary.tldr: Analyzing exponential Gaussian noise identifies when distribution changes improve randomized-smoothing certificates, including stronger ImageNet results.

title: Effects of Exponential Gaussian Distribution on (Double Sampling) Randomized Smoothing

abstract: Smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) is omnipresent in modern engineering and scientific disciplines. SPH is a class of Lagrangian schemes that discretize fluid dynamics via finite material points that are tracked through the evolving velocity field. Due to the particle-like nature of the simulation, graph neural networks (GNNs) have emerged as appealing and successful surrogates. However, the practical utility of such GNN-based simulators relies on their ability to faithfully model physics, providing accurate and stable predictions over long time horizons - which is a notoriously hard problem. In this work, we identify particle clustering originating from tensile instabilities as one of the primary pitfalls. Based on these insights, we enhance both training and rollout inference of state-of-the-art GNN-based simulators with varying components from standard SPH solvers, including pressure, viscous, and external force components. All Neural SPH-enhanced simulators achieve better performance than the baseline GNNs, often by orders of magnitude in terms of rollout error, allowing for significantly longer rollouts and significantly better physics modeling. Code available under https://github.com/tumaer/neuralsph.

paragraphs: Smoothed particle hydrodynamics represents fluid using material points that move with the evolving flow. This particle structure makes graph neural networks attractive substitutes for conventional simulators. Their practical usefulness, however, depends on maintaining accurate and physically faithful predictions over many successive simulation steps.

The paper identifies particle clustering caused by tensile instabilities as a major source of difficulty. Guided by that diagnosis, Neural SPH incorporates components from standard SPH solvers into both training and rollout inference for existing graph neural simulators. The components include pressure, viscosity, and external forces, with different enhancements using varying combinations.

All of the enhanced simulators in the reported evaluation outperform their baseline graph neural networks. Rollout error often improves by orders of magnitude, enabling substantially longer rollouts and better modeling of the physics. The findings link a particular instability to a practical remedy: bringing established fluid-simulation components into learned simulators at both learning and prediction time. The reported improvements concern the evaluated enhancements and baselines, with the largest error reductions occurring often rather than in every case.
summary.tldr: Neural SPH adds conventional fluid-solver components to graph neural simulators, improving accuracy and enabling longer rollouts.

title: Neural SPH: Improved Neural Modeling of Lagrangian Fluid Dynamics

abstract: Distribution shifts are ubiquitous in real-world machine learning applications, posing a challenge to the generalization of models trained on one data distribution to another. We focus on scenarios where data distributions vary across multiple segments of the entire population and only make local assumptions about the differences between training and test (deployment) distributions within each segment. We propose a two-stage multiply robust estimation method to improve model performance on each individual segment for tabular data analysis. The method involves fitting a linear combination of the based models, learned using clusters of training data from multiple segments, followed by a refinement step for each segment. Our method is designed to be implemented with commonly used off-the-shelf machine learning models. We establish theoretical guarantees on the generalization bound of the method on the test risk. With extensive experiments on synthetic and real datasets, we demonstrate that the proposed method substantially improves over existing alternatives in prediction accuracy and robustness on both regression and classification tasks. We also assess its effectiveness on a user city prediction dataset from Meta.

paragraphs: This paper addresses prediction when training and deployment data differ across segments of a population. It makes local assumptions about distribution changes within each segment. That focus matters because the learning problem is organized around improving performance for individual segments while drawing on data available across multiple domains.

The proposed method has two stages. First, it fits a linear combination of base models learned from clusters of training data spanning multiple segments. It then refines the result separately for each segment. The design works with commonly used, off-the-shelf machine learning models, making the contribution a way of combining and adapting predictors for tabular data.

The authors establish a generalization bound for test risk and evaluate the method on synthetic and real datasets. They report substantial improvements over existing alternatives in prediction accuracy and robustness for both regression and classification. They also assess it on a Meta user-city prediction dataset. These findings support combining information across segments with local refinement under the paper’s assumptions about distribution shifts.
summary.tldr: A two-stage method combines models across population segments and refines them locally to improve prediction under local distribution-shift assumptions.

title: Multiply Robust Estimation for Local Distribution Shifts with Multiple Domains

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown great promise in tasks like node and graph classification, but they often struggle to generalize, particularly to unseen or out-of-distribution (OOD) data. These challenges are exacerbated when training data is limited in size or diversity. To address these issues, we introduce a theoretical framework using Rademacher complexity to compute a regret bound on the generalization error and then characterize the effect of data augmentation. This framework informs the design of GRATIN, an efficient graph data augmentation algorithm leveraging the capability of Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) to approximate any distribution. Our approach not only outperforms existing augmentation techniques in terms of generalization but also offers improved time complexity, making it highly suitable for real-world applications.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can struggle when asked to handle unseen or out-of-distribution data, particularly when their training examples are limited or insufficiently diverse. This paper studies data augmentation as a response to that problem. Its approach connects a theoretical analysis of generalization with the design of an efficient augmentation algorithm.

The theoretical framework uses Rademacher complexity to derive a regret bound on generalization error and characterize how augmentation affects it. This analysis informs GRATIN, an augmentation method based on Gaussian mixture models. The method draws on the ability of Gaussian mixtures to approximate distributions, making distribution modeling central to how additional graph data is constructed.

The authors report better generalization than existing augmentation techniques together with improved time complexity. These findings make the contribution twofold: the framework supplies a way to reason about augmentation's effect, and GRATIN turns that reasoning into a practical method. The result supports distribution-based augmentation as a promising means of improving graph learning when the original data offers limited size or diversity.
summary.tldr: GRATIN uses Gaussian mixture models and generalization theory to improve graph data augmentation, with reported gains in generalization and time complexity.

title: Graph Neural Network Generalization With Gaussian Mixture Model Based Augmentation

abstract: Maximum entropy reinforcement learning (MaxEnt-RL) has become the standard approach to RL due to its beneficial exploration properties. Traditionally, policies are parameterized using Gaussian distributions, which significantly limits their representational capacity. Diffusion-based policies offer a more expressive alternative, yet integrating them into MaxEnt-RL poses challenges—primarily due to the intractability of computing their marginal entropy. To overcome this, we propose Diffusion-Based Maximum Entropy RL (DIME). DIME leverages recent advances in approximate inference with diffusion models to derive a lower bound on the maximum entropy objective. Additionally, we propose a policy iteration scheme that provably converges to the optimal diffusion policy. Our method enables the use of expressive diffusion-based policies while retaining the principled exploration benefits of MaxEnt-RL, significantly outperforming other diffusion-based methods on challenging high-dimensional control benchmarks. It is also competitive with state-of-the-art non-diffusion based RL methods while requiring fewer algorithmic design choices and smaller update-to-data ratios, reducing computational complexity.

paragraphs: Maximum entropy reinforcement learning encourages exploration alongside reward seeking. Conventional Gaussian policies restrict the distributions of actions a policy can represent. Diffusion policies offer greater flexibility, but their marginal entropy is difficult to compute, creating an obstacle to using them within the maximum entropy objective.

DIME addresses that obstacle using approximate inference methods for diffusion models. The authors derive a lower bound on the maximum entropy objective, providing a tractable basis for learning expressive policies. They also introduce a policy iteration scheme and prove that it converges to the optimal diffusion policy. The guarantee concerns that policy setting, rather than unrestricted optimality across every possible policy representation.

On challenging high-dimensional control benchmarks, DIME substantially outperforms other diffusion-based methods. It is also competitive with leading methods that do not use diffusion, while requiring fewer algorithmic design choices and smaller update-to-data ratios. Together, these findings support diffusion policies as a practical way to expand policy expressiveness while retaining the exploration rationale of maximum entropy learning.
summary.tldr: DIME uses a lower-bound objective to combine expressive diffusion policies with maximum entropy reinforcement learning.

title: DIME: Diffusion-Based Maximum Entropy Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Modern machine learning applications are characterized by the increasing size of deep models and the growing diversity of data modalities. This trend underscores the importance of efficiently adapting pre-trained multi-modal models to the test distribution in real time, i.e., multi-modal test-time adaptation. In practice, the magnitudes of multi-modal shifts vary because multiple data sources interact with the impact factor in diverse manners. In this research, we investigate the the under-explored practical scenario uni-modal distribution shift, where the distribution shift influences only one modality, leaving the others unchanged. Through theoretical and empirical analyses, we demonstrate that the presence of such shift impedes multi-modal fusion and leads to the negative transfer phenomenon in existing test-time adaptation techniques. To flexibly combat this unique shift, we propose a selective adaptation schema that incorporates multiple modality-specific adapters to accommodate potential shifts and a “router” module that determines which modality requires adaptation. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of our proposed method through extensive experimental evaluations. Code available at https://github.com/chenmc1996/Uni-Modal-Distribution-Shift.

paragraphs: A multimodal model may encounter a change in only one of its input sources while the others remain stable. This paper studies that specific test-time adaptation problem. It matters because applying adaptation across a combined model must account for the unequal effects of a distribution shift on its different modalities.

Through theoretical and empirical analysis, the authors show that a shift affecting one modality can disrupt multimodal fusion and cause negative transfer in existing adaptation methods. Their proposed system uses separate adapters for individual modalities, together with a router that determines which modality needs adaptation. The architecture explicitly separates detecting the affected input source from adjusting its processing.

Extensive experiments support the effectiveness of this selective scheme. The central finding is that adaptation decisions should reflect where a shift occurs within multimodal data. Under the studied setting, routing adaptation toward the affected modality offers a way to respond to changing inputs while accounting for the fact that other sources remain unchanged.
summary.tldr: Modality-specific adapters and a router improve test-time adaptation when a distribution shift affects only one modality.

title: Test-Time Selective Adaptation for Uni-Modal Distribution Shift in Multi-Modal Data

abstract: Actor-critic algorithms have been instrumental in boosting the performance of numerous challenging applications involving continuous control, such as highly robust and agile robot motion control. However, their theoretical understanding remains largely underdeveloped. Existing analyses mostly focus on finite state-action spaces and on simplified variants of actor-critic, such as double-loop updates with i.i.d. sampling, which are often impractical for real-world applications. We consider the canonical and widely adopted single-timescale updates with Markovian sampling in continuous state-action space. Specifically, we establish finite-time convergence by introducing a novel Lyapunov analysis framework, which provides a unified convergence characterization of both the actor and the critic. Our approach is less conservative than previous methods and offers new insights into the coupled dynamics of actor-critic updates.

paragraphs: Actor-critic methods are widely used in continuous control, but much of their theoretical analysis focuses on simplified settings. These include finite state and action spaces, separate update loops, or independently sampled data. This paper studies a formulation closer to common practice: single-timescale updates in continuous spaces with Markovian sampling.

In this setting, the actor and critic evolve together, while samples retain the dependence associated with a Markov process. The authors introduce a Lyapunov analysis framework that characterizes convergence of both components jointly. This allows their interaction to be treated as part of the central mathematical problem.

The paper establishes finite-time convergence and describes the analysis as less conservative than previous approaches. Its main contribution is theoretical: it provides a unified account of the coupled learning dynamics under the stated update and sampling setup. By addressing continuous spaces and dependent sampling together, the result strengthens the connection between actor-critic convergence analysis and the algorithms commonly used for continuous-control applications.
summary.tldr: A joint Lyapunov analysis establishes finite-time convergence for single-timescale actor-critic updates in continuous spaces with Markovian sampling.

title: On the Convergence of Continuous Single-timescale Actor-critic

abstract: Vision Transformers (ViT) are remarkable at 3D pose estimation, yet they still encounter certain challenges. One issue is that the popular ViT architecture for pose estimation is limited to images and lacks temporal information. Another challenge is that the prediction often fails to maintain pixel alignment with the original images. To address these issues, we propose a systematic framework for 3D pose estimation, called ExtPose. ExtPose extends image ViT to the challenging scenario and video setting by taking in additional 2D pose evidence and capturing temporal information in a full attention-based manner. We use 2D human skeleton images to integrate structured 2D pose information. By sharing parameters and attending across modalities and frames, we enhance the consistency between 3D poses and 2D videos without introducing additional parameters. We achieve state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on multiple human and hand pose estimation benchmarks with substantial improvements to 34.0mm (-23%) on 3DPW and 4.9mm (-18%) on FreiHAND in PA-MPJPE over the other ViT-based methods respectively.

paragraphs: Vision Transformers can estimate three-dimensional poses, but image-based architectures lack temporal information and may produce predictions that do not align well with image pixels. ExtPose extends these models to incorporate additional two-dimensional pose evidence and information across video frames, aiming for more consistent three-dimensional predictions.

The method represents structured pose evidence using images of human skeletons. It then uses attention across modalities and frames to connect this evidence with the visual input and temporal context. Parameter sharing allows these extensions without adding parameters. The design brings spatial structure and temporal information into a common attention-based framework.

summary.tldr: ExtPose adds structured 2D pose evidence and temporal attention to ViTs without extra parameters, improving human and hand pose estimation.

title: ExtPose: Robust and Coherent Pose Estimation by Extending ViTs

abstract: In-context learning (ICL) is a remarkable capability of pretrained transformers that allows models to generalize to unseen tasks after seeing only a few examples. We investigate empirically the conditions necessary on the pretraining distribution for ICL to emerge and generalize out-of-distribution. Previous work has focused on the number of distinct tasks necessary in the pretraining dataset. Here, we use a different notion of task diversity to study the emergence of ICL in transformers trained on linear functions. We find that as task diversity increases, transformers undergo a transition from a specialized solution, which exhibits ICL only within the pretraining task distribution, to a solution which generalizes out of distribution to the entire task space. We also investigate the nature of the solutions learned by the transformer on both sides of the transition, and observe similar transitions in nonlinear regression problems. We construct a phase diagram to characterize how our concept of task diversity interacts with the number of pretraining tasks. In addition, we explore how factors such as the depth of the model and the dimensionality of the regression problem influence the transition.

It investigates the question empirically using transformers trained on linear functions, emphasizing a notion of task diversity that differs from simply counting distinct training tasks.

As diversity increases, the authors observe a transition in the learned behavior. On one side, the model performs in-context learning only within the pretraining task distribution. On the other, it generalizes across the entire task space in the studied setting. They also examine the kinds of solutions learned on both sides and observe similar transitions in nonlinear regression.

A phase diagram describes how diversity interacts with the number of pretraining tasks. Additional experiments explore model depth and regression dimensionality as influences on the transition. The findings suggest that understanding generalization requires examining how training tasks are distributed as well as how many there are, with the evidence grounded in the regression problems studied.
summary.tldr: Regression experiments reveal a task-diversity-driven transition from specialized in-context learning to generalization beyond the pretraining task distribution.

title: When can in-context learning generalize out of task distribution?

abstract: Long-term time series forecasting (LTSF) has traditionally relied on large parameters to capture extended temporal dependencies, resulting in substantial computational costs and inefficiencies in both memory usage and processing time. However, time series data, unlike high-dimensional images or text, often exhibit temporal pattern similarity and low-rank structures, especially in long-term horizons. By leveraging this structure, models can be guided to focus on more essential, concise temporal data, improving both accuracy and computational efficiency. In this paper, we introduce TimeBase, an ultra-lightweight network to harness the power of minimalism in LTSF. TimeBase 1) extracts core basis temporal components and 2) transforms traditional point-level forecasting into efficient segment-level forecasting, achieving optimal utilization of both data and parameters. Extensive experiments on diverse real-world datasets show that TimeBase achieves remarkable efficiency and secures competitive forecasting performance. Additionally, TimeBase can also serve as a very effective plug-and-play complexity reducer for any patch-based forecasting models. Code is available at https://github.com/hqh0728/TimeBase.

TimeBase starts from the observation that time series often contain similar temporal patterns and low-rank structure, particularly over long horizons. These properties suggest that a compact representation may capture much of the useful forecasting information.

The method extracts core temporal basis components and changes the forecasting unit from individual points to segments. Together, these choices direct the network toward a concise representation of the time series and reduce the complexity of producing long forecasts. The architecture is designed to make efficient use of both the data and its parameters.

Experiments on diverse real-world datasets show strong efficiency with competitive forecasting performance. The abstract also reports that TimeBase can act as a plug-and-play complexity reducer for patch-based forecasting models. The results support exploiting recurring temporal structure when seeking lower computational cost without losing competitive accuracy.
summary.tldr: TimeBase uses compact temporal components and segment-level forecasting to achieve strong efficiency with competitive long-term forecasting performance.

title: TimeBase: The Power of Minimalism in Efficient Long-term Time Series Forecasting

abstract: Pathology image segmentation plays a pivotal role in artificial digital pathology diagnosis and treatment. Existing approaches to pathology image segmentation are hindered by labor-intensive annotation processes and limited accuracy in tail-class identification, primarily due to the long-tail distribution inherent in gigapixel pathology images. In this work, we introduce the Laplace Diffusion Model, referred to as L-Diffusion, an innovative framework tailored for efficient pathology image segmentation. L-Diffusion utilizes multiple Laplace distributions, as opposed to Gaussian distributions, to model distinct components—a methodology supported by theoretical analysis that significantly enhances the decomposition of features within the feature space. A sequence of feature maps is initially generated through a series of diffusion steps. Following this, contrastive learning is employed to refine the pixel-wise vectors derived from the feature map sequence. By utilizing these highly discriminative pixel-wise vectors, the segmentation module achieves a harmonious balance of precision and robustness with remarkable efficiency. Extensive experimental evaluations demonstrate that L-Diffusion attains improvements of up to 7.16%, 26.74%, 16.52%, and 3.55% on tissue segmentation datasets, and 20.09%, 10.67%, 14.42%, and 10.41% on cell segmentation datasets, as quantified by DICE, MPA, mIoU, and FwIoU metrics. The source are available at https://github.com/Lweihan/LDiffusion.

These findings support the proposed feature-learning pipeline for segmentation, with the stated gains representing maxima in the evaluations.

title: L-Diffusion: Laplace Diffusion for Efficient Pathology Image Segmentation

abstract: An important question today is whether a given text was used to train a large language model (LLM). A completion test is often employed: check if the LLM completes a sufficiently complex text. This, however, requires a ground-truth definition of membership; most commonly, it is defined as a member based on the n-gram overlap between the target text and any text in the dataset. In this work, we demonstrate that this n-gram based membership definition can be effectively gamed. We study scenarios where sequences are non-members for a given n and we find that completion tests still succeed. We find many natural cases of this phenomenon by retraining LLMs from scratch after removing all training samples that were completed; these cases include exact duplicates, near-duplicates, and even short overlaps. They showcase that it is difficult to find a single viable choice of n for membership definitions. Using these insights, we design adversarial datasets that can cause a given target sequence to be completed without containing it, for any reasonable choice of n. Our findings highlight the inadequacy of n-gram membership, suggesting membership definitions fail to account for auxiliary information available to the training algorithm.

paragraphs: A model's ability to finish a passage exactly is often used as evidence that the passage appeared in training. Interpreting that test requires a definition of training-set membership. This paper examines definitions based on n-gram overlap, which assess membership using matching sequences of a chosen length between the target and training data.

The authors find cases where completion succeeds even though the target is a non-member under the selected definition. They retrain models from scratch after removing training samples that had been completed and identify natural cases involving duplicates, near-duplicates, and short overlaps. These observations make it difficult to select one overlap length that yields a consistently useful membership definition.

Using those insights, the authors construct adversarial datasets that cause a target sequence to be completed without containing it under any reasonable chosen n. The findings challenge the adequacy of overlap-based membership and its interpretation through completion tests. Their explanation emphasizes auxiliary information available during training, which can support exact completion without the target satisfying the chosen membership rule.
summary.tldr: Exact text completion can succeed for sequences classified as absent by n-gram membership rules, exposing weaknesses in those definitions.

title: Language Models May Verbatim Complete Text They Were Not Explicitly Trained On

abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting has become a widely used strategy for improving large language and multimodal model performance. However, it is still an open question under which settings CoT systematically reduces performance. In this paper, we seek to identify the characteristics of tasks where CoT reduces performance by drawing inspiration from cognitive psychology, focusing on six representative tasks from the psychological literature where deliberation hurts performance in humans. In three of these tasks, state-of-the-art models exhibit significant performance drop-offs with CoT (up to 36.3% absolute accuracy for OpenAI o1-preview compared to GPT-4o), while in others, CoT effects are mixed, with positive, neutral, and negative changes. While models and humans do not exhibit perfectly parallel cognitive processes, considering cases where thinking has negative consequences for humans helps identify settings where it negatively impacts models. By connecting the literature on human verbal thinking and deliberation with evaluations of CoT, we offer a perspective for understanding the impact of inference-time reasoning.

paragraphs: Asking a model to reason step by step often improves performance, but the effect depends on the task. This paper investigates settings where chain-of-thought reasoning can make results worse. It takes inspiration from cognitive psychology, selecting six representative tasks where deliberate thinking has been found to harm human performance.

On three of those tasks, the evaluated state-of-the-art models show significant performance declines with chain of thought. The abstract reports a drop of up to 36.3 percentage points in accuracy for OpenAI o1-preview compared with GPT-4o. On the remaining tasks, the effects vary, including improvements, little change, and declines. The reported pattern therefore does not support treating deliberation as uniformly helpful or harmful.

The authors emphasize that model and human cognitive processes are not perfectly parallel. Their contribution is to use known human difficulties as a guide for locating model failures. Connecting psychological findings with model evaluations offers a way to study when additional inference-time reasoning helps and when it can interfere with successful task performance.
summary.tldr: Tasks where deliberation harms humans help identify cases where chain-of-thought reasoning also reduces model performance, although effects vary.

title: Mind Your Step (by Step): Chain-of-Thought can Reduce Performance on Tasks where Thinking Makes Humans Worse

abstract: We address the challenge of optimizing meta-parameters (hyperparameters) in machine learning, a key factor for efficient training and high model performance. Rather than relying on expensive meta-parameter search methods, we introduce MetaOptimize: a dynamic approach that adjusts meta-parameters, particularly step sizes (also known as learning rates), during training. More specifically, MetaOptimize can wrap around any first-order optimization algorithm, tuning step sizes on the fly to minimize a specific form of regret that considers the long-term impact of step sizes on training, through a discounted sum of future losses. We also introduce lower-complexity variants of MetaOptimize that, in conjunction with its adaptability to various optimization algorithms, achieve performance comparable to those of the best hand-crafted learning rate schedules across diverse machine learning tasks.

paragraphs: Learning rates control the size of parameter updates and strongly affect how efficiently a model trains. Choosing them through repeated hyperparameter searches can be expensive. MetaOptimize instead adjusts these training controls during the training run itself, with particular emphasis on step sizes.

The framework can wrap around any first-order optimization algorithm. Its objective is a specific form of regret that accounts for the longer-term effects of learning-rate choices through a discounted sum of future losses. This makes the consequences for subsequent training part of the tuning criterion, giving the method a way to assess step sizes beyond their immediate effect.

The authors also introduce variants with lower computational complexity. Across diverse machine learning tasks, these variants, together with the framework’s compatibility with different optimizers, achieve performance comparable to the best handcrafted learning-rate schedules considered. The contribution is an adaptive mechanism for tuning the training process, reducing reliance on an externally selected schedule while explicitly considering how current choices influence later losses.
summary.tldr: MetaOptimize adjusts learning rates during training using an objective that accounts for their longer-term effects on loss.

title: MetaOptimize: A Framework for Optimizing Step Sizes and Other Meta-parameters

abstract: Generalist robots that can perform a range of different tasks in open-world settings must be able to not only reason about the steps needed to accomplish their goals, but also process complex instructions, prompts, and even feedback during task execution. Intricate instructions (e.g., "Could you make me a vegetarian sandwich?" or "I don’t like that one") require not just the ability to physically perform the individual steps, but the ability to situate complex commands and feedback in the physical world. In this work, we describe a system that uses vision-language models in a hierarchical structure, first reasoning over complex prompts and user feedback to deduce the most appropriate next step to fulfill the task, and then performing that step with low-level actions. In contrast to direct instruction following methods that can fulfill simple commands ("pick up the cup"), our system can reason through complex prompts and incorporate situated feedback during task execution ("that’s not trash"). We evaluate our system across three robotic platforms, including single-arm, dual-arm, and dual-arm mobile robots, demonstrating its ability to handle tasks such as cleaning messy tables, making sandwiches, and grocery shopping. Videos are available at https://www.pi.website/research/hirobot
