paragraphs: A robot handling everyday tasks needs to interpret more than isolated movement commands. Requests can express preferences, involve several steps, or change as a person comments on what is happening. Hi Robot addresses the connection between this richer language and the physical actions needed to carry out a task.

The system arranges vision-language models in a hierarchy. A higher level reasons about the user's request and feedback to choose an appropriate next step. A lower level executes that step through physical actions. This structure connects interpretation to execution while allowing feedback received during the task to influence what the robot does next.

The authors evaluate the system on single-arm, dual-arm, and mobile dual-arm robots. Demonstrated tasks include table cleanup, sandwich preparation, and grocery shopping. These evaluations show the system handling complex requests and feedback grounded in the ongoing physical situation. The contribution is therefore a demonstrated way to connect open-ended instructions with stepwise robotic execution across several platforms and everyday task settings.
summary.tldr: Hi Robot uses hierarchical vision-language reasoning to turn complex requests and ongoing feedback into executable robotic actions.

title: Hi Robot: Open-Ended Instruction Following with Hierarchical Vision-Language-Action Models

abstract: Low-precision training is considered an effective strategy for reducing both training and downstream inference costs. Previous scaling laws for precision mainly focus on integer quantization, which pay less attention to the constituents in floating-point (FP) quantization, and thus cannot well fit the LLM losses in this scenario. In contrast, while FP quantization training is more commonly implemented in production, it’s research has been relatively superficial. In this paper, we thoroughly explore the effects of FP quantization targets, exponent bits, mantissa bits, and the calculation granularity of the scaling factor in FP quantization training performance of LLM models. In addition to an accurate FP quantization unified scaling law, we also provide valuable suggestions for the community: (1) Exponent bits contribute slightly more to the model performance than mantissa bits. We provide the optimal exponent-mantissa bit ratio for different bit numbers, which is available for future reference by hardware manufacturers; (2) We discover the formation of the critical data size in low-precision LLM training. Too much training data exceeding the critical data size will inversely bring in degradation of LLM performance; (3) The optimal FP quantization precision is directly proportional to the computational power, but within a wide computational power range. We estimate that the best cost-performance precision should lie between 4-8 bits.

paragraphs: Low-precision training can reduce training and inference costs, but floating-point precision involves more than a single bit count. The paper studies how quantization targets, exponent bits, mantissa bits, and scaling-factor granularity affect language-model performance. It argues that scaling laws centered on integer quantization do not adequately capture these floating-point choices.

The authors develop a unified scaling law for floating-point quantization and derive guidance for allocating bits. Their findings indicate that exponent bits contribute slightly more to performance than mantissa bits, and they provide preferred ratios for different total precisions. They also identify a critical training-data size beyond which additional data degrades performance in the low-precision setting they analyze.

The resulting picture links numerical format, dataset size, and available computation rather than treating precision as an isolated setting. The authors report that optimal precision grows with computational power and estimate that four to eight bits offers the best cost-performance balance over a broad compute range. This is a scaling-based estimate, with the recommended precision tied to the computational setting.
summary.tldr: A floating-point scaling law connects bit allocation, data size, and compute, estimating a broad cost-performance sweet spot at four to eight bits.

title: Scaling Laws for Floating–Point Quantization Training

abstract: Different from its counterpart outcome reward models (ORMs), which evaluate the entire responses, a process reward model (PRM) scores a reasoning trajectory step by step, providing denser and more fine-grained rewards. However, training a PRM requires labels annotated at every intermediate step, presenting significant challenges for both manual and automatic data collection. This paper aims to address this challenge. Both theoretically and empirically, we show that an implicit PRM can be obtained at no additional cost, by simply training an ORM on the cheaper response-level labels. The only assumption is to parameterize the outcome reward as the log-likelihood ratios of the policy and reference models r$\phi$(y) = $\beta$ log $\pi$$\phi$(y) $\pi$ref(y) , which can be optimized regardless of the specific choice of loss objectives. In experiments, we instantiate our implicit PRMs with various objectives and evaluate their performance on MATH. We show that our implicit PRM outperforms a strong MCTS-based baseline á la Math-Shepherd (Wang et al., 2023) using less than 1/38 of the training data. Its performance can be further improved with majority voting. We further find that scaling up instructions and responses benefits our implicit PRM, and the latter brings a larger gain. Particularly, we find that our implicit PRM, when instantiated with the cross-entropy (CE) loss, is more data-efficient and can keep improving generation models even when trained with only one response per instruction, the setup that suffers from extreme data scarcity and imbalance. Further, instructions should be relevant to downstream tasks while the diversity of responses does not bring gains. Surprisingly, training on extra Math-Shepherd step labels brings no further improvements to our implicit PRM trained on only outcome data. We hope that our work will encourage a rethinking of PRM training approaches and contribute to making training PRMs more accessible.

These findings identify conditions under which cheaper outcome supervision can supply useful stepwise feedback.
summary.tldr: With a specific likelihood-ratio reward parameterization, response-level training yields useful implicit process rewards without step-level labels.

title: Free Process Rewards without Process Labels

abstract: Recent advancements in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have leveraged pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to improve the generalization capabilities. VLMs, typically pre-trained on vision-language understanding tasks, provide rich semantic knowledge and reasoning abilities. However, prior research has shown that VLMs often focus on high-level semantic content and neglect low-level features, limiting their ability to capture detailed spatial information and understand physical dynamics. These aspects, which are crucial for embodied control tasks, remain underexplored in existing pre-training paradigms. In this paper, we investigate the training paradigm for VLAs, and introduce UP-VLA, a Unified VLA model training with both multi-modal Understanding and future Prediction objectives, enhancing both high-level semantic comprehension and low-level spatial understanding. Experimental results show that UP-VLA achieves a 33% improvement on the Calvin ABC-D benchmark compared to the previous state-of-the-art method. Additionally, UP-VLA demonstrates improved success rates in real-world manipulation tasks, particularly those requiring precise spatial information.

Prior research shows that vision-language models can emphasize meaning while overlooking low-level features and physical dynamics.

UP-VLA changes the training paradigm by combining multimodal understanding with future prediction. These objectives are intended to strengthen both semantic comprehension and low-level spatial understanding in one model. The motivation is that embodied action benefits from understanding the current situation and learning to predict what follows, bringing physical detail into the training objective.

Experiments report a 33% improvement over the previous state of the art on the Calvin ABC-D benchmark. Real-world manipulation evaluations also show improved success rates, especially for tasks requiring precise spatial information. The findings support combining understanding and prediction objectives as a way to address the spatial demands of embodied control in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: UP-VLA combines multimodal understanding and future prediction to improve embodied control, particularly tasks requiring precise spatial information.

title: UP-VLA: A Unified Understanding and Prediction Model for Embodied Agent

abstract: Advances in large language models have driven strong performance across many tasks, but their memory and compute costs still hinder deployment. SVD-based compression reduces storage and can speed up inference via low-rank factors, yet performance depends on how rank is allocated under a global compression ratio. Prior methods often use homogeneous ranks for similarly sized matrices, despite large differences in loss sensitivity, or rely on expensive iterative pre-truncation optimization to determine per matrix ranks. We propose Zero Sum SVD (ZS-SVD), a post-training method that performs global singular component selection using activation whitening and first-order calibration loss estimates in whitened coordinates. ZS-SVD prunes components across the whole model with a zero sum rule that keeps the cumulative predicted loss change near zero, automatically yielding heterogeneous ranks without solving a rank allocation optimization. Motivated by evidence that gradients near pretrained solutions exhibit low rank structure, we also introduce an optional lightweight correction that applies a single projected gradient update after truncation, followed by re-truncation. Extensive experiments across multiple LLM architectures show consistent gains across diverse benchmarks and compression ratios. Code is available at https://github.com/mint-vu/Zero-Sum-SVD

paragraphs: Low-rank compression replaces large weight matrices with smaller factors, reducing storage and potentially accelerating inference. Its effectiveness depends on how much rank each matrix retains. Giving similarly sized matrices the same rank ignores differences in their effect on model quality, while optimizing ranks through repeated preliminary truncations can be expensive.

Zero Sum SVD selects singular components across the whole model. It uses activation whitening and first-order estimates of calibration-loss changes to assess components in the transformed coordinates. Its zero-sum rule keeps the cumulative predicted loss change near zero, automatically producing different ranks for different matrices without a separate rank-allocation optimization.

The method also offers a lightweight correction: one projected gradient update after compression, followed by another truncation. This is motivated by evidence of low-rank gradient structure near pretrained solutions. Experiments across multiple architectures, benchmarks, and compression ratios show consistent gains. The approach makes global loss sensitivity the organizing principle for deciding which components to retain.
summary.tldr: Zero Sum SVD allocates compression globally by balancing predicted loss changes across singular components.

title: Zero Sum SVD: Balancing Loss Sensitivity for Low Rank LLM Compression

abstract: Compute-In-Memory (CIM) accelerators are promising for energy-efficient edge inference, yet they faces fundamental challenges when deploying Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), as hardware-induced weight perturbations from intrinsic noise and device drift degrade accuracy and impede reliable inference. To tackle this challenge, we propose Diversity-aware Weight Perturbation (DWP), an immune-system-inspired training method that emulates affinity-based selection by exploiting sample-level prediction disagreement under diverse noise realizations to guide adaptive sample weighting, building robustness to weight perturbation. Experiments show that DWP-trained models consistently yield superior robustness, achieving over 15% accuracy improvements compared to standard-trained models under severe weight perturbations (mismatch level up to 70%) and maintaining inference accuracy at 90% over a simulated one-year CIM operation with only 2%–4% variation in accuracy. Moreover, under matched model and inference configurations, deployment on low-precision CIM hardware reduces inference energy by 38% compared to a GPU baseline. These results demonstrate that DWP enables robust and energy-efficient neural network deployment on resource-constrained edge devices with inherent hardware uncertainties.

paragraphs: Compute-in-memory hardware can reduce inference energy, but device noise and drift perturb model weights and degrade predictions. This paper trains networks to tolerate those hardware uncertainties. Diversity-aware Weight Perturbation uses differences in sample predictions under varied noise realizations to decide where training effort should concentrate.

The adaptive sample-weighting rule is inspired by affinity-based selection in immune systems. By emphasizing disagreement produced by diverse perturbations, the method encourages robustness to changes in deployed weights. The relevant uncertainty comes from hardware behavior, rather than only input noise or ordinary distribution shift.

Experiments report accuracy improvements above 15% over standard training under severe perturbations and around 90% accuracy through a simulated year of operation with small variation. A matched low-precision deployment reduces inference energy by 38% relative to a GPU baseline. The long-term stability result is simulated, and the energy comparison applies to the stated matched configurations.
summary.tldr: Diversity-aware noise training improves robustness to compute-in-memory weight perturbations while supporting the reported energy-efficient deployment.

title: Diversity-aware Weight Perturbation Promotes Robust Adaptation

abstract: Oscillatory neural signals such as electroencephalography (EEG) and local field potentials (LFPs) show phase relationships that coordinate communication across brain regions. Modern recordings capture hundreds of channels across many frequency bins, yet standard phase analyses are restricted to only a few variables. The Torus Graph (TG) model, an exponential-family distribution over phases whose univariate and pairwise potentials generalize von Mises distributions, infers principled structure among oscillations but models only static, undirected dependencies and is limited to $\sim \! 100$ variables because its score matching inference scales as $\mathcal{O}(d^{6})$. We introduce a stochastic score matching procedure that reduces the per-iteration cost to $\mathcal{O}(d^{2})$, enabling inference on datasets with thousands of variables. This scalable foundation supports analyses of 1,860 frequency-phase features from multi-electrode LFPs and enables two extensions previously inaccessible to TGs or classical circular statistics: (i) a TG Hidden Markov Model capturing state-dependent phase-coupling changes (e.g., spindle-related states during sleep) and (ii) an autoregressive TG inferring directional interactions via transfer-entropy estimation. Applied to LFP recordings, these models reveal state-dependent phase-interaction patterns between wakefulness and NREM sleep. Together, they enable systematic, large-scale mapping of dynamic and directional phase relationships across brain and cognitive states.

paragraphs: Relationships between the phases of brain oscillations help describe coordination across regions. Torus Graphs model dependencies among these circular variables, but their existing inference procedure limits analysis to roughly 100 variables. This paper introduces stochastic score matching with quadratic per-iteration cost, replacing the previous sixth-power scaling.

The computational change enables analysis of thousands of variables, including 1,860 frequency-phase features from multielectrode local field potentials. It also supports two extensions beyond static, undirected dependence. A Torus Graph Hidden Markov Model captures coupling patterns that change between states, while an autoregressive version estimates directional interactions through transfer entropy.

The contribution combines scalable inference with models of changing and directional statistical relationships. Reducing per-iteration cost makes these richer analyses accessible at a scale closer to modern multichannel recordings, allowing many frequencies and recording channels to be studied together.
summary.tldr: Scalable Torus Graph inference enables analysis of thousands of neural phase variables and extensions for changing and directional interactions.

title: Torus Graphs for Large Scale Neural Phase Analysis

abstract: Neural tangent kernels (NTKs) are a powerful tool for analyzing deep, non-linear neural networks. In the infinite-width limit, NTKs can easily be computed for most common architectures, yielding full analytic control over the training dynamics. However, at infinite width, important properties of training such as NTK evolution or feature learning are absent. Nevertheless, finite width effects can be included by computing corrections to the Gaussian statistics at infinite width. We introduce Feynman diagrams for computing finite-width corrections to NTK statistics. These dramatically simplify the necessary algebraic manipulations and enable the computation of layer-wise recursion relations for arbitrary statistics involving preactivations, NTKs and certain higher-derivative tensors (dNTK and ddNTK) required to predict the training dynamics at leading order. We demonstrate the feasibility of our framework by extending stability results for deep networks from preactivations to NTKs and proving the absence of finite-width corrections for scale-invariant nonlinearities such as ReLU on the diagonal of the Gram matrix of the NTK. We numerically implement the complete set of equations necessary to compute the first-order corrections for arbitrary inputs and demonstrate that the results follow the statistics of sampled neural networks for widths $n\gtrsim 20$.

paragraphs: Neural tangent kernels provide a mathematical way to study neural network training. They become especially tractable when network width is taken to infinity, but that limit omits effects such as feature learning and changes in the kernel during training. This paper develops tools for calculating corrections that bring finite network width back into the analysis.

The authors introduce Feynman diagrams to simplify the algebra needed for these corrections. Their framework yields layer-by-layer recursions for statistics involving preactivations, neural tangent kernels, and higher-derivative tensors used to predict leading-order training dynamics. The contribution is a systematic computational language for quantities that otherwise require complicated manipulations.

They extend deep-network stability results to neural tangent kernels and prove that finite-width corrections vanish on the kernel Gram matrix diagonal for scale-invariant nonlinearities such as ReLU. This statement concerns those diagonal entries. Numerical first-order corrections for arbitrary inputs follow sampled-network statistics at widths around 20 and above, demonstrating the framework's empirical feasibility in the tested setting.
summary.tldr: Feynman diagrams simplify finite-width corrections to neural tangent kernels, enabling theoretical and numerical analysis beyond infinite-width networks.

title: Finite-Width Neural Tangent Kernels from Feynman Diagrams

abstract: Multi-vector retrieval (MVR) models, exemplified by ColBERT, have established new benchmarks in retrieval accuracy by preserving fine-grained token-level interactions. However, this granularity imposes prohibitive storage and retrieval efficiency bottlenecks: to manage the immense memory footprint and computational overhead of billion-scale token vectors, state-of-the-art systems are forced to rely on aggressive dimension reduction and complex clustering (e.g., K-means). This compromise introduces two critical limitations: excessive indexing latency of clustering large-scale corpora and semantic information loss inherent to compression. In this paper, we propose Single-stage Sparse Retrieval (SSR, a paradigm shift that replaces expensive clustering with efficient sparse coding. Instead of compressing features into low-dimensional dense vectors, we utilize Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) to project token embeddings into a high-dimensional but highly sparse representation. This transformation enables us to bypass vector clustering entirely and leverage inverted indexing for precise, high-throughput retrieval. Extensive experiments on the BEIR benchmark demonstrate that SSR achieves a "trifecta" of improvements: it reduces indexing time by 15x compared to ColBERTv2, halves retrieval latency, and simultaneously improves retrieval performance over leading baselines.

paragraphs: Multi-vector retrieval keeps token-level representations to capture fine-grained matches, but storing and searching those vectors can be expensive. Existing systems manage the burden through dimension reduction and clustering, which add indexing work and can discard semantic information. Single-stage Sparse Retrieval changes the representation used to organize these token vectors.

SSR uses a sparse autoencoder to map token embeddings into a high-dimensional representation with relatively few active entries. This allows the system to use an inverted index and bypass vector clustering. The approach therefore changes how token information is encoded and accessed, while retaining the fine-grained retrieval setting that motivates multi-vector methods.

On the BEIR benchmark, the authors report indexing that is 15 times faster than ColBERTv2, retrieval latency reduced by half, and improved retrieval performance over leading baselines. These findings show simultaneous gains in preparation cost, search speed, and retrieval quality in the reported evaluation. The paper's central contribution is demonstrating sparse coding as an effective alternative to the clustering-heavy indexing pipeline.
summary.tldr: SSR replaces clustering with sparse token representations and inverted indexing, improving indexing speed, retrieval latency, and benchmark retrieval quality.

title: No More K-means: Single-Stage Sparse Coding for Efficient Multi-Vector Retrieval

abstract: Regular expressions (regexes) frequently exhibit super-linear worst-case behavior in regex engines, exposing software to Regex Denial-of-Service (ReDoS) attacks. Detecting such vulnerabilities is challenging, especially for extended features such as lookarounds and backreferences: existing static approaches are efficient but often lack support for extended features, whereas dynamic and hybrid approaches reduce false positives by executing regex matching on real engines, but incur high runtime overhead. To address this trade-off, we propose ReDoS-MotifGNN (RMGNN), a motif-based graph learning framework for ReDoS detection that leverages the low inference latency of graph neural networks (GNNs). RMGNN converts regexes into Heterogeneous Regex Graphs (HRGs) and encodes three ReDoS-related motifs into HRGs to incorporate domain priors, while preserving the syntactic structure and extended features of the input regex. Furthermore, it applies heterogeneous propagation with kernel-guided motif learning to capture multi-scale semantics, which are fused via residual cross-attention for robust prediction. Comprehensive evaluation on four real-world datasets (over 317k regexes) demonstrates that RMGNN outperforms six state-of-the-art baselines in F1-score and achieves an average 244$\times$ speedup over the top F1-performing baseline.

paragraphs: Some regular expressions can require disproportionately long matching times, creating opportunities for denial-of-service attacks. Detecting these expressions involves a trade-off: static analysis is efficient but often struggles with features such as lookarounds and backreferences, while methods that execute matches can reduce false alarms at a substantial runtime cost.

RMGNN represents each regular expression as a heterogeneous graph that retains its syntax and extended features. It adds three motifs associated with ReDoS, giving the learning system explicit domain knowledge about relevant structural patterns. Different graph relationships are processed through heterogeneous propagation and kernel-guided motif learning. Residual cross-attention then combines information captured at multiple scales to make a vulnerability prediction.

Across four real-world datasets containing more than 317,000 expressions, RMGNN achieves higher F1-scores than six state-of-the-art baselines. It is also 244 times faster on average than the baseline with the strongest F1-score. These results support using structured graph representations to combine accurate detection with low inference latency.
summary.tldr: RMGNN detects vulnerable regular expressions using graph structure and attack-related motifs, improving reported accuracy and inference speed.

title: Exploring Motif-based Heterogeneous Graph Learning for ReDoS Detection

abstract: The diversity of robot embodiments and action spaces makes it challenging to build robot world models that generalize across different embodiments. We introduce the Latent Action-Conditioned Robot World Model (LAC-WM), which operates within a learned unified latent action space shared across diverse embodiments. This unified action space improves the world model’s performance when adapted to previously unseen robot embodiments. We compare LAC-WM with an Explicit Action-Conditioned World Model (EAC-WM), which conditions on explicit motion labels. Our results shows that explicit action conditioning leads to disjoint action representations across embodiments, limiting downstream performance when adapting to new robots. We evaluate both models on dexterous manipulation tasks and a modified LIBERO benchmark. LAC-WM improves downstream performance over EAC-WM by up to 46.7% on dexterous manipulation and 11.7% on LIBERO. Crucially, the unified latent action space allows LAC-WM’s downstream performance to scale positively with the number of embodiments used during pretraining. In contrast, the disjoint action space in EAC-WM leads to decreased performance as the number of pretraining embodiments increases. These results highlights the importance of a unified action space for efficient cross-embodiment learning, addressing a key challenge in robotics.

paragraphs: Training a world model across different robots is difficult because their bodies and action spaces differ. An action representation that works for one robot may not connect naturally to another robot’s movements. This paper investigates whether learning a shared internal action space can make experience from diverse robots more useful when adapting to an unseen embodiment.

The proposed LAC-WM conditions its world model on learned latent actions shared across embodiments. The comparison model, EAC-WM, instead uses explicit motion labels. In the reported results, explicit conditioning produces separated action representations across robots, limiting downstream adaptation. The shared latent space provides a common representation through which experience from different embodiments can contribute.

On dexterous manipulation and a modified LIBERO benchmark, LAC-WM improves downstream performance over EAC-WM by up to 46.7% and 11.7%, respectively. Its performance also improves as pretraining includes more embodiments, whereas EAC-WM’s declines. These findings suggest that representation choice determines whether greater robot diversity helps or hinders transfer in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: A shared learned action space helps robot world models transfer to unseen embodiments and benefit from more diverse pretraining.

title: Cross-Embodiment Robot Foundation World Models with Latent Actions

abstract: Understanding physical transformations is fundamental for reasoning in dynamic environments. While Vision Language Models (VLMs) show promise in embodied applications, whether they genuinely understand physical transformations remains unclear. We introduce ConservationBench evaluating conservation—whether physical quantities remain invariant under transformations. Spanning four properties with paired conserving/non-conserving scenarios, we generate 23,040 questions across 112 VLMs. Results reveal systematic failure: performance remains near chance with improvements on conservation tasks accompanied by drops on controls. Control experiments show strong textual priors favoring invariance, yet models perform worse with visual content. Neither temporal resolution, prompting, nor curated sampling helps. These findings show that current VLMs fail to maintain transformation-invariant representations of physical properties across dynamic scenes.

paragraphs: Reasoning about physical change requires recognizing which quantities remain the same as a scene transforms. ConservationBench tests this ability through paired scenarios in which a property either is or is not conserved. It covers four properties, generating 23,040 questions and evaluating 112 vision–language models.

The paired design matters because a model can appear successful by repeatedly assuming that quantities stay unchanged. The results reveal near-chance performance, with improvements on conserving scenarios accompanied by declines on controls. Additional experiments find strong textual preferences for invariance, while providing visual content makes performance worse. This pattern points to answers driven by prior expectations rather than reliable interpretation of the transformations.

The tested changes to temporal resolution, prompting, and curated sampling do not resolve the problem. The authors conclude that current evaluated models fail to maintain representations of physical properties that remain consistent across dynamic scenes. The benchmark therefore exposes a systematic weakness in tracking conservation, using controls to distinguish actual sensitivity to physical change from a general tendency to answer that something stayed the same.
summary.tldr: ConservationBench finds systematic failures in tested vision–language models’ ability to track conserved physical properties across changing scenes.

title: Vision Language Models Cannot Reason About Physical Transformation

abstract: Forecasting the evolution of dynamic environments is crucial for autonomous agents. While generative world models have achieved high photorealism in 2D video synthesis by mixing ego-motion and environmental dynamics within the image plane, they exhibit physical inconsistencies, such as morphing or vanishing objects, especially over long time horizons. In this paper, we propose FR3D, a world-modeling approach that predicts a persistent 3D latent representation for future dynamic 3D reconstruction. Unlike prior works that treat the world as a sequence of image-based features, FR3D explicitly decouples the 3D evolution of the scene from the agent’s trajectory, treating the inferred ego-motion as a latent proxy for action. This disentanglement resolves ambiguities between self-motion and world-motion, ensuring geometric consistency into the future. Furthermore, we introduce a teacher-student distillation strategy that leverages the spatial "common sense" of off-the-shelf foundation models, leading to robust zero-shot generalization. Extensive experiments demonstrate FR3D’s strong performance for future dynamic 3D reconstruction from monocular observations across multiple datasets, even 2 seconds into the future. Project page: https://fr3d-wm.github.io.

paragraphs: Predicting future visual observations requires separating changes in the world from changes caused by the observer’s movement. Image-based world models can mix these effects, producing realistic-looking videos with inconsistent objects that morph or disappear. FR3D addresses this ambiguity by predicting a persistent three-dimensional latent representation of the evolving scene.

The approach explicitly separates scene evolution from the agent’s trajectory. It treats inferred ego-motion—the agent’s own movement—as a latent proxy for action, allowing future geometry to be modeled separately from viewpoint changes. This separation is the paper’s mechanism for resolving ambiguity between self-motion and world-motion and maintaining geometric consistency into the future.

FR3D also uses teacher-student distillation to transfer spatial knowledge from existing foundation models. The authors report that this supports robust zero-shot generalization. Experiments across multiple datasets show strong future dynamic 3D reconstruction from monocular observations, including predictions two seconds ahead. The findings connect a persistent spatial representation with motion separation and transferred spatial knowledge, providing an approach to forecasting the changing world in three dimensions.
summary.tldr: FR3D forecasts persistent 3D scenes by separating environmental motion from the agent’s own movement and distilling foundation-model spatial knowledge.

title: Future Dynamic 3D Reconstruction: Toward 3D World Modeling with Disentangled Ego-Motion

abstract: In this paper, we present a novel federated independence testing (FedIT) method that addresses both theoretical and practical challenges arising from client heterogeneity. We begin by revisiting existing federated independence testing methods and showing why they fail to provide valid guarantees or maintain statistical power under data distributional shift across clients. Building on this analysis, we develop a copula-based marginal alignment technique together with a stacking-based aggregation strategy that amplifies intra-client dependence while mitigating inter-client variation, resulting in a theoretically sound and powerful global test. For practicality, we further accelerate the aggregation step and incorporate a privacy-preserving mechanism. On the theoretical side, we prove both the correctness of our method and the validity of the test. Empirically, we conduct extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, which demonstrate the superiority of our solution over existing methods.

For practicality, we further accelerate the aggregation step and incorporate a privacy-preserving mechanism. paragraphs: Federated independence testing asks whether variables are statistically dependent using data distributed across clients. When clients have different data distributions, combining their evidence becomes difficult. The paper revisits existing methods and explains how this heterogeneity can undermine either the validity of their guarantees or their ability to detect dependence.

The proposed FedIT method combines copula-based marginal alignment with stacking-based aggregation. Alignment addresses differences in individual variable distributions, while aggregation emphasizes dependence within clients and reduces variation between clients. This division matters because a global test needs to retain the relationships present locally without letting client-to-client distribution shifts dominate the combined evidence.

The authors also accelerate aggregation and incorporate a privacy-preserving mechanism to make the approach more practical. They prove correctness and test validity, then evaluate performance on synthetic and real-world datasets. The experiments show superiority over existing methods in the studied settings. Together, the results connect a theoretically supported global test with an aggregation strategy designed specifically for heterogeneous clients.
summary.tldr: FedIT aligns client distributions and aggregates within-client dependence to deliver a theoretically valid and empirically powerful federated independence test.

title: Powerful and Theoretically Guaranteed Independence Testing on Heterogeneous Federated Clients

abstract: We propose a minimal agentic baseline that enables systematic comparison across different AI-based theorem prover architectures. This design implements the core features shared among state-of-the-art systems: iterative proof refinement, library search and context management. We evaluate this agentic approach using qualitatively different benchmarks and compare various frontier language models and design choices. Our results show competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art approaches, while using a significantly simpler architecture and a fraction of their cost. Additionally, we demonstrate consistent advantages of an iterative approach over multiple single-shot generations, especially in terms of sample efficiency and cost effectiveness. The implementation is released open-source as a candidate reference for future research and as an accessible prover for the community.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a compact theorem-proving agent intended to make comparisons between AI proof systems more systematic. It includes three capabilities shared by leading approaches: refining proofs over repeated attempts, searching a mathematical library, and managing the context available to the language model. These capabilities form a simple reference architecture.

The authors evaluate the agent across qualitatively different benchmarks, using several frontier language models and alternative design choices. They report performance competitive with leading approaches despite a substantially simpler architecture and a fraction of their cost. The result suggests that these core agent capabilities can account for strong performance without requiring the full complexity of existing systems.

A separate comparison finds consistent benefits from iterative refinement over generating multiple independent, single-shot proof attempts. The advantages are particularly clear in sample efficiency and cost effectiveness. The open-source implementation is offered both as an accessible prover and as a candidate research reference, helping future studies compare model and architecture choices within a shared framework.
summary.tldr: A simple theorem-proving agent achieves competitive results at lower cost, with iterative refinement outperforming repeated single-shot attempts.

title: A Minimal Agent for Automated Theorem Proving

abstract: While Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) offer structural advantages for global planning, efficiently verifying that they arrive at correct answers via valid reasoning traces remains a critical challenge. In this work, we propose a geometric perspective: Reasoning on the Manifold. We hypothesize that valid generation trajectories reside as stable attractors on the high-density manifold of the learned distribution, whereas invalid paths exhibit off-manifold drift. To operationalize this, we introduce Bidirectional Manifold Consistency (BMC), a training-free, unsupervised metric that quantifies the stability of the generated sequence through a forward-masking and backward-reconstruction cycle. Empirically, we demonstrate BMC’s versatility across the full reasoning lifecycle: (1) in Diagnosis, it serves as a robust discriminator of solution validity without ground truth answer; (2) in Inference, it enables rejection resampling to effectively concentrate computational resources on complex reasoning tasks; and (3) in Alignment, it functions as a dense geometric reward that transforms sparse outcome supervision into fine-grained guidance, empowering models to self-evolve beyond standard baselines. Our results establish intrinsic geometric stability as a robust indicator of correctness for dLLMs.
originalAbstract: While Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) offer structural advantages for global planning, efficiently verifying that they arrive at correct answers via valid reasoning traces remains a critical challenge. To operationalize this, we introduce Bidirectional Manifold Consistency (BMC), a training-free, unsupervised metric that quantifies the stability of the generated sequence through a forward-masking and backward-reconstruction cycle. Empirically, we demonstrate BMC’s versatility across the full reasoning lifecycle: (1) in Diagnosis, it serves as a robust discriminator of solution validity without ground truth answer; (2) in Inference, it enables rejection resampling to effectively concentrate computational resources on complex reasoning tasks; and (3) in Alignment, it functions as a dense geometric reward that transforms sparse outcome supervision into fine-grained guidance, empowering models to self-evolve beyond standard baselines. paragraphs: This paper investigates how diffusion language models can assess their own reasoning without a known correct answer. Its starting hypothesis is geometric: valid reasoning trajectories behave like stable attractors in high-density regions of the learned distribution, while invalid trajectories tend to drift away. The authors turn that hypothesis into a measurable consistency test.

Bidirectional Manifold Consistency masks a generated sequence and then reconstructs it, measuring stability across that cycle. The metric requires neither training nor supervised labels. Its purpose is to provide an internal signal about whether a solution is valid by testing how reliably the model returns to the generated sequence.

Experiments explore three uses. The score distinguishes valid solutions without ground-truth answers, guides rejection resampling during inference, and supplies a dense reward for alignment. In the alignment setting, it turns sparse outcome supervision into finer-grained guidance and supports improvement beyond standard baselines. These findings support geometric stability as an empirical indicator of correctness in the studied diffusion models, building on the paper’s proposed hypothesis.
summary.tldr: A masking-and-reconstruction consistency score helps diffusion language models assess reasoning, guide resampling, and obtain finer-grained alignment rewards.

title: Reasoning on the Manifold: Bidirectional Consistency for Self-Verification in Diffusion Language Models

abstract: Diffusion-based large language models generate text by gradually filling in masked tokens, yet they remain slow because they usually decode only a few tokens per step. Parallel decoding, which unmasks multiple tokens simultaneously, promises acceleration but often degrades quality when too many tokens are predicted at once. We identify the root cause: when decoding is viewed as iterative token grouping, overly permissive grouping places interdependent tokens in the same step, violates the conditional independence assumption, and amplifies reliance on noisy context even when the top prediction is already correct. We introduce SPEED, a framework that enlarges safe parallel groups through complementary training and inference designs. At training time, a sharpened teacher distillation objective selectively aligns the student to teacher-correct positions using a temperature-scaled KL term together with a masked language modeling loss, producing a student that assigns more probability mass to correct token identities and elevates more positions above the decoding threshold. At inference time, Slow-Fast Decoding partitions tokens by sensitivity to revealed context using token-wise Jensen-Shannon Divergence computed with and without access to the preceding block, decoding low-sensitivity tokens jointly in parallel while deferring high-sensitivity tokens until sufficient context resolves them. Through extensive experiments, our framework attains up to 12.2$\times$ speedup on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and 6.7$\times$ on Dream-7B-Instruct with accuracy close to greedy decoding across standard reasoning and code benchmarks.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models generate text by repeatedly filling masked positions. Predicting many positions together can accelerate generation, but quality suffers when tokens that depend on one another are grouped into the same step. SPEED addresses this grouping problem through complementary changes to training and decoding, aiming to enlarge the sets of tokens that can safely be generated in parallel.

During training, the student learns from positions where the teacher is correct, using a temperature-scaled distribution-matching loss alongside masked language modeling. This concentrates more probability on correct token identities and brings more positions above the decoding threshold. During inference, Slow-Fast Decoding compares each token's predictions with and without the preceding block to estimate sensitivity to revealed context.

Low-sensitivity tokens are decoded together, while sensitive tokens wait for additional context. Experiments report speedups of up to 12.2 times on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and 6.7 times on Dream-7B-Instruct, with accuracy close to greedy decoding on reasoning and code benchmarks. The result ties acceleration to more selective parallel grouping, with the stated speedups representing the best reported cases.
summary.tldr: SPEED combines selective teacher distillation with context-sensitive token grouping to accelerate diffusion decoding while keeping accuracy close to greedy decoding.

title: SPEED: Sharpened-Teacher Distillation for Parallel Decoding of Diffusion Language Models

abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer substantial speed advantages through parallel decoding, but the lack of token dependencies limits generation quality compared to autoregressive (AR) models. Recent progress attempts to bridge the gap via importance sampling, with DLM being the proposal and AR being the target. However, due to the huge gap between their distributions, the sampling requires a large number of particles and is thus expensive to compute. In this paper, we introduce PoE-Bridge, a novel decoding framework that drastically improves generation speed and accuracy by introducing an intermediate distribution to bridge the gap. The distribution is constructed as a Product-of-Experts (PoE) of the DLM proposal and the AR target. With the intermediate distribution, we first use the DLM to draft multiple continuations in parallel, then apply rejection sampling to verify the drafted tokens and move the resulting candidates toward the PoE. We then use importance sampling to further correct the PoE-aligned candidates toward the AR target. We further propose several improved techniques, including mixed-temperature sampling for enhanced diversity and elastic rejection windows for reducing wasted verification. Empirically, PoE-Bridge achieves significantly improved accuracy with $5\times$ speedup over the standard DLM decoding approach, and recovers at least 95% of the target AR model’s performance, efficiently advancing most of the quality gap on challenging mathematical reasoning and coding tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/juntongshi48/poe-bridge.

Those performance ratios refer to the evaluated tasks and decoding comparison, rather than proving identical outputs or universal runtime gains.
summary.tldr: A product-of-experts bridge improves correction between parallel diffusion drafts and an autoregressive target, boosting reported speed and quality.

title: Diffusion Language Model Parallel Decoding via Product-of-Experts Bridge

abstract: Why depth yields a genuine computational advantage over shallow methods remains a central open question in learning theory. We study this question in a controlled high-dimensional Gaussian setting, focusing on compositional target functions. We analyze their learnability using an explicit three-layer fitting model trained via layer-wise spectral estimators. Although the target is globally a high-degree polynomial, its compositional structure allows learning to proceed in stages: an intermediate representation reveals structure that is inaccessible at the input level. This reduces learning to simpler spectral estimation problems, well studied in the context of multi-index models, whereas any shallow estimator must resolve all components simultaneously. Our analysis relies on Gaussian universality, leading to sharp separations in sample complexity between two and three-layer learning strategies.

paragraphs: A function can be complicated when viewed directly from its inputs yet become simpler when expressed as a sequence of intermediate computations. This paper uses that compositional structure to study why an additional network layer can provide a real learning advantage. The analysis takes place in a controlled setting with high-dimensional Gaussian inputs.

The authors examine an explicit three-layer fitting model trained through spectral estimators applied layer by layer. Although the overall target is a high-degree polynomial, the intermediate representation exposes structure unavailable at the input level. Learning can therefore proceed through simpler spectral estimation problems, whereas a shallow estimator must resolve the components together.

Using Gaussian universality, the analysis establishes sharp differences in sample complexity between the two-layer and three-layer strategies. The result gives a concrete mechanism connecting depth to data requirements: intermediate representations change which structure becomes accessible at each stage. Its theoretical force comes from the specified compositional targets and Gaussian setting, rather than from a claim that adding depth improves every learning problem.
summary.tldr: For compositional targets under Gaussian inputs, layer-wise spectral learning reveals structure that yields sharp sample-complexity advantages for three layers over two.

title: Deep Learning of Compositional Targets with Hierarchical Spectral Methods

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to provide automated assessment signals for evaluating model-generated outputs. However, practical deployment faces three persistent challenges: heterogeneous reliability across models, substantial latency and token costs, and the absence of principled strategies for allocating evaluation resources. We introduce R$^2$Eval, a routing-aware automated assessment framework that formulates evaluation as a resource allocation and aggregation problem rather than relying on a single monolithic evaluator. R$^2$Eval combines difficulty-aware routing with reasoned evaluation signals to dynamically select evaluator models on a per-instance basis under explicit accuracy, latency, and cost constraints. Our study makes three contributions. First, we construct six difficulty-aware datasets spanning both reasoning-intensive (mathematics, logic, code) and non-reasoning (knowledge, roleplay, writing) tasks, with human-annotated reference assessments. Second, we provide a systematic empirical analysis of how reasoning traces produced by different evaluator models correlate with assessment outcomes, revealing substantial variance and systematic mismatches across difficulty regimes. Third, we develop and evaluate both offline and online routing strategies that adaptively allocate evaluation queries, achieving substantially improved accuracy–efficiency trade-offs compared to static baselines. Experiments across 19 language models demonstrate that R$^2$Eval significantly reduces evaluation cost and latency while maintaining close alignment with human assessments. These results highlight the importance of routing-aware automated assessment and establish R$^2$Eval as a scalable and reliable framework for large-scale model evaluation.

The findings support adapting evaluation resources to the instance, with routing forming a substantive part of assessment quality and efficiency.
summary.tldr: R²Eval routes assessment queries by difficulty to reduce evaluation cost and latency while retaining close agreement with human judgments.

title: Routing and Reasoned Evaluation with Large Language Models

abstract: Hierarchical decision-making frameworks are pivotal for addressing complex control tasks, enabling agents to decompose intricate problems into manageable subgoals. Despite their promise, existing hierarchical policies face critical limitations: (i) reinforcement learning (RL)-based methods struggle to guarantee strict constraint satisfaction, and (ii) optimal control (OC)-based approaches often rely on myopic and computationally prohibitive formulations. To reconcile these trade-offs, hierarchical RL-OC architectures have emerged as a promising paradigm. However, the formulation of the lower-level optimization within these frameworks remains underexplored, often relying on heuristic or myopic objectives. In this work, we propose a principled framework that systematically integrates upper-level goal abstraction with structured lower-level decision making. We adopt an inverse optimization approach to inform the structure of the lower-level problem from expert demonstrations, ensuring that the objective of the lower-level policy remains aligned with the overall long-term task goal. To validate the approach, our framework is evaluated on distinct decision making tasks: network-based resource allocation and continuous collision avoidance. Empirical results demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms strong baselines based on end-to-end RL, learning-augmented optimal control, and existing hierarchical RL approaches in both efficiency and decision quality.

paragraphs: Hierarchical decision making divides a difficult control problem into high-level goals and lower-level decisions. Reinforcement learning can struggle to enforce strict constraints, while optimal-control formulations can be shortsighted or computationally expensive. Combining the two is promising, but the lower-level optimization problem is often designed using heuristics that may not align with the overall task.

This paper uses inverse optimization to learn the structure of that lower-level problem from expert demonstrations. Instead of specifying its objective only through manual design, the framework uses demonstrated decisions to inform how the structured policy should optimize. The purpose is to connect upper-level goal abstraction with lower-level choices that remain aligned with long-term task goals.

The researchers evaluate the framework on network resource allocation and continuous collision avoidance, covering distinct kinds of decisions. It consistently outperforms the tested end-to-end reinforcement learning, learning-augmented optimal-control, and hierarchical reinforcement-learning baselines in efficiency and decision quality. The results support treating the design of the lower-level objective as a learnable part of a hierarchical architecture.
summary.tldr: The framework learns lower-level optimization structure from expert demonstrations to better align hierarchical decisions with long-term goals.

title: Hierarchical Decision Making with Structured Policies: A Principled Design via Inverse Optimization

abstract: In self-supervised goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (RL) without external rewards, goals are typically specified by observations sampled from experience. However, depending on the observation structure, such a fixed representation of goals may be either too concrete (requiring exact pixel-level matches) or too abstract (involving ambiguous observations). Here we propose the construction of hierarchical latent goal spaces that integrate both concrete and abstract goals. To this end, we use an energy function to learn a partially ordered space, in which a subset relation between observations naturally induces a hierarchy from concrete to abstract goals. This representation enables agents to disambiguate specific states while also generalizing to shared concepts. In experiments on navigation and robotic manipulation, agents trained with our hierarchical goal space achieve higher task success and greater generalization to novel tasks compared to agents limited to purely observational goals.

paragraphs: In self-supervised goal-conditioned reinforcement learning, agents often use previously observed states as goals without receiving external rewards. A fixed observation-based goal representation can be awkward: it may demand an exact visual match or leave distinct states ambiguous. This paper develops a goal space that includes both specific targets and broader concepts.

The method learns a latent space with a partial ordering using an energy function. Subset relations between observations organize goals into a hierarchy running from concrete to abstract. This structure allows the representation to distinguish particular states while also capturing concepts shared across them. The agent therefore has access to different levels of specificity within one learned goal space.

In navigation and robotic manipulation experiments, agents trained with this hierarchy achieve higher task success and better generalization to novel tasks than agents using purely observational goals. The findings support learning relationships among goals as part of the representation itself. Those relationships help connect the precision needed to identify a particular state with the abstraction useful for transferring behavior to new tasks.
summary.tldr: Learning subset relations among goals gives reinforcement-learning agents a hierarchy that combines precise targets with transferable abstract concepts.

title: Hierarchical Goal Abstractions via Learned Subset Relations

abstract: Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) empowers pre-trained models to adapt online to distribution shifts during inference, but such online updates often become unstable in long-horizon deployments. Prevailing approaches attribute this failure to error accumulation from noisy pseudo-labels, relying on heuristics to gate samples used for updates. We argue that this statistical view is insufficient: the problem lies not only in sample quality but also in the directionality of gradients. In this work, we identify a geometric failure mode termed manifold erosion. Through spectral analysis, we find that reliable gradients concentrate in a stable low-rank subspace, while gradients from confident mispredictions are high-rank yet exhibit a persistent directional leakage into this protected subspace. This leakage can accumulate coherently and gradually erode core representations, eventually leading to collapse. To address this, we propose Manifold-Aware Gradient Projection (MGP), a geometric intervention that tracks the dominant subspace online and projects gradients onto its orthogonal complement. By blocking the leakage path, MGP decouples stability from plasticity. Extensive experiments on diverse TTA benchmarks demonstrate its long-horizon stability, whereas prior methods often fail.

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation updates a trained model as it encounters changing inputs during deployment. These updates can become unstable over long periods. The paper argues that filtering unreliable training examples addresses only part of the problem: even confident predictions can produce harmful updates because of the directions those updates take.

Spectral analysis identifies a failure mode called manifold erosion. Reliable gradients occupy a stable, low-dimensional subspace, but gradients from confident mistakes repeatedly leak into that same subspace. Although these mistaken gradients spread across more directions overall, their persistent component in the protected space can accumulate and damage core representations.

Across the evaluated test-time adaptation benchmarks, the method remains stable over long horizons where earlier methods often fail, supporting gradient direction as an important intervention point.
summary.tldr: MGP stabilizes long-running test-time adaptation by blocking gradient directions that can gradually damage core representations.

title: Blocking the Leakage: Manifold-Aware Gradient Projection for Long-Horizon Test-Time Adaptation

abstract: Recent advances in image generation have been largely driven by image tokenization, which compresses raw pixels into compact latent representations. While existing tokenizers excel at preserving low-level visual details through reconstruction-based training, they often lack explicit semantic guidance, which limits their ability to capture semantically structured representations and thus hinders their performance on downstream tasks like image generation. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel tokenization framework that incorporates high-level semantics through two key innovations: (1) a text-integrated encoder that jointly processes images and textual descriptions to produce semantically enriched latent representations, and (2) a concept-guided training objective that leverages sparse autoencoders to decompose pre-trained vision-language model features to a semantic concept space, employing sparse and disentangled concept indices for guidance. Our approach achieves strong alignment with semantic concepts, maintaining high reconstruction fidelity with an rFID of 1.39 on ImageNet, while achieving a gFID of 2.65 on the class-conditional image generation task and 10.73 on the text-to-image generation task. By infusing high-level semantic structures into low-level visual fidelity, our method bridges the reconstruction-generation divide and drives generative modeling as a powerful foundation. The code is available at https://github.com/hustyyq/ConceptTok

paragraphs: Image tokenizers compress pixels into compact representations that later support reconstruction and generation. This paper argues that training primarily to reconstruct visual detail can leave those representations insufficiently organized around meaning. Its proposed tokenizer adds explicit semantic guidance so that preserving appearance and representing high-level concepts become connected training goals.

The framework introduces two complementary components. A text-integrated encoder processes images together with textual descriptions to enrich their latent representations. A separate concept-guided objective uses sparse autoencoders to decompose features from a pretrained vision-language model into a semantic concept space. Sparse, disentangled concept indices then guide the tokenizer, providing a more explicit semantic target than reconstruction alone.

These findings support the stated goal of retaining visual fidelity while making image representations useful for generation. The contribution lies in integrating semantic organization directly into tokenization, rather than relying solely on the downstream generator to supply it.
summary.tldr: Concept-guided tokenization combines text-aware encoding with sparse semantic supervision to support both faithful reconstruction and image generation.

title: Concept-Guided Tokenization: Closing the Gap Between Reconstruction and Generation

abstract: Multi-agent debate has shown promise for improving the reasoning of large language models, yet recent theory suggests its benefits are highly regime-dependent. While interaction can amplify informative signals under corrective conditions, symmetric debate dynamics are neutral in expectation, often making majority voting preferable. We reconcile these views by arguing that debate is effective only when invoked at the right time and with appropriate structure. Based on this insight, we propose LASE: Leader-Adaptive Structured Engagement, a leader-centric multi-agent debate framework that selectively engages interaction only in non-neutral regimes. LASE introduces an asymmetric leader–supporter architecture that enables directed information flow and selective signal amplification, while defaulting to simple aggregation otherwise. Experiments across diverse reasoning benchmarks show that LASE achieves multi-agent-level performance with near single-agent token cost, substantially improving efficiency over static debate and voting baselines.

paragraphs: Having several language models debate an answer can improve reasoning, but interaction is not equally useful in every setting. The paper draws on a distinction between corrective dynamics, where interaction amplifies useful information, and symmetric dynamics, which are neutral in expectation. In the latter case, majority voting may be preferable to spending tokens on discussion.

LASE, short for Leader-Adaptive Structured Engagement, makes the decision to debate part of the framework. It uses a leader–supporter structure to direct information flow and selectively amplify useful signals. Interaction is engaged only in regimes identified as non-neutral; otherwise, the system falls back to simple aggregation. This combines selective participation with an intentionally asymmetric discussion structure.

Across diverse reasoning benchmarks, LASE achieves performance associated with multi-agent systems while using close to a single agent's token budget. It also improves efficiency over static debate and voting baselines. The findings support the paper's central argument that the value of debate depends on when it is invoked and how information moves between participants.
summary.tldr: LASE selectively organizes leader–supporter debate to achieve multi-agent reasoning performance at near single-agent token cost.

title: Efficient Multi-Agent Reasoning via Confidence-Guided Adaptive Debate

abstract: High-curvature regions in 3D point clouds encapsulate critical fine-grained geometric semantics yet exhibit a distinct long-tail sparsity in their spatial distribution. The inherent limitations of polynomial volume growth in Euclidean space frequently render these intricate geometric features challenging to adequately resolve within a uniform-scale feature space. Consequently, these regions are frequently overshadowed by smooth global features dominated by low-curvature regions, thereby limiting the discriminative capacity of the network. To address this issue, we propose PointCHR, a curvature-aware hyperbolic rectification (CHR) for point cloud analysis. Utilising the property of exponential volume expansion in the vicinity of hyperbolic manifolds, CHR presents a learnable curvature-guided radial rectification mechanism. By adaptively projecting high-curvature points towards boundary regions endowed with larger effective embedding capacities, PointCHR effectively mitigates the representation crowding problem inherent in Euclidean settings. Extensive experimentation has demonstrated that PointCHR significantly enhances the ability of backbone to capture fine-grained geometric details, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks.
originalAbstract: High-curvature regions in 3D point clouds encapsulate critical fine-grained geometric semantics yet exhibit a distinct long-tail sparsity in their spatial distribution. The inherent limitations of polynomial volume growth in Euclidean space frequently render these intricate geometric features challenging to adequately resolve within a uniform-scale feature space. Consequently, these regions are frequently overshadowed by smooth global features dominated by low-curvature regions, thereby limiting the discriminative capacity of the network. To address this issue, we propose PointCHR, a curvature-aware hyperbolic rectification (CHR) for point cloud analysis. Utilising the property of exponential volume expansion in the vicinity of hyperbolic manifolds, CHR presents a learnable curvature-guided radial rectification mechanism. By adaptively projecting high-curvature points towards boundary regions endowed with larger effective embedding capacities, PointCHR effectively mitigates the representation crowding problem inherent in Euclidean settings. Extensive experimentation has demonstrated that PointCHR significantly enhances the ability of backbone to capture fine-grained geometric details, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks.

paragraphs: Regions with high curvature contain important geometric detail in a 3D point cloud, but they are relatively sparse. A representation dominated by abundant smooth regions can obscure those details. The paper connects this difficulty to the limited room available for separating intricate features within a uniform-scale Euclidean feature space.

PointCHR introduces curvature-aware hyperbolic rectification to redistribute representational capacity. Its learnable mechanism uses curvature to adjust points’ radial positions in a hyperbolic representation. High-curvature points are projected toward boundary regions with greater effective embedding capacity. The method draws on the exponential volume expansion of hyperbolic geometry to reduce crowding among features that need more room to remain distinguishable.

Experiments report that PointCHR significantly improves the ability of backbone networks to capture fine geometric details and achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks. The contribution is a geometry-based way to address imbalance in which parts of a point cloud receive expressive representation, allocating more capacity to sparse regions that carry important local shape information.
summary.tldr: PointCHR uses curvature-guided hyperbolic embeddings to give sparse, detailed point-cloud regions more representational capacity.

title: PointCHR: Point Cloud Analysis via Curvature-Aware Hyperbolic Rectification

abstract: Bridging high-level semantic understanding with low-level physical control remains a persistent challenge in embodied intelligence, stemming from the fundamental spatiotemporal scale mismatch between cognition and action. Existing generative VLA policies typically adopt a "Generation-from-Noise" paradigm, which disregards this disparity, leading to representation inefficiency and weak condition alignment during optimization. In this work, we propose ResVLA, an architecture that shifts the paradigm to "Refinement-from-Intent." Recognizing that robotic motion naturally decomposes into global intent and local dynamics, ResVLA utilizes spectral analysis to decouple control into a deterministic low-frequency anchor and a stochastic high-frequency residual. By anchoring the generative process on the predicted intent, our model focuses strictly on refining local dynamics via a residual diffusion bridge. Extensive simulation experiments show that ResVLA achieves competitive performance, strong robustness to language and robot embodiment perturbations, and faster convergence than standard generative baselines. ResVLA also demonstrates strong performance in real-world robot experiments.

paragraphs: Vision-language-action policies must connect broad instructions and scene understanding to detailed robot movements. The paper identifies a mismatch between the spatial and temporal scales of understanding and control. It argues that generating actions from noise does not adequately account for this mismatch, weakening representation efficiency and alignment with conditioning information during optimization.

ResVLA starts with a predicted movement intent and then refines its details. Spectral analysis separates control into a deterministic low-frequency anchor and a stochastic high-frequency residual. The anchor represents the broad movement component, while a residual diffusion bridge handles local dynamics. This gives the generative process a structured starting point and concentrates its role on refinement.

Simulation experiments show competitive performance, faster convergence than standard generative baselines, and strong robustness to changes in language and robot embodiment. The authors also report strong performance in real-world robot experiments. These findings support separating global intent from local dynamics as a useful architectural choice for connecting high-level conditioning to physical control.
summary.tldr: ResVLA anchors robot action generation on predicted movement intent and uses residual diffusion to refine local dynamics, with competitive performance and faster reported convergence.

title: From Noise to Intent: Anchoring Generative VLA Policies with Residual Bridges

abstract: This position paper argues that adopting AI in organizational practice does not guarantee productivity gains, because human and environmental factors critically moderate the relationship between AI deployment and realized productivity improvements. Following the advent of high-performance generative models, AI use has been rapidly encouraged in some sectors while being restricted in others. Most practitioners assume that AI brings productivity boosts owing to enhanced technical capabilities, but regardless of apparent performance advances in AI technology, human and environmental factors of the organization may substantially attenuate—or even negate—the effective productivity benefits. We identify five key moderating factors: human resource composition, baseline capability of individuals, learning curve of practitioners, incentives for fair use, and flexibility of objectives. Drawing on the partial equilibrium model of Gries and Naudé (2022), we argue that existing economic frameworks may inadvertently overlook these factors. We revise the existing framework to redefine effective organizational determinants and shed light on practical implications including industry and education, responding to alternative views and calling for action of stakeholders.

paragraphs: This position paper challenges the assumption that stronger AI capabilities automatically translate into more productive organizations. Its central argument is that the relationship depends on the people using the technology and the environment in which they work. Those conditions can substantially reduce, or even eliminate, the benefits that technical improvements appear to promise.

The authors identify five factors that shape this relationship: workforce composition, individuals’ starting capabilities, the learning required to use AI, incentives for fair use, and how flexibly objectives can change. Together, these factors make productivity an organizational question as well as a technical one. Assessing a model’s capabilities alone therefore does not establish what an organization will gain from deploying it.

The paper revises an existing partial equilibrium economic framework to better represent these organizational determinants. It uses that revision to discuss implications for industry and education, address competing views, and call for stakeholder action. The contribution is an argument about how to understand effective productivity, rather than a claim that AI adoption consistently helps or harms it.
summary.tldr: AI adoption does not guarantee productivity gains because organizational conditions and human capabilities shape its practical benefits.

title: Position: Adopting AI in Practice Does Not Guarantee the Productivity Boost

abstract: Semi-supervised clustering employs a small amount of labeled data to aidunsupervised learning. Previous work in the area has utilized supervised datain one of two approaches: 1) constraint-based methods that guide theclustering algorithm towards a better grouping of the data, and 2)distance-function learning methods that adapt the underlying similarity metricused by the clustering algorithm. This paper provides new methods for the twoapproaches as well as presents a new semi-supervised clustering algorithm thatintegrates both of these techniques in a uniform, principled framework.Experimental results demonstrate that the unified approach produces betterclusters than both individual approaches as well as previously proposedsemi-supervised clustering algorithms.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised clustering uses a small amount of labeled information to help organize otherwise unlabeled data. Existing approaches have used that information in two main ways: directing which groupings the clustering algorithm should prefer, or changing the distance function that determines which examples appear similar. This paper develops both approaches and brings them together.

Constraint-based guidance influences the grouping process itself. Metric learning changes the similarity relationships on which that process depends. The proposed algorithm integrates these two uses of supervision within a single principled framework, allowing the labeled information to shape both the grouping decisions and the underlying notion of distance.

The authors report that the unified approach produces better clusters in their experiments than either component used individually. It also outperforms previously proposed semi-supervised clustering algorithms in those comparisons. The result supports the value of combining direct guidance with a learned similarity measure: in the tested settings, the two sources of influence work better together than either does alone.
summary.tldr: Combining clustering constraints with metric learning produces better clusters than either approach alone in the reported experiments.

title: Integrating constraints and metric learning in semi-supervised clustering

abstract: The conditional distribution of a discrete variable y, given another discrete variable x, is often specified by assigning one multinomial distribution to each state of x. The cost of this rich parametrization is the loss of statistical power in cases where the data actually fits a model with much fewer parameters. In this paper, we consider a model that partitions the state space of x into disjoint sets, and assigns a single Dirichlet-multinomial to each set. We treat the partition as an unknown variable which is to be integrated away when the interest is in a coarser level task, e.g., variable selection or classification. Based on two different computational approaches, we present two exact algorithms for integration over partitions. Respective complexity bounds are derived in terms of detailed problem characteristics, including the size of the data and the size of the state space of x. Experiments on synthetic data demonstrate the applicability of the algorithms.
