paragraphs: When predicting one discrete variable from another, a common approach assigns a separate outcome distribution to every possible input state. This is flexible, but it can sacrifice statistical power when many states could share a simpler description. The paper studies a model that groups input states into disjoint sets and assigns one Dirichlet-multinomial model to each group.

The grouping itself is unknown. Instead of choosing a single partition and treating it as settled, the authors integrate over possible partitions when addressing broader tasks such as variable selection or classification. This keeps uncertainty about the grouping within the calculation used for the final task.

The main contribution is computational: two exact algorithms, based on different approaches, perform this integration. The authors derive complexity bounds that depend on detailed problem characteristics, including dataset size and the number of input states. Synthetic-data experiments demonstrate that the algorithms can be applied in practice. Together, these results explain how to compute with the partition model and how its computational demands depend on the problem.
summary.tldr: Two exact algorithms integrate over uncertain groupings of discrete input states in Bayesian partition models.

title: Computational aspects of Bayesian partition models

abstract: In many prediction tasks, selecting relevant features is essential for achieving good generalization performance. Most feature selection algorithms consider all features to be a priori equally likely to be relevant. In this paper, we use transfer learning — learning on an ensemble of related tasks — to construct an informative prior on feature relevance. We assume that features themselves have meta-features that are predictive of their relevance to the prediction task, and model their relevance as a function of the meta-features using hyperparameters (called meta-priors). We present a convex optimization algorithm for simultaneously learning the meta-priors and feature weights from an ensemble of related prediction tasks which share a similar relevance structure. Our approach transfers the “meta-priors” among different tasks, which makes it possible to deal with settings where tasks have nonoverlapping features or the relevance of the features vary over the tasks. We show that learning feature relevance improves performance on two real data sets which illustrate such settings: (1) predicting ratings in a collaborative filtering task, and (2) distinguishing arguments of a verb in a sentence.

paragraphs: Feature selection often begins by treating every feature as equally likely to matter. This paper learns a more informative starting point from related prediction tasks. Its central assumption is that features have descriptive meta-features that predict their relevance, and that the tasks share a similar structure governing which features are useful.

The method models relevance as a function of these meta-features, controlled by shared hyperparameters called meta-priors. A convex optimization algorithm jointly learns the meta-priors and task feature weights. What transfers between tasks is knowledge about feature relevance, making the approach applicable even when tasks use nonoverlapping features or individual features have different relevance across tasks.

This matters because transferable knowledge need not depend on matching the same input coordinates everywhere. The paper demonstrates improved performance on two real datasets: predicting ratings in collaborative filtering and distinguishing the arguments of verbs in sentences. These applications illustrate the stated settings where sharing relevance information can help despite differences in the features used by individual tasks.
summary.tldr: Learning shared priors from feature meta-features improves prediction across related tasks, including tasks with different or nonoverlapping features.

title: Learning a meta-level prior for feature relevance from multiple related tasks

abstract: This paper focuses on a new clustering task, called self-taught clustering . Self-taught clustering is an instance of unsupervised transfer learning , which aims at clustering a small collection of target unlabeled data with the help of a large amount of auxiliary unlabeled data. The target and auxiliary data can be different in topic distribution. We show that even when the target data are not sufficient to allow effective learning of a high quality feature representation, it is possible to learn the useful features with the help of the auxiliary data on which the target data can be clustered effectively. We propose a co-clustering based self-taught clustering algorithm to tackle this problem, by clustering the target and auxiliary data simultaneously to allow the feature representation from the auxiliary data to influence the target data through a common set of features. Under the new data representation, clustering on the target data can be improved. Our experiments on image clustering show that our algorithm can greatly outperform several state-of-the-art clustering methods when utilizing irrelevant unlabeled auxiliary data.

paragraphs: The paper introduces self-taught clustering: grouping a small unlabeled target dataset with help from a much larger unlabeled auxiliary dataset. The two datasets may differ in their topic distributions. The motivation is that the target collection alone may be too small to support learning a useful feature representation.

The proposed algorithm uses co-clustering to process the target and auxiliary data simultaneously. A common set of features lets representations learned from the auxiliary collection influence the target collection. The method therefore transfers information through shared features even when the auxiliary examples do not match the target's topical distribution.

Under the resulting representation, target clustering can improve. Image-clustering experiments show that the algorithm can greatly outperform several state-of-the-art clustering methods when using irrelevant unlabeled auxiliary data. The finding supports the possibility that data need not directly match the target topic to help organize it. The reported benefit depends on learning useful shared features, and the experimental result establishes that this transfer can work in the evaluated image-clustering setting.
summary.tldr: Co-clustering transfers useful features from auxiliary unlabeled data to improve clustering of a small target collection.

title: Self-taught clustering

abstract: Identifying the most influential documents in a corpus is an important problem in many fields, from information science and historiography to text summarization and news aggregation. Unfortunately, traditional bibliometrics such as citations are often not available. We propose using changes in the thematic content of documents over time to measure the importance of individual documents within the collection. We describe a dynamic topic model for both quantifying and qualifying the impact of these documents. We validate the model by analyzing three large corpora of scientific articles. Our measurement of a document�s impact correlates significantly with its number of citations.

paragraphs: Measuring a document's influence is difficult when citation records are unavailable. This paper proposes using the language of a document collection and how its themes change over time. The central idea is to assess individual documents through their relationship to the collection's evolving thematic content, providing a way to study influence using the documents themselves.

The authors develop a dynamic topic model that both measures impact and characterizes it. These are complementary goals: estimating how influential a document appears to be and describing the thematic nature of that influence. The temporal component matters because the proposed measure depends on changes across documents over time, rather than only on their content viewed independently.

The model is validated on three large collections of scientific articles. Its impact estimates correlate significantly with citation counts, supporting a relationship between the language-based measure and an established bibliometric signal. This finding supports its usefulness as an alternative source of evidence about influence, particularly when citation information is absent; it does not establish that thematic change proves causal influence.
summary.tldr: A dynamic topic model estimates scholarly impact from thematic changes over time, producing scores significantly correlated with citation counts.

title: A Language-based Approach to Measuring Scholarly Impact

abstract: We present a simple and scalable graph clustering method called power iteration clustering (PIC). PIC finds a very low-dimensional embedding of a dataset using truncated power iteration on a normalized pair-wise similarity matrix of the data. This embedding turns out to be an effective cluster indicator, consistently outperforming widely used spectral methods such as NCut on real datasets. PIC is very fast on large datasets, running over 1,000 times faster than an NCut implementation based on the state-of-the-art IRAM eigenvector computation technique.

paragraphs: Power Iteration Clustering, or PIC, groups data by first building a very low-dimensional representation from pairwise similarities. The method applies a truncated power iteration to a normalized similarity matrix. This turns the similarity information into a compact embedding that can indicate which examples belong together.

The key finding is that this small representation works effectively as a cluster indicator. On the real datasets studied, the authors report that PIC consistently outperforms widely used spectral methods such as normalized cuts. The result supports the usefulness of the truncated computation for clustering, rather than treating it merely as an intermediate numerical calculation.

The paper also reports substantial computational savings on large datasets: PIC runs more than a thousand times faster than the compared normalized-cuts implementation using IRAM eigenvector computation. That comparison concerns the implementation and datasets reported. Together, the findings make the case that a simple, compact similarity-based embedding can offer both effective clustering and markedly lower computational cost.
summary.tldr: PIC uses truncated power iteration to produce compact cluster indicators, with strong clustering results and major speedups in the reported comparisons.

title: Power Iteration Clustering

abstract: Many clustering algorithms only find one clustering solution. However, data can often be grouped and interpreted in many different ways. This is particularly true in the high-dimensional setting where different subspaces reveal different possible groupings of the data. Instead of committing to one clustering solution, here we introduce a novel method that can provide several non-redundant clustering solutions to the user. Our approach simultaneously learns non-redundant subspaces that provide multiple views and finds a clustering solution in each view. We achieve this by augmenting a spectral clustering objective function to incorporate dimensionality reduction and multiple views and to penalize for redundancy between the views.

Instead of committing to one clustering solution, here we introduce a novel method that can provide several non-redundant clustering solutions to the user. Our approach simultaneously learns non-redundant subspaces that provide multiple views and finds a clustering solution in each view. We achieve this by augmenting a spectral clustering objective function to incorporate dimensionality reduction and multiple views and to penalize for redundancy between the views.

paragraphs: A dataset can support several meaningful ways of grouping its examples. This is especially relevant in high dimensions, where different subsets or combinations of dimensions can expose different structures. This paper develops a clustering method intended to present several distinct views of the same data to the user.

The method jointly learns subspaces and a clustering within each subspace. Its objective extends spectral clustering to include dimensionality reduction, multiple views, and a penalty for redundancy between views. The subspaces determine how the data are represented, while the clusterings describe the groupings visible within those representations.

Learning these components together makes the search for alternative views part of the clustering problem itself. The redundancy penalty encourages the views to contribute different information instead of repeatedly exposing the same grouping. The contribution is a formulation for exploring multiple interpretations of a dataset, with both the representations and their associated clusterings selected through a shared optimization objective.
summary.tldr: An extended spectral-clustering objective jointly learns multiple subspaces and clusterings while penalizing redundancy between views.

title: Multiple Non-Redundant Spectral Clustering Views

abstract: We propose a non-convex training objective for robust binary classification of data sets in which label noise is present. The design is guided by the intention of solving the resulting problem by adiabatic quantum optimization. Two choices are prompted by the engineering constraints of existing quantum hardware: training problems are formulated as quadratic unconstrained binary optimization; and model parameters are represented as binary expansions of low bit-depth. In the present work we validate this approach by using a heuristic classical solver as a stand-in for quantum hardware. Testing on several popular data sets and comparing with a number of existing convex and non-convex losses solved by convex optimization, we find substantial advantages in robustness as measured by test error under increasing label noise. Robustness is enabled by the non-convexity of our hardware-compatible loss function, which we name q -loss . We emphasize that we do not claim any theoretical superiority of q -loss over other non-convex losses. In fact if solving them to optimality was possible, they could be just as good or better, but q -loss has one important property that all others are lacking—namely that it is compatible with quantum hardware.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a binary-classification objective designed to remain robust when training labels contain errors. Its non-convex loss, called q-loss, is developed with adiabatic quantum optimization in mind. Hardware constraints shape the formulation: training becomes quadratic unconstrained binary optimization, and model parameters use low-bit-depth binary representations.

The experiments use a heuristic classical solver as a stand-in for quantum hardware. Across several popular datasets, the authors compare test error as label noise increases against existing convex and non-convex loss approaches. They report substantial robustness advantages and attribute that robustness to the non-convexity of the hardware-compatible objective.

The claimed advantage is carefully qualified. The authors do not establish theoretical superiority over other non-convex losses; those losses could perform equally well or better if solved optimally. The distinctive contribution is an objective that combines observed robustness with compatibility with the targeted quantum hardware. The experiments validate the approach through classical optimization, so they do not constitute a demonstration of quantum-computing performance.
summary.tldr: Quantum-hardware-compatible q-loss improves robustness to label noise in classical-solver experiments without claiming theoretical superiority over other non-convex losses.

title: Robust Classification with Adiabatic Quantum Optimization

abstract: We propose a new, nonparametric approach to learning and representing transition dynamics in Markov decision processes (MDPs), which can be combined easily with dynamic programming methods for policy optimisation and value estimation. This approach makes use of a recently developed representation of conditional distributions as embeddings in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). Such representations bypass the need for estimating transition probabilities or densities, and apply to any domain on which kernels can be defined. This avoids the need to calculate intractable integrals, since expectations are represented as RKHS inner products whose computation has linear complexity in the number of points used to represent the embedding. We are able to provide guarantees for the proposed applications in MDPs: in the context of a value iteration algorithm, we prove convergence to either the optimal policy, or to the closest projection of the optimal policy in our model class (an RKHS), under reasonable assumptions. In experiments, we investigate a learning task in a typical classical control setting (the under-actuated pendulum), and on a navigation problem where only images from a sensor are observed. For policy optimisation we compare with least-squares policy iteration where a Gaussian process is used for value function estimation. For value estimation we also compare to the recent NPDP method. Our approach achieves better performance in all experiments.

paragraphs: Planning in a Markov decision process requires reasoning about what may happen after an action. This paper represents those transition dynamics through embeddings of conditional distributions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. The nonparametric representation can be combined with dynamic programming for policy optimization and value estimation, without explicitly estimating transition probabilities or densities.

The computational benefit comes from expressing expectations as inner products in the kernel space. This bypasses potentially intractable integrals, with computation linear in the number of points representing an embedding. The approach applies wherever suitable kernels can be defined. Under stated reasonable assumptions, the authors prove convergence in value iteration to the optimal policy or its closest projection within their model class.

Experiments cover control of an under-actuated pendulum and navigation using only sensor images. Policy optimization is compared with least-squares policy iteration using Gaussian-process value estimation, and value estimation is also compared with NPDP. The proposed method performs better in all reported experiments, providing empirical support alongside its conditional convergence guarantee.
summary.tldr: Kernel embeddings represent MDP transitions without explicit density estimation and support efficient planning with conditional convergence guarantees.

title: Modelling transition dynamics in MDPs with RKHS embeddings

abstract: Context-Dependent Deep-Neural-Network HMMs, or CD-DNN-HMMs, combine the classic artificial-neural-network HMMs with traditional context-dependent acoustic modeling and deep-belief-network pre-training. CD-DNN-HMMs greatly outperform conventional CD-GMM (Gaussian mixture model) HMMs: The word error rate is reduced by up to one third on the difficult benchmarking task of speaker-independent single-pass transcription of telephone conversations.
originalAbstract: Context-Dependent Deep-Neural-Network HMMs, or CD-DNN-HMMs, combine the classic artificial-neural-network HMMs with traditional context-dependent acoustic modeling and deep-belief-network pre-training. CD-DNN-HMMs greatly outperform conventional CD-GMM (Gaussian mixture model) HMMs: The word error rate is reduced by up to one third on the difficult benchmarking task of speaker-independent single-pass transcription of telephone conversations.

paragraphs: This paper studies transcription of telephone conversations using context-dependent deep neural network hidden Markov models, abbreviated CD-DNN-HMMs. The proposed system combines three ingredients: neural-network HMMs, context-dependent acoustic modeling, and deep-belief-network pre-training. The contribution lies in bringing these components together within a speech-recognition model evaluated on conversational audio.

The comparison is with conventional context-dependent HMM systems that use Gaussian mixture models. Both approaches retain context-dependent acoustic modeling and the HMM framework, while the proposed combination incorporates deep neural networks and their pre-training. This makes the reported result evidence for the combined modeling approach; the abstract does not separately attribute the improvement to each component.

On the demanding benchmark of speaker-independent, single-pass telephone-conversation transcription, the authors report word error rate reductions of up to one third. That is a relative reduction in the stated error measure, with one third describing the upper end of the reported improvement. The finding demonstrates a substantial advantage over the conventional comparison system on this particular transcription task.
summary.tldr: Context-dependent deep neural network HMMs reduce word error rate by up to one third on a telephone-conversation transcription benchmark.

title: Conversational Speech Transcription Using Context-Dependent Deep Neural Networks
